entries.title: Ecclesiastes Introduction
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
INTRODUCTION TO ECCLESIASTES

  1. THE NAME OF THE BOOK

    1. The Hebrew name for the book is the phrase from Eccl. 1:1, "the Words of Qoheleth, the son of David, king in Jerusalem." Its short designation was "Qoheleth" (BDB 875, KB 1080).
      1. The VERB (i.e., "assembled") was used of Solomon in 1 Kgs. 8:1.
      2. It is a FEMININE PARTICIPLE from the Hebrew word Qahal, "congregation" or "assembly" (see Introduction IV. F.).
      3. It seems to designate an office, however, it is used with the ARTICLE in Eccl. 12:8.

    2. The book is known as "Ecclesiastes," which is a Latinized form from the Septuagint (Koine Greek translation done in the B.C. period). This is the Greek term for "one who assembles," from the root "to call out" and the PREPOSITION ek, "out"
      SPECIAL TOPIC: SEPTUAGINT

    3. The term Qoheleth
      1. can mean one who assembles an audience, therefore, a teacher, preacher, debater (cf. Eccl. 12:9, Eccl. Rab.)
      2. can be used as imagery for one who gathers truth, a philosopher or sage (i.e., Rashi)
      3. can mean one who gathers different opinions and decides which is more accurate, a researcher (Metzudat Zion)
      4. in the LXX, it means "a member of an Assembly"

  2. CANONIZATION

    1. Ecclesiastes is an example of a type of ANE wisdom literature. It is an extended treatment of a subject and, like Job, which often challenges traditional wisdom teachings.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: WISDOM LITERATURE, I. B. #1. b.

    2. It is part of the third and last division of the Hebrew canon called "the Writings."

    3. It is also part of a special grouping of five small books called the Megilloth or "five scrolls." Each of these was read at an annual feast day. Ecclesiastes was read at the feast of Booths or Tabernacles.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW CANON, #3. c.

    4. Because of the skeptical, negative nature of this book, it was rejected by the conservative rabbinical school of Shammai, but advocated by the liberal rabbinical school of Hillel. This discussion continued even until the time of the Pharisaic revival at Jamnia after the fall of Jerusalem (A.D. 70-90).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: PHARISEES

    5. Several of the canonical books of the OT had difficulty being accepted by later rabbis
      1. Ecclesiastes ‒ bitter, negative, non-traditional spirit
      2. Song of Songs ‒ affirmation of physical love
      3. Esther ‒ no mention of
        1. God
        2. the Jewish temple and its rites
        3. teaching from the Torah
      4. Ezekiel ‒ his temple (chapters 40-48) different from Moses' tabernacle and Solomon's temple
      5. and to some extent, Daniel ‒ apocalyptic prophecies of Daniel 7-12

    6. Ecclesiastes was finally accepted because
      1. it was attributed to Solomon (see Authorship, IV)
      2. it has a traditional conclusion (i.e., Eccl. 12:13-14)
      3. it rings true to human experience and reveals the confusion of the Jewish faith community. As an aside, its scepticism truly addresses the age of post-modernity

  3. GENRE

    1. Ecclesiastes, like Job, must be interpreted as a whole (beware of proof-texting). It is a sustained focus on the tensions of human existence.

    2. It is a tongue-in-cheek sarcastic look at life without God. The two key theological phrases are
      1. "under the sun," Eccl. 1:3, 9, 14; 2:11, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22; 3:16; 4:1, 3, 7, 15; 5:13, 18; 6:1, 5, 12; 7:11; 8:9, 15, 17; 9:3, 6, 9, 11, 13; 10:5; 11:7; 12:2 (31 times; see note at 1:14)
      2. vanity of vanities, all is vanity" repeated often (first in 1:2 and last in 12:8; see note at 1:14)

    3. The book is characterized by opposites (antithetical parallelism). Notice:
      1. wisdom vs. folly
      2.  good vs. evil
      3. light vs. dark
      4. love vs. hate
      5. life vs. death
      6.  this world vs. afterlife

        The mysteries of fallen human existence are admitted and documented, but there is more! There is God; there will be justice one day. Because humans do not know the answers does not mean there are no answers! This book is written in the style of OT Wisdom Literature (monotheistic, judgment day, future hope, goodness and fairness of God, revelation (Scripture).

          SPECIAL TOPIC: EASTERN LITERATURE (biblical paradoxes)
          SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

    4. A very helpful book on hermeneutics, Cracking Old Testament Codes, by D. Brent Sandy and Ronald Giese, calls Ecclesiastes "counter-wisdom or anti-widsom." It also states, "It forces the reader (or listener) to be brutally honest with both self and God," pp. 270-271.

  4. AUTHORSHIP

    1. The book is anonymous, like most OT books, although "Qoheleth" (see F. below) is mentioned often.

    2. Jewish tradition said it was one of three books written by Solomon (Midrash Shir hasherem Rabbah I, 1, sect. 10)
      1. Song of Songs when he was young
      2. Proverbs when he was middle aged
      3. Ecclesiastes when he was old and bitter (Rashi)

    3. Solomon is surely the literary foil of Ecclesiastes 1-2 because of his wisdom, wealth and position. But there are hints that he is not the true author:
      1. in Eccl. 1:12, "I was king over Israel in Jerusalem" (NIV) ‒ PAST TENSE
      2. in Eccl. 1:16, ". . . more than all who were over Jerusalem before me" (NASB) ‒ only David was king in Jerusalem before Solomon
      3. in Eccl. 4:1-3, 5:8 and 8:9 governmental abuse is discussed but its correction is hopeless
      4. obviously the author is not King Solomon in Eccl. 8:2-4, where advice on how to act in the King's presence is given
      5. the name, Solomon, does not occur in the book

    4. For a scholarly argument for Solomon's authorship see Introduction to the OT, by C. F. Keil, vol. 1, pp. 516-529.

    5. Baba Bathra 15a (a book of the Talmud) said the men of Hezekiah wrote Proverbs (cf. Prov. 25:1), Ecclesiastes, and Song of Songs, but this obviously meant they edited or compiled these wisdom books.

    6. The term Qoheleth (BDB 875, KB 1080) can be a proper name or a title. It looks like a title because
      1. it has the DEFINITE ARTICLE in Eccl. 7:27 and 12:8
      2. it is a FEMININE form which implies an office, but uses MASCULINE VERBS
      3. it is a rare term found seven times, only in this book

    7. The only section of the book that reveals a later editor(s) is Eccl. 12:9-10,11-12,13-14. They were obviously added by someone familiar with Genesis, Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Proverbs. They express traditional Mosaic theology. They were added to make the book more acceptable to the rabbis.

    8. The apparent paradoxes or contradictions have been explained as
      1. sarcasm, life without God ("under the sun")
      2. traditional Jewish wisdom and challenges to it (quoted to be refuted)
      3. a wisdom teacher and his enthusiastic young student and a narrator (dialogue)
      4. the conflict within fallen mankind (a life's journal)
      5. later editors, example, Eccl. 12:9-12 (positive toward Qoheleth) and Eccl. 12:13-14 (negative toward Qoheleth)
      6. I think #1 is best (cf. Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, p. 228)

  5. DATE

    1. There are two issues related to the date of Ecclesiastes:
      1. when the book was composed
      2. when it was put in its final canonical form

    2. The historical setting must be after Solomon's day. He is used as a literary foil in Ecclesiastes 1-2.

    3. The final form of the book points to a later date:
      1. stylistic form of the Hebrew is post-exilic but before 400-300 B.C.
        1. Aramaic words and expressions (i.e., "parks," Eccl. 2:5; "sentence," Eccl. 8:11)
        2. the form of the Hebrew
      2. there are literary parallels in Phoenician wisdom literature of about 600-400 B.C.
      3. allusions to Ecclesiastes appear in the writing of Ben Sirach, Ecclesiasticus, which was written about 180 B.C.
      4. there have been several small parts of Ecclesiastes found in the Dead Sea Scrolls (4Q). These have been dated as late as the second century B.C.

  6. LITERARY UNITS

    1. This book is difficult to outline. It is more like a life's journal than a structured literary work. It is similar to rabbinical teaching called "pearls on a string." However, there are:
      1. unifying words (i.e., "vanity," but also "good")
      2. unifying phrases (i.e., "under the sun")
      3. unifying motifs (i.e., happenings)
      4. and a unifying theme (Eccl. 1:2 and 12:8)

    2. It is possible that there have been editorial additions:
      1. the opening, Eccl. 1:1
      2. inclusive literary form, Eccl. 1:2 and 12:8 imply that Eccl. 1:1 and 12:9-14 are additions
      3. two added epilogues:
        1. Eccl. 12:9-12 (in the third person)
        2. Eccl. 12:13-14 (traditional Mosaic theology)

    3. It is obvious that Ecclesiastes 1-2 uses Solomon as a literary foil.

    4. Chapter 3 is a wonderful poem about the common experiences of human life.

    5. Chapter 12:9-14 is a double epilogue.

    6. The remainder does not outline easily!

  7. THEOLOGICAL ISSUES

    1. The very fact of this book's presence in the Canon seems to imply that God does not reject the sincere, doubtful seeker.

    2. The asking of ultimate questions is not discouraged.

    3. Ecclesiastes assumes the existence of Israel's God and is written within the stream of the OT faith.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: MONOTHEISM

    4. Evil is a result of mankind's fall, not God (cf. Eccl. 7:29; 9:3). This is not the world God intended it to be!
      SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

    5. God's ways cannot be known. Mankind can struggle for meaning in life, but it cannot be found without God, and even then, many subjects are veiled.

    6. It doubts the easy orthodox views on the afterlife and doubts mankind's ability to know God, but still God is gracious and present.
      SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

    7. The world, as it is, is unfair and cruel; there must be something more, if God's promises are true!

    8. Be content with the simple pleasures of life—they are from God. Enjoy them when and where you can (Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12, 13, 22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).

    9. Simplistic answers that do not fit life experiences are "no" answers. We must face the reality of the meaninglessness of life if there is no God (i.e., naturalism).

  8. MAIN TRUTHS

    1. Its main purpose was to show the futility of human existence apart from God. It is a tract to convert self-sufficient materialists or intellectuals. B. H. Carroll said that in the days of his infidelity, Ecclesiastes and Job exercised an unearthly power on him, expressing the emptiness of life and pointing him toward God.
       The dictionary section of NIDOTTE, vol. 4, pp. 552-554, lists a similar option as one of several: "if the vanity of all reality is truly Qoheleth's own conclusion, it is only because he limits his observations initially to a reality without the God of the OT; then when he does introduce God, this pessimistic view of life dissipates and is supplanted by a more orthodox attitude expressed in the epilogue (Eccl. 12:13-14)."

    2. Happiness and contentment are found in the simple daily pleasures of life, cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:12-13,22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-9; 12:13-14
      1. faith and obedience toward God
      2. pleasures of home and family
      3. one's work, vocation

    3. This book is agnostic about God and the afterlife. It does not answer the questions of ultimate reality, but it does ask the questions of current reality:
      1. For Jews, it showed the error of simplistic overstatements made by traditional theologians ("the two ways"), cf. Deut. 30:1,15,19; Ps. 1:1.
      2. For pagans, it shows the bankruptcy of earthly life without God.
      3. Easy answers to life's questions are usually wrong. There is mystery even for faith! Revelation does not reveal all!

    4. This author is using natural revelation, not special revelation (although he is familiar with Genesis, Deuteronomy, Psalms, and Proverbs), to examine life. The covenant name for God, YHWH, does not appear in the book. As in all wisdom literature, the general name for God, Elohim, is used.

      SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

    5. This book forms a balance to the neat maxims of Proverbs that offer success in life ("the two ways," e.g., Psalm 1). There is mystery in life, in nature, in humanity, and in God. The key is found
      1. in faith, not knowledge
      2. in family, not possessions
      3. in God, not human wisdom, faith, or actions

        The simple pleasures of life: family, work, friends, and food provide happiness in this life. The next life is veiled, but God is there!

 * Although they are not inspired, paragraph divisions are the key to understanding and following the original author's intent. Each modern translation has divided and summarized the paragraphs. Every paragraph has one central topic, truth, or thought. Each version encapsulates that topic in its own distinct way. As you read the text, ask yourself which translation fits your understanding of the subject and verse divisions.
 In every chapter we must read the Bible first and try to identify its subjects (paragraphs), then compare our understanding with the modern versions. Only when we understand the original author's intent by following his logic and presentation can we truly understand the Bible. Only the original author is inspired—readers have no right to change or modify the message. Bible readers do have the responsibility of applying the inspired truth to their day and their lives.
 Note that all technical terms and abbreviations are explained fully in the following SPECIAL TOPICS: Hebrew Grammatical Terms and Glossary.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

GENERAL BACKGROUND TO THE BOOK

  1. Ecclesiastes is a part of the literary genre known as "Wisdom Literature."
    SPECIAL TOPIC: WISDOM LITERATURE

  2. It is characterized by a practical orientation to daily life without reference to the historical acts of God or the cultus of Israel. The book focuses on practical advice for individuals not the nation.

  3. I personally do not believe Solomon is the author (see Introduction, Authorship), although I think he is used in Chapter 1 and 2 as a literary foil (cf. H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Ecclesiastes, pp. 8-17), someone who had it all but was not happy!

  4. This is one book that must be taken as a whole. It is a sustained argument through chapter 12. It must not be prooftexted or great theological contradictions occur. See Fee and Stuart, How To Read the Bible for All Its Worth, pp. 225-248.

  5. In my opinion the key to interpreting the book is the phrase "under the sun." The author is going to analyze life with and without God. He is challenging traditional religious philosophy (i.e., the two ways, blessing and cursing of the Mosaic covenant, cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28-30).

  6. The author uses natural revelation (i.e., Ps. 19:1-6), not special revelation (i.e., Ps. 19:7-10; 119), to examine life. The name YHWH does not appear at all in this book, but the general name for God, Elohim.
    SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C., D.

  7. This teacher does not provide answers so much as he asks the right questions, the tough questions about mankind's existence. He is not afraid to challenge traditional thought and traditions.

  8. Ecclesiastes 1-2 can be seen as a list of things that humans seek which they think will give them joy and contentment, but without God life cannot be full!
    1. wisdom, Eccl. 1:13-18
    2. pleasure, Eccl. 2:1-3
    3. possessions or wealth, Eccl. 2:4-8a
    4. sex, Eccl. 2:8b
    5. fame and popularity, Eccl. 2:9-11

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

1:1
NASB, NKJV, LXX  "The Preacher"
NRSV, NET  "the Teacher"
TEV  "the Philosopher"
NJB  "Qoheleth"
REB  "the Speaker"
JPSOSA (footnote)  "the Assembler"
Peshitta  "Kohlat" ("Preacher" in Lamsa's footnote)

There is no DEFINITE ARTICLE here, although it does appear in Eccl. 7:27; 12:8. This is a function more than a title. The best translation would be "professor" or "teacher" (BDB 875, KB 1080). See Introduction, Name of the Book, C. and Authorship, F.

▣ "the son of David" This verse and verse 12 imply that this is speaking of Solomon, but other references throughout the book do not fit Solomon. I believe that an unknown wisdom teacher(s) used Solomon's wisdom, wealth, power, and position as a literary foil to critique life. See Introduction, Authorship, C.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:2 "vanity of vanities"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:2 "vanity of vanities" This is a Hebrew superlative (cf. Eccl. 1:2 and 12:8). The word means "vapor," "breath" (i.e., name of Adam and Eve's second child), or "mist" (BDB 210 I, KB 236 I, cf. James 4:14). Its emphasis is either

  1. nothingness of human aspirations (cf. Eccl. 2:11,15; as well as the reality of idols)
  2. in Arabic, the root means "foul"
  3. the transitoriness of human life (cf. Ps. 39:5,11; 144:4)
  4. NIDOTTE, vol. 4. p. 553, says it means "temporary"
  5. the context supports #3 (cf. H. C. Leupold, Exposition of Ecclesiastes, p. 41)

This is a key term and recurrent phrase in this book (i.e., used 38 times, cf. Eccl. 1:2,14; 2:1,11,15,17, 19,21,23,26; 3:19; 4:4,7,8,16; 5:7,10; 6:2,4,9,11,12; 7:6,15; 8:10,14; 9:9; 11:8,10; 12:8). Notice how it begins and ends the book! The term is used sparingly in other wisdom books; Job, 5 times; Psalms, 9 times; and Proverbs, 3 times.

For different theories about how it affects the strong statements in this book, see Introduction, Authorship, H. I prefer option #1.

This theological presupposition will be the lexical grid through which I interpret the book (i.e., this is what life without God would be like).

▣ "all is vanity" Notice the root, "vanity" (BDB 210 I, KB 236 I), is used five times in this one verse! The Handbook on Ecclesiastes by UBS, says the term should be understood as

  1. incomprehensible
  2. enigmatic
  3. mysterious
  4. impossible to understand

Therefore, it communicates the reality that life is full of unanswerable questions (p. 4). The person knowledgeable in wisdom will know this, but will continue to trust God and keep His commandments (i.e., traditional conclusion of the book, chapter 12).

This refers to the uncertain and unpredictable activities of life. These are a result of fallen humanity trying to live life in his own strength, independent from God. This is the condition left by the Fall!  See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

The Hebrew term "all" (BDB 481, KB 474), often translated "everything," is a common word, but is used unusually often in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 9 times in chapter 1; 17 times in chapter 2; 13 times in chapter 3, etc.). Qoheleth uses this inclusive language to express his theological emphasis on

  1. God's control and sovereignty
  2. human ineffectiveness and transitoriness

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:3 "what advantage does man have in all his works"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3 "what advantage does man have in all his works" All human efforts, as well as all other human activities, are meaningless if there is no God (atheistic humanism, naturalism).

  1. If these worlviews are true, then humans are the chance result of physical forces.
  2. There is no purpose, no meaning, no afterlife, no god, just the physical universe (naturalism)!

Oh my, what a terrible worldview!

NASB, LXX  "advantage"
NKJV, NJB, REB, Peshitta  "profit"
NRSV  "gain"
TEV  "what do you have to show for it"
JPSOA  "real value"

This Hebrew root (BDB 452, KB 404) has several meanings:

  1. I ‒ reminder, excess, pre-eminence
  2. II ‒ cord, rope, bowstring
  3. III ‒ abundance
  4. A Translator's Handbook on Ecclesiastes, by UBS, suggests it refers to eternity or the afterlife, possibly "a lasting benefit" (pp. 5-6).

The form here is found only in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:11,13 [twice]; 3:9; 5:8,15; 7:12; 10:11; another form of the term is a substantive from the Qal PARTICIPLE, cf. Eccl. 6:11; 7:11,16; 12:9,12). It is obviously a key term because it describes the goal of mankind's search for meaning, purpose, and contentment!

NASB  "work"
NKJV, REB, LXX, Peshitta  "labor"
NRSV, NJB  "toil"
JPSOA  "gains"
NET  "effort"

The VERB "work" (BDB 765, KB 845, Qal IMPERFECT), used twice, has several connotations. The root can mean

  1. trouble, sorrow
  2. trouble, mischief
  3. toil, labor
  4. JPSOA footnote, "'amal usually means 'gain' in Eccl., cf. Ps. 105:44:

In this context #3 fits best, but one feels the presence of the other connotations in the root (there are several verses where the root is used twice, cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:10,11,18,19, 20,21,22; 4:8; 5:18; 9:9).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:3, 9, 13, 14 "under the sun"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:3, 9, 13, 14 "under the sun" In my opinion this is a second key phrase (PREPOSITION, BDB 1065; DEFINITE ARTICLE and NOUN, BDB 1039) in interpreting the entire book. It is used twenty-five times and only in Ecclesiastes. It reflects mankind's futile efforts without God (i.e., "under the sun"; the parallel phrase, "under the heavens," is also used several times.).

Qoheleth examines physical life (by observation, i.e., natural revelation) and comes to the conclusion that it is vanity (cf. Dictionary of Biblical Imagery, p. 228).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:4ff
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:4ff This begins a poetic stanza:

  1. NASB ‒ vv. 3-11
  2. NKJV ‒ vv. 3-11
  3. NRSV ‒ vv.1-11
  4. TEV ‒ prose
  5. NJB ‒ prose
  6. JPSOA ‒ vv. 2-9
  7. NIV ‒ vv. 3-11
  8. REB ‒ prose

It is obvious that the genre and structure are not easy to identify and outline in this book.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:4 The phrase "remains forever" is used in a relative sense (cf. Exod. 21:6).

This verse is expressing the fleetingness of conscious life (cf. Job 14:2; Ps. 90:5-6; 103:15-16; Isa. 40:6-7) versus the stability of the spiritual creation (as an aspect of YHWH's permanence, cf. Ps. 104:5; 119:90).

The Hebrew 'olam must be interpreted in light of a given literary context. It has a wide semantical field.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:5 Psalm 19:4-6 presents this same truth in great poetic majesty, but here the sun's daily task is seen as a vain, meaningless, wearisome repetition (i.e., the natural order and stability of physical creation of Gen. 8:22).

▣ "hastening" This term can mean "panting" (BDB 983 I, KB 1375, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE), as in weariness or desire (i.e., Ps. 119:131). The sun grows weary hurrying every day to finish its course (cf. Ps. 19:4-6). This is the first in a series of eleven Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLES reflecting nature (cf. Eccl. 1:5-7). The wind, like the sun, hurries to finish its repetitive course.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:6 The Septuagint and Vulgate relate the first part of this verse to the sun, but in context it refers to the wind (a word play with "vanity") as another meaningless activity (as is the flowing of rivers to the sea, v. 7).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 1:7 The Aramaic Targums and Rashi speculate the water returned through underground tunnels.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:8 "All things are wearisome"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:8 "All things are wearisome" Physical creation is in a repetitive, mysterious routine (i.e., Eccl. 1:9):

  1. human life, Eccl. 1:4
  2. heavenly bodies, Eccl. 1:5
  3. wind, Eccl. 1:6
  4. rivers, Eccl. 1:7

This premise is the author's first and primary presupposition about earthly existence (i.e., "there is nothing new or significant in an endless cycle of physical creation"). The principle is begun in Eccl. 1:8a and followed by three explanatory phrases:

  1. man cannot tell it
  2. eye is not satisfied in seeing it
  3. ear is not filled with hearing it

These describe the generations that come and go (cf. Eccl. 1:4a). They all experience

  1. the cycles in nature
  2. frustrations at the mysteries of fallen existence
  3. seeking answers but not finding them (another cycle)
NASB  "man is not able to tell it"
NKJV  "man cannot express it"
NRSV  "more than one can express"
TEV  "a weariness too great for words"
REB  "no one can describe them all"
LXX  "a man will not be able to speak of them"
Peshitta  "a man is not satisfied with utterance"
JPSOA  "no man can ever state them"

The author's list of meaningless repetition in nature could be multiplied endlessly. The implication is not only fallen human's inability to state clearly the meaninglessness and hopelessness brought about by the cycles of nature, but also the sense of purposelessness it brings to human existence!

Humans cannot tell because they do not know (i.e., apart from divine revelation). Human searching for answers is hopeless without divine revelation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:9 "That which has been is that which will be"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:9 "That which has been is that which will be" This refers to meaningless repetition with no apparent purpose or attainable goal (this is sarcasm of human activity without God. Compare Isa. 55:6-13!). This describes humanistic atheism and, for that matter, eastern religious philosophy (i.e., wheel of karma).

▣ "there is nothing new under the sun" This repeated theme is one of two keys to interpreting the book. The author is showing the meaninglessness and hopelessness of life without God; without purpose; without eternity! The readers are forced to contemplate human existence, earthly life, if there is no God!

This is where the modern issue over origins takes on its sharpest focus.

  1. Is the universe, in all its size, power, and violence all there was, all there is, and all there will be? (Carl Sagan)
  2. Is human life an accident, a passing purposeless evolution of constant change?
  3. Is change the only absolute?

These are the ultimate questions of human worth, dignity. Are we really made in the divine image (cf. Gen. 1:26-27) for fellowship with our Creator (cf. Gen. 3:8)?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:10 "See this, it is new"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:10 "See this, it is new" "See" (BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE) is from a supposed objector (i.e., diatribe). He is answered by his faulty remembrance of history (cf. Eccl. 1:10- 11). The only constant is the empty repetition (both physical and existential).

1:11
NASB  "earlier things"
NKJV  "former things"
NRSV  "people of long ago"
TEV  "what happened in the past"
NJB  "of the past"
JPSOA  "the earlier ones"
REB  "those who lived in the past"
LXX  "the first things"
Peshitta  "former generations"

This MASCULINE PLURAL ADJECTIVE (BDB 911, KB 1168) refers to people, Lev. 26:45; Deut. 19; Ps. 79:8, while the FEMININE PLURAL refers to events, Isa. 41:22; 42:9; 43:9; 46:9; 48:3; and possibly Isa. 61:4. Therefore, the NRSV has the better translation.

This verse is characterized well by Robert Gordis, Koheleth, the Man and His World, a Study of Ecclesiastes, p. 208, as "This verse gives the reason for Eccl. 1:10. Things appear new only because the past is forgotten (Levy)—an additional element in the vanity of human existence; not only can nothing be accomplished, but the memory of the effort is wiped out (Hertz)."

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:12 "the preacher"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:12 "the preacher" See note at Eccl. 1:1.

▣ "have been king" This is the first of several reasons why Solomon was not the author, but a literary foil (see Introduction, IV. Authorship, C).

The VERB "was" (BDB 224, KB 243, Qal PERFECT) is used often in the previous paragraph (Eccl. 1:9 [twice], Eccl. 1:10 [six times]). Time implications in Hebrew verbs must be determined from the context. The perfect tense implies a past condition, not a current one. Was there ever a time when Solomon was not king after once becoming king? The rabbis felt this problem and surmised that Solomon experienced a judgment similar to Nebuchadnezzar (cf. Daniel 4) and was removed from active leadership over Israel for a period of time (Targum on Eccl. 1:12; J. Sanhedrin 20c). This is just supposition and imagination trying to explain away the grammatical features of this text.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW GRAMMAR

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:13 "mind"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:13 "mind" This is literally "heart," which is Hebrew imagery for the entire person.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART

▣ "seek" This word means "seek with application" (BDB 205, KB 233, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, cf. Ps. 111:2; 119:45).

▣ "explore" This word means "to investigate" or "to go to the root of a matter" (BDB 1064, KB 1707, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, cf. Eccl. 7:25). It was used often of exploring the land of Canaan in Numbers 13, but here it refers to a search for truth (cf. Prov. 2:4).

▣ "wisdom" There are two words used in Wisdom Literature that related to knowing. A good example is Prov. 1:7:

  1. knowledge (BDB 395, KB 228)
  2. wisdom (BDB 315, KB 313)

They form a complementary pair. One focuses on practical living and the other on academic knowledge. They are both needed to live life well. They should not be contrasted, but both be sought after (cf. Job 28:28; Ps. 111:10; Prov. 9:10; 15:33).

▣ "concerning all that has been done under heaven" See note at Eccl. 1:3. This is a key concept, crucial for a proper interpretation of the book. It is parallel to the phrase "under the sun."

▣ "God" This is the Hebrew name Elohim. It is used for God as Creator, Provider, and Sustainer of all life on this planet. This is the only name used for Deity in the book.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

NASB  "a grievous task"
NKJV  "this grievous task"
NRSV, JPSOA  "an unhappy business"
TEV  "a miserable fate"
NJB  "what a wearisome task"
LXX  "a worthless task"
Peshitta  "a difficult task"
NET  "a burdensome task"

The word "task" (BDB 775, KB 857) is used several times in the book (cf. Eccl. 2:26; 3:10; 4:8; 5:13; 8:16). God has given humans, made in His image (i.e., Gen. 1:26-27), a desire to know and understand their place and purpose in creation, but sin has destroyed our ability to find the answer.

The ADJECTIVE (BDB 948, KB 1250-1256) basically means "evil" or "bad." It is used several times in the book (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 2:17; 4:3,8; 5:1,14; 6:2; 8:3,5,9,11,12; 9:2,3 [twice],12; 10:13; 12:14) to describe life!

God has given humans who are made in His image an insatiable desire to know, to understand, but it cannot be satisfied in this fallen world. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was a disaster, not a blessing! We know evil and ignorance, but not God or ultimate questions. Life is a mystery!

Notice the definition from NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 452.

"Qohelet's evaluation of human concerns or tasks is negative; they are an evil or misfortune (rā; Eccl. 1:13) perpetrated against the human race, causing frustration and pain (2:23) and of no advantage whatever (2:11). This state of affairs exists not because of human moral failure or want of skillful exercise of human industry, but because the Creator has irrevocably determined and arranged it so (1:13; 3:10-11; cf. 1:15). Qohelet's theology of creation is in striking contrast and tension with the profoundly affirmative theology of creation reflected in the Pentateuchal creation accounts of the creation hymns in the Psalms (→ br' I, create, separate, # 1343). Qoheleth's theology of creation is also in tension with the early Christian theology of the apostle Paul, who situates the creation-human order within the soteriological framework of primordial human sin and subsequent curse/futility destined for eschatological reversal (Rom. 8:20-21). Qohelet, in contrast to Israel's traditional wisdom assumptions, postulates an enigmatic, frustrating created order. For him, the latter reflects the character of a labyrinthine deity, inimical to the triumphalist human quest for a secure and meaningful mastery of existence. On the problem of correlating this aspect of Qohelet's thought with the positive affirmations present in the final form of the book, see M. Fox. Qohelet and His Contradictions, 1990 (→ Ecclesiastes: Theology)."

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:14 "under the sun"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:14 "under the sun" See note at Eccl. 1:3. Notice the number of times this phrase or a parallel phrase is used (cf. Eccl. 1:3,9,13,14; 2:11,17,18,19,20,22; 3:16; 4:1,3,7,15; 5:13,18; 6:1,5,12; 7:11; 8:15 [twice],17; 9:3,9 [twice],11,13; 10:5). This is one of two key theological phrases to understanding the book (see Introduction III. B.)!

▣ "all is vanity and striving after wind" This is another repeated phrase (and parallel) which characterizes this book (cf. Eccl. 1:2,14; 2:1,11,15,17,19,21,23,26; 3:19; 4:4,6,8,16; 5:7,16; 6:2,4,9,11; 7:6,15; 8:10,14[twice]; 9:9; 11:8,10; 12:8). See word study at Eccl. 1:17. It characterizes human's search for meaning, happiness, and purpose without God.

  1. Life without God in a fallen world is frustrating and empty!
  2. Life with God in a fallen world is mysterious and unexplainable!
  3. Our hope is in the unseen God of revelation (Scripture). He has revealed Himself, but we still live in a fallen world and reap its chaos and evil!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:15 "crooked. . .straightened"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:15 "crooked. . .straightened" The words "crooked" (BDB 736, KB 804) and "straight" (BDB 1075, KB 1784, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) are often used in moral senses. This phrase is found only in Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 1:15; 7:13; 12:9). They form the basis for the Hebrew concepts of righteousness and sin (see Special Topic below). This may have been an oft quoted proverb (i.e., NIV, cf. Eccl. 7:13)..

Not only can fallen mankind (even covenant humanity) not "know" or "find," but they cannot "fix." Life is a mystery and it cannot be understood or changed by those walking through it. In historical context, this may be a slap at divination or simply a realistic statement of mankind's inability to correct the human condition (but God can, cf. Eccl. 7:13; Job 12:14; Isa. 14:27). Wisdom knows that some things cannot be changed and goes on with life, but it also knows some things can be changed by godly living and godly choices. The problem is knowing which is which!

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: DIVINATION

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:16 "I said to myself"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:16 "I said to myself" This statement reflects the ego problem in the human search for wisdom and happiness. The essence of the Fall (i.e., Genesis 3) was "self-centered independence from God." This characterizes our fallen world. A life turned inward toward "me," "mine" can never find God's wisdom and God's peace (even a Davidic king)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

▣ "I have magnified and increased wisdom" This is a claim to be wiser than all the Jewish leaders in Jerusalem before him (cf. 1 Kgs. 3:12; 4:29-34).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:16; 2:7,12 "more than all who were over Jerusalem"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:16; 2:7,12 "more than all who were over Jerusalem" This is another example of how Solomon will not historically fit as author. Only David preceded him. See Introduction, Authorship, C.

NASB, NRSV, REB  "I applied my mind"
NKJV  "I set my heart"
TEV  "I was determined"
NJB  "I have applied myself"
JPSOA  "I set my mind"
LXX, Peshitta  "I perceived"

This theme of sincere, dedicated, aggressive human effort (cf. Eccl. 1:13,17; 8:9,16) is not enough to find wisdom or purpose in an ever-changing, yet always the same, physical creation.

▣ "to know" This VERB (BDB 393, KB 390) is used three times in this context (two are Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS and one is a Qal PERFECT VERB).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW (using mostly Deuteronomy as a paradigm)

▣ "wisdom. . .madness and folly" These contrasting pairs:

  1. wisdom ‒ BDB 315
  2. madness ‒ BDB 239 (cf. Eccl. 9:3)
  3. folly ‒ BDB 698

show the futility of mankind's search for ultimate answers about the mysteries of human existence (cf. Eccl. 2:12). Biblical faith is not a human search, but a divine revelation. God wants His special creatures to know Him, but without faith and revelation, it is impossible (i.e., "striving after the wind")!

NASB  "striving after the wind"
NKJV  "grasping for the wind"
NRSV, NJB  "chasing after wind"
TEV, REB  "chasing the wind"
LXX  "waywardness of spirit"
Peshitta  "vexation of spirit"

This CONSTRUCT (BDB 946 [KB 1265 II] and 924) can mean:

  1. search for pleasure
  2. pasturing (i.e., controlling, cf. UBS' A Handbook on Ecclesiastes, p. 4), which is an impossible task

From Eccl. 1:14 it is obvious that "vanity" (BDB 210 I) and "wind" (BDB 924) are in a synonymous/parallelism.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 1:18 "in much wisdom there is much grief"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
1:18 "in much wisdom there is much grief" This, like Eccl. 1:15, may have been a well known cultural proverb from the sages. The search for meaning and happiness cannot be accomplished without God (cf. Eccl. 2:23; 12:12; Prov. 1:1-7; 1 Cor. 13:2). As a matter of fact, it becomes maddening!

The more you know, the more you know you do not know!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Who is the author?
  2. What was his purpose in writing this book?
  3. Is he a pessimist or cynic?
  4. What are the two key phrases in interpreting this book? Why?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:1 "I said to myself"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:1 "I said to myself" Chapters 1-2 form a literary unit. This is a recurrent refrain (cf. Eccl. 1:16,17; 2:1,15). The author is verbalizing (i.e., in writing) his unspoken thoughts.

▣ "Come now" There are three IMPERATIVES in this verse:

  1. "come" ‒ BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE (a Hebrew way to introduce a new thought, e.g., Ps. 34:12; 46:8; 66:5,16)
  2. "I will test" ‒ BDB 650, KB 702, Piel IMPERFECT used in a cohortative sense
  3. "enjoy yourself" ‒ BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE (literally, "and look on goodness." The UBS Handbook for Translators says this can be understood as "see what good there is in it?" or "see what pleasure can offer?" (p. 52)

▣ "I will test you with pleasure" The VERB "test" (BDB 650, KB 702, Piel COHORTATIVE) clarifies the experiment. Qoheleth is trying to ascertain if worldly, physical pleasure is the key to "gain" (see note at Eccl. 1:3), but alas, it is not! All physical pleasure fades with the doing. It becomes routine and common (as do possessions).

Pleasure (BDB 970, KB 1336) is used in Ecclesiastes in two different senses:

  1. gaiety, laughter (Eccl. 2:1,2,10; 7:4), where periods of pleasure briefly dull the mind and heart to humanity's existential existence in a fallen world, but it does not last; it does not satisfy!
  2. daily pleasure in life's personal relationships and activities (Eccl. 8:15; 9:7). Here pleasure is not the goal, but the result of a lifestyle attitude of trust in God (cf. Eccl. 2:26; 5:19) and thankfulness about common, daily life experiences (food, drink, family, friends, work, cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).

It is these contrasts between the proper use and attitude toward things in this world versus a "me first," "me at any cost," emphasis of fallen humanity that characterize this book. All things have their proper place (cf. Ecclesiastes 3).

▣
NASB, NRSV  "So enjoy yourself"
NKJV  "so enjoy pleasure"
TEV  "find out what happiness is"
REB  "get enjoyment"
NJB  "see what enjoyment has to offer"
JPSOA  "taste mirth"
Peshitta  "therefore enjoy good things"
NET  "if it is worthwhile"

The MT has "and look on goodness." The issue is, "What is good?" This is repeated in v. 3; or to use another Ecclesiastes image, "What is profitable?" "What is lasting?" These are the questions of life! Where is happiness found?

The Hebrew root "good" (BDB 373 II) is used abut 40 times in this book and is the key issue in ascertaining where lasting gain/profit/good is found.

NASB  "futility"
NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "vanity"
TEV  "useless"
NJB, REB, JPSOA, NET  "futile"

See note at Eccl. 1:2.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:2 Notice the two parallel comments about "laughter" and "pleasure," which are unrelated to a person's life of faith, are useless. They bring no lasting peace, joy, or hope! No profit (cf. v. 11)). See full note on "profit" at Eccl. 1:3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:3 "stimulate my body with wine. . .while my mind was guiding me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:3 "stimulate my body with wine. . .while my mind was guiding me" This may refer to drunkenness, but with limits, safeguards (i.e., the wisdom of the sages). This is similar to the use of "mind expanding" drugs today, which have temporary pleasurable results, but long term addiction and destruction!

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

▣ "folly" The VERB form (BDB 698, KB 754) in Aramaic means "to know," "to be intelligent," or "to cause to understand." This connotation seems to fit the context best (cf. Eccl. 1:17; 2:12,13; 7:25).

▣ "under heaven" This phrase (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 2:3; 3:1) is a synonym for "under the sun," used twenty-nine times in Ecclesiastes (see NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 165, #10). See note on the theological meaning at Eccl. 1:3.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:4-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4-11 These verses describe what the author attributes to King Solomon. These are things and accomplishments that he had done (a series of 23 PERFECT TENSE VERBS), but, there was no lasting peace, joy, hope, and happiness. St. Augustine said there is a God-shaped hole in every person. Nothing can fill that hole except God. Only when we know Him can physical things and life experiences have meaning (cf. chapter 3).

The NIV Study Bible adds an interesting note about how vv. 4-6 use so many terms found in Genesis 1-2 that it seems the author is surely alluding to the Garden of Eden. However, this garden in chapter 2 is a garden of Eden without God, but a garden built by a fallen, powerful, rich human.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:4 "I enlarged my works"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:4 "I enlarged my works" BDB 152, KB 178, Hiphil PERFECT.

  1. houses, Eccl. 2:4
  2. vineyards, Eccl. 2:4
  3. parks, Eccl. 2:5
  4. orchards, Eccl. 2:5
  5. ponds, Eccl. 2:6
  6. slaves, Eccl. 2:7
  7. flocks and herds, Eccl. 2:7

Notice the number of times "myself" appears in Eccl. 2:4-8.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:5 "parks"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:5 "parks" This is a Persian loan word (BDB 825) describing a wealthy person's garden.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:7 "male and female slaves"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:7 "male and female slaves" Slavery was common in the ancient world. It was not all bad! Many poor Hebrews sold themselves into slavery to another Hebrew to have a better life (cf. Deut. 15:12-18)! Of course, forced slavery (military, economic) was, and is, a tragedy! There was, and is, human exploitation in this area.

▣ "larger than all who preceded me in Jerusalem" This clearly shows the egocentric nature of these pursuits (cf. Eccl. 2:9; see note at Eccl. 1:16).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:8 "I collected"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:8 "I collected" (BDB 888, KB 1111, Qal PERFECT):

  1. silver and gold, Eccl. 2:8
  2. treasure, Eccl. 2:8 (taxes or tribute)
  3. singers, Eccl. 2:8
  4. concubines, Eccl. 2:8

▣ "provinces" This may refer to the administrative divisions set up by Solomon (cf. Eccl. 5:8; 1 Kgs. 4:17-19; 20:14-19). Again, Solomon is the literary foil in chapters 1-2.

▣ "male and female singers" This (BDB 1010, KB 1479) possibly refers to

  1. the artistic aspect of life
  2. temple singers
  3. regular festivals (i.e., door keepers)

Music was a major part of the life of the Israelite people. They express to God every human emotion from joy to saddness. Let me suggest several categories, some which overlap. This is just a suggestive list.

  1. victory songs
    1. Exodus 15:1-18
    2. Judges 5:1-3
    3. Psalm 68:4,32; 104:33
  2. temple worship music
    1. 1 Chronicles 13:8; 15:16; 25:1
    2. 2 Chronicles 23:13
    3. Nehemiah 12:27
  3. palace songs
    1. Ezra 2:65
    2. Ecclesiastes 2:8
    3. Amos 8:3,10; also note 5:23; 6:5
  4. secular songs of partying
    1. 2 Samuel 19:35
    2. Proverbs 25:20
    3. Ecclesiastes 7:5; 12:4 (imagery)
    4. Ezekiel 26:13
  5. love songs
    1. Psalm 45 (king's wedding)
    2. Song of Songs (whole book)
    3. Isaiah 5:1 (YHWH's love for Israel)
    4. Ezekiel 33:32
  6. funeral songs (dirge)
    1. 1 Chronicles 35:25
    2. Isaiah 24:7-13
  7. laments (with implied singing or chanting)
    1. Psalm 13:1-7; 42:1-11; 89:30-48; 130:1-8
    2. 2 Chronicles 35:25
    3. Lamentations (whole book)
  8. praise songs (often called "new song")
    1. Psalm 13:6; 27:6; 28:7; 40:1-3; 57:7; 59:16; 69:30; 96:1; 98:1; 101:1; 108:1-6; 144:9
    2. Jeremiah 20:13
  9. songs of ascent sung as pilgrims approached Jerusalem during feast days — Psalm 122-134
NASB, NRSV  "concubines"
NKJV  "musical instruments of all kinds"
TEV  "all the women a man could want"
NJB, JPSOA  "every human luxury, chest upon chest of it"
NIV  "harem"
REB  "everything that affords delight"
LXX  "a butler and female cupbearers"

The Hebrew word (BDB 994, KB 950) is very uncertain (see NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 49). Obviously from the varied translations the meaning of this Hebrew hapax legomenon is unknown. The possibilies come from the Semitic root:

  1. From the term for "woman's breast" (BDB 994), NASB, NRSV, TEV, NIV (in apposition to "the delights of men"). UBS Hebrew Text Project gives this option a "B" rating.
  2. The NIV Study Bible's footnote says that an early Egyptian letter uses a similar Canaanite term for concubines (p. 993). This fits Solomon (cf. 1 Kings 11:3).
  3. In later Hebrew (Mishnah) it refers to a chest or coffer, NJB, JPSOA (in apposition to "the treasure of kings")
  4. KJV, ASV, NKJV see it as in apposition to "singers" (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 99).
  5. The LXX took the meaning from the Aramaic root, "to pour out (wine)" (NET Bible, p. 116).
  6. The REB seems to connect it to "delights of men," but in the sense of luxuries (cf. Prov. 19:10).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:9-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:9-11 This strophe is a summary statement. All of these "things" did provide a moment of joy and satisfaction, but it did not last! If the wisest, wealthiest, and most powerful person (i.e. Solomon) cannot find real lasting joy and satisfaction, how can anyone? This is the conclusion of Eccl. 2:11 (cf. Eccl. 1:14; 2:17,22-23)! This is the question of how to find purpose in life without God; without God, life becomes just physical existence! Where is lasting value or gain found?

The NKJV and NIV translations see Eccl. 2:10 and 11, as well as 12-16, as poetry, but other English translations have not followed this approach.

For the key phrase, "under the sun," see note at Eccl. 1:3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:10 "all that my eyes desired I did not refuse them. I did not withhold my heart from any pleasure"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:10 "all that my eyes desired I did not refuse them. I did not withhold my heart from any pleasure" These are balanced lines. It is hard to know when Qoheleth moves from prose to poetry. Notice the VERBS:

  1. "refuse" ‒ BDB 69, KB 82, Qal PERFECT, meaning "withhold"
  2. "withhold" ‒ BDB 586, KB 602, Qal PERFECT; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 991, says this implies that "the searcher for meaning has abandoned all restraint in search of pleasure."

For "heart" see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "my labor" The author (here speaking as Solomon, i.e. a literary foil) rejoices in his works (cf. Eccl. 2:10 [twice],11), but in Eccl. 2:18,20,22 he "hates" them! The question of Eccl. 3:9, "What does the worker gain from his toil?" resounds! Earthly effort will fail, fade, and forever pass away!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:11 "there was no profit"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:11 "there was no profit" This is a crucial theological concept in Ecclesiastes. The NOUN only occurs in Ecclesiastes ten times (i.e., Eccl. 1:3; 2:11,23; 3:9; 5:8,25; 7:12; 10:10,11). It could be translated "profit," "advantage," or "gain." See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:12 Our author returns to wisdom to find lasting value, but he has tried that before also (cf. Eccl. 1:16-18). There are advantages to wisdom as opposed to folly (cf. Eccl. 7:11,12,19; 9:18; 10:10; Proverbs 8; see good note in NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 679 and same concept in vol. 3, pp. 254-255), but they are not ultimate advantages (cf. Eccl. 2:14-16).

  1. one fate befalls them both (cf. Eccl. 9:11; Ps. 49:10)
  2. there will be no lasting remembrance of either (note the opposite in Ps. 112:6; Prov. 10:7)
▣
NASB  "for what will the man do who will come after the king"
NRSV  "for what can the one do who will come after the the King"
NKJV, JPSOA  "for what will the men be like who will succeed"
REB    ‒‒omit‒‒
NJB, NET  "what can the successor of a king do"
Peshitta  "who is the man who can enter into judgment with the King"
TEV  "After all, a king can only do what previous kings have done"

I think the TEV catches the meaning best. It explains v. 16. There is no thing new under the sun!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:13 "wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:13 "wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness" There is value in wisdom, but it is not ultimate (cf. Eccl. 7:11,12,19; 9:18; 10:10). Human wisdom is always tenuous and partial.

▣ The NASB translation has left out the significant term "profit" or "advantage" (BDB 452, KB 404). See note at Eccl. 1:3.

2:14
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, REB, LXX, Peshitta  "eyes are in his head"
TEV  "see where they are going"
NJB  "have their eyes open "

The two dynamic equivalent translations (TEV, NJB) show the Hebraic imagery.

▣ "the fool" This is the Hebrew term "the self-confident one" (BDB 493, KB 489).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE, #2

▣ "one fate befalls them both" This fate (BDB 899, KB 629) is a euphemism for death. Qoheleth feels the pain of the future common experience of all human beings (cf. Eccl. 2:15; 3:19 [twice]; 9:2,3).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:15 "As is the fate of the fool"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:15 "As is the fate of the fool" The VERB (BDB 899, KB 1137, Qal IMPERFECT) denotes that which is unexpecterd or surprising. It denotes an underlying divine process and purpose (see NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 984).

▣
NASB, NRSV  "Why then have I been extremely wise?"
NKJV, Peshitta  "And why was I then more wise?"
TEV  "So what have I gained from being wise?"
REB  "To what purpose have I been wise?"
NJB  "What is the point of my having been wise?"
JPSOA  "To what advantage, then, have I been wise?"

The textual question, is it

  1. an ADVERB, "so very"
  2. a sentence, "there is no gain/profit"

The UBS Hebrew Text Project, p. 568, gives option #1 a "B" rating. But option #2 makes perfect sense in this context.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:16 "lasting"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:16 "lasting" This is literally "forever." See SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam).

▣ "all will be forgotten" This VERB (BDB 1013, KB 1489, Niphal PERFECT) denotes the completed action of a yet future event as if it were already complete. What looks new is just something done before but has been forgotten (cf. Eccl. 1:9-11).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:17 "hated life"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:17 "hated life" This VERB (BDB 971, KB 1338, Qal PERFECT) means "hate," but with the connotation of "disgusted" with life (cf. NJB) because of the futility that all he had worked for and built (cf. Eccl. 2:18; 2:11) had no lasting value or gain/profit/advantage.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:18 "I must leave it to the man who will come after me"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:18 "I must leave it to the man who will come after me" Traditional wisdom teachers put great faith in one's prosperity, not so Qoheleth. Everyone leaves everything (cf. v. 21; Ps. 39:6; 49:10).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:18-21
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:18-21 There is an obvious poetic parallel between Eccl. 2:18-19 and Eccl. 2:20-21 (cf. NET Bible, p. 1119).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:19 "who knows. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:19 "who knows. . ." This is the author's major concern. He is obviously a trained sage, but this does not help knowing

  1. future events
  2. answer to ultimate questions (i.e., Eccl. 3:21)
  3. why life is so unfair

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:19,21 "he gives his legacy to one who has not labored with them"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:19,21 "he gives his legacy to one who has not labored with them" Often that which is passed on to the next generation is not appreciated, and is even squandered away!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:20 What a lament! What a realization! In Hebrew there is a repetition (NOUN and VERB, BDB 765, KB 845) of the term "labor," "toil," which strengthens the lament.

The VERBAL (BDB 384, KB 382, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) means "despair," "be hopeless," "desperate." Qoheleth uses strong language to describe the depth of his emotions about the utter futility of human effort!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:21 "there is"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:21 "there is" This Hebrew phrase (BDB 441) introduces a hypothetical, but often occurring, human experience or example (cf. Eccl. 2:21; 4:8; 5:13; 6:1,11; 7:15 [twice]; 8:14 [thrice]; 10:5). It is used many times in Wisdom Literature (e.g., Prov. 11:24; 12:8; 13:7; 14:12; 16:25; 18:24; 20:15).

NASB, NKJV, NRSV, LXX  "a great evil"
TEV  "it isn't right"
NJB  "grossly evil"
JPSOA  "a grave evil"
REB  "a great wrong"
Peshitta  "a great misfortune"
NET  "an awful injustice"

These translations reflect the Hebrew word "evil" (BDB 948-949, KB 1262). It is used in this context as "grievous injustice" (cf. Eccl. 2:17; 5:13 [twice],16; 6:1; 9:12; 10:5). The unfairness and randomness of this fallen world lies heavy on this author! See note at Eccl. 5:13.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:22 "What does a man get in all his labor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 2:22 "What does a man get in all his labor" What are the ultimate results of physical labors? Is there anything beyond the grave? See note at Eccl. 1:3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:23 "his task is painful and grievous"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:23 "his task is painful and grievous" This is the recurrent description of fallen humanity's search for happiness. It always turns to despair (cf. Eccl. 1:18; 2:23; 5:17; 11:10).

▣ "even at night his mind does not rest" Those who possess worldly things worry about them constantly (i.e. day, Eccl. 2:23a and night, Eccl. 2:23b; i.e., no rest). Those who seek wisdom realize "the more you know, the more you know you do not know"! There is a race no one can win (cf. Eccl. 1:18).

The word translated "does not rest" is really the VERB "lie down" (BDB 1011, KB 1486, Qal PERFECT). This is a good place to briefly discuss how Hebrew roots develop into several connotations. This basic action of someone lying down developed into a wide semanitc field of possibilities.

  1. lie down to sleep
  2. lie down for sexual purposes
  3. lay somethig down (i.e., place it) on (i.e., about something)
  4. the place one sleeps

All words start with a concrete meaning/usage, but become extended in their meanings. This is why I say again and again, "words have meaning only in sentences and sentences have meaning only in paragraphs." Context, context, context!!

  1. historical
  2. literary
  3. imagery

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:24 "This also I have seen, that it is from the hand of God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:24 "This also I have seen, that it is from the hand of God" The simple pleasures of life are gifts from God (cf. Eccl. 3:13; 5:19; 9:7; Prov. 13:22; Job 27:16-17). See note at Eccl. 2:1. This is one of just a few great truths in this book!

  1. enjoy the simple pleasures of daily life (Eccl. 2:1,24; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9)
    1. food (fellowship)
    2. drink (although this can refer to revelry [cf. Exod. 32:6; 1 Sam. 30:16; 1 Kgs. 1:25] in this context it refers to daily family and social life)
    3. sense of self-worth from life's work
    4. rejoicing in life (Eccl. 9:8)
    5. marriage and family (Eccl. 9:9)
  2. fear God, keep the commandments (Eccl. 2:25; 12:13-14)

▣ "from the hand of God" See Special Topic below.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:24-26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:24-26 The Jewish Study Bible (p. 1608) asserts that these verses offer a new perspective on the author's previous comments about the futility of life (i.e., enjoy the immediate). However, they seem to answer the question of Eccl. 1:3. It is true there is no lasting benefit (cf. Eccl. 2:11) apart from God, but Eccl. 2:24-26 finally brings "above the sun" into focus. There is more to life than birth, life, and inevitable death. There is God, judgment, and an afterlife. Things will be set straight (cf. Eccl. 1:15), but not here, not now. Unfairness, injustice, and vanity seem to reign (because of the Fall, cf. Genesis 3), but wait, God reigns! He and His (i.e., humans made in His image, cf. Gen. 1:26-27) will spend eternity together. For now, the righteous must trust in His revelation and enjoy the simple daily pleasures that this world offers (when and while one can).

Qoheleth being an OT sage, did not know the whole picture (i.e., the new Covenant, cf. Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36 and the complete, ultimate revelation in Jesus Christ).

There is an interesting list concerning Qoheleth's understanding of God's actions in this fallen, temporal world (i.e., NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 553):

  1. creator, Eccl. 11:5; 12:1,7 (like Psalms)
  2. judge, Eccl. 3:17,18; 11:9
  3. benefactor, Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:13; 5:18-20
  4. one to be feared, Eccl. 3:14; 5:1-7; 7:18 (like Proverbs)
  5. one to be obeyed, Eccl. 5:4; 7:26; 8:2; 13:13-14 (like Proverbs)
  6. one causality in the universe, Eccl. 3:11; 5:18-6:2; 7:13-14 (like Psalms)
  7. unknowable, Eccl. 3:11; 8:16-9:1 (like Job)
  8. fair, Eccl. 8:12,13

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ONE CAUSALITY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:25 "have enjoyment"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:25 "have enjoyment" This is a rare Hebrew term used only here in the OT. Most English translations take the meaning from the Arabic "feel" or "perceive by the senses" (BDB 301 II). However, the NJB has "drink," following the Septuagint, which tried to make Eccl. 2:24 and 25 parallel. The UBS Hebrew Text Project, p. 569, gives "enjoys" a "B" rating.

NASB  "without Him"
NKJV, MT  "more than I"
NRSV, NIV, LXX,  "apart from him"
TEV   ‒‒omit‒‒
NJB  "came from Him"
JPSOA  "but myself"
REB  "without God"
Peshitta  "except he"

The MT has "apart from me." A Hebrew textual variation ("apart from Him") in some medieval Hebrew manuscripts is preserved in the Septuagint, Peshitta, and Vulgate. Does this phrase reflect Qoheleth's thinking or has a major theological insight been reached (i.e. "gift from God," "from the hand of God") beginning in Eccl. 2:24? I think Eccl. 2:24-26 should be seen as a whole new thought.

The UBS Text Project, p. 570, gives "apart from me" a "B" rating (some doubt).  It suggests it refers to Qoheleth, not Elohim.  I prefer, from context, that it refers to God (NASB, NJB, REB).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 2:26
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
2:26 The question of this verse is how is a person "good in His sight?" This question must be related to Eccl. 12:13-14. Notice the benefits:

  1. wisdom (BDB 315, KB 313)
  2. knowledge (BDB 395, KB 228)
  3. joy (BDB 970, KB 1336)

Notice the consequences for a selfish, godless life:

  1. gathering and collecting
  2. only to be given to another ("person who is good in His sight")

Obviously Eccl. 2:24-26 are contrasting Eccl. 2:12-23! Exactly how they relate is uncertain.

Qoheleth is also challenging traditional wisdom about prosperity (i.e., the Two Ways, cf. Job; Psalm 73). The wicked rich are actually gathering for the righteous (cf. Job 27:16,17; Prov. 13:22)!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. List the things in Eccl. 2 that Qoheleth says proclaim vanity.
  2. Why does the author use Solomon as a backdrop in these two opening chapters?
  3. Why does he seem to contradict himself about the advantages or disadvantages of wisdom and pleasure?
  4. What great insights do Eccl. 2:24-26 convey?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:1 "There is an appointed time for everything"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:1 "There is an appointed time for everything" The "appointed time" (lit. "for everything a season") seems to refer to the common events of human life. The "appointed time" does not speak of the advantageous human time, but of the divinely appointed time (i.e., Eccl. 2:24-26 and full note at 3:14). The emphasis of this chapter is on divine appointment. It speaks of the mystery of human effort ("under heaven") as it is compared with the sovereignty of God. In Wisdom Literature "appointed time" is often imagery for "appropriate time."

NASB  "event"
NKJV  "purpose"
NRSV  "matter"
TEV  "happens"
NJB  "occupation"
REB  "activity"
JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "a season"

The Hebrew word (BDB 343, KB 340) means "delight" or "pleasure," but here it has the added connotation of activity that brings joy (cf. Eccl. 3:17; 8:6; Prov. 31:13). Enjoy life each day! Smell the roses along the path! All humans have is the immediate. All future events are in God's hand.

▣ "under heaven" See full note of the key phrase, "under the sun," at 1:3,9.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Although this chapter is usually interpreted as dealing with the timeliness or appropriateness of human actions, in context, it deals with God's sovereignty (see NRSV, i.e., Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:14).

  2. When interpreting the book of Ecclesiastes it is very important that we see it is satire based on two key phrases:
    1. "all is vanity" (i.e., transitoriness of human life and effort; see full note at Eccl. 1:2)
    2. "under the sun" (i.e., physical life, earthly life viewed apart from God; see Eccl. 1:3,9)

  3. The central answer to a meaningless and frustrated life is found in
    1. fear God (cf. Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12,13; 12:13)
    2. faith and obedience (cf. Eccl. 12:13-14)
    3. the simple daily pleasures of life as provided by God (cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:12-13, 22; 5:18; 6:12; 8:15; 9:7)

  4. Ecclesiastes is one of the books of the Bible that must be interpreted in its totality. Prooftexting this book or missing its tongue-in-cheek worldview will prove to be a hermeneutical disaster.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:2 "A time to give birth, and a time to die"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:2 "A time to give birth, and a time to die" There is a series of events which refer to the cycle of human development from birth to death.

▣ "A time to plant, and a time to uproot what is planted" There is a grammatical connection between the efforts of the sinner (Eccl. 2:26, two Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS) and that of Eccl. 3:2-9 (a series of 27 INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS).

This speaks of the annual harvest (i.e., M. Dahood, Phoenician Background of Qohelet).  Israel was an agricultural culture. "Uproot" here means to harvest the matured crop.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:2-8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:2-8 Almost all English translations see Eccl. 3:2-8 in a poetic structure. Within each line there is a contrast, but the relationship between lines is not completely clear. There is a series of 27 INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS (three more in 2:26).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:3 "A time to kill, and a time to heal"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:3 "A time to kill, and a time to heal" Since war is mentioned in Eccl. 3:8 the killing referred to here seems to have another focus. Some have assumed that it refers to

  1. capital punishment within the nation of Israel (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HANG and SPECIAL TOPIC: STONE TO DEATH)
  2. the defense of one's home, or person, in the event of an attack
  3. The Jewish Publication Society of America (JPSOA) translates this phrase as "A time for slaying and a time for healing," but in the footnote it suggests a possible emendation based on 1 Kgs. 18:30, "A time for wrecking and a time for repairing."

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:4 "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; A time to mourn, and a time to dance"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:4 "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; A time to mourn, and a time to dance" Some believe these two poetic lines refer to funerals (ie., a time to weep) and weddings (i.e., a time to laugh) or to other regular social events.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:5 "A time to throw stones, and a time to gather stones"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:5 "A time to throw stones, and a time to gather stones" Many have assumed that

  1. this is agricultural imagery of one removing stones from a field
  2. however, this could be construction imagery of using stones for a rock fence or a home
  3. It has been the consensus among Jewish commentators that this has sexual connotations (cf. TEV "making love"). This is stated specifically in the Midrash. The context of Eccl. 3:5b seems to reinforce this understanding. This would mean that there is time, Levitically speaking, when men could have sexual relations and a time when they could not because of a woman's menstrual cycle or the man's military commitments.

▣ "A time to embrace, and a time to shun embracing" This could refer to

  1. sexual love within marriage (cf. Sol 2:6)
  2. sexual love outside of marriage (cf. Prov. 5:20)
  3. a family's caring love for each other
  4. friends kissing one another on the cheek, which was common in the Near East.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:6 "A time to search, and a time to give up as lost"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 3:6 "A time to search, and a time to give up as lost" The first term "search" (BDB 134, KB 152, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) means to seek after something. However, there comes a time in life where it becomes obvious that that something or someone cannot be obtained! One must get on with life!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:7 "A time to tear apart, and a time to sew together"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:7 "A time to tear apart, and a time to sew together" This may refer to one of the mourning practices of the Jews. They would rip the front of their robe at the neckline about five inches (e.g., 1 Sam. 4:12; 2 Sam. 1:2; 13:31; 15:32; 2 Kgs. 18:3;7; Jer. 41:5); when the mourning was over they would sew it up again.

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES

▣ "A time to be silent, and a time to speak" This may also refer to

  1. the mourning rites
  2. sharing information

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:8 "A time to love and a time to hate"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:8 "A time to love and a time to hate" This speaks to the range of human emotions from the positive to the negative (i.e., true antonyms). Unfortunately, fallen humans are involved in both. One brings lasting advantage but the other does not.

▣ "A time for war and a time for peace" Most Jewish commentators understand Eccl. 3:1-8 as referring to

  1. national Israel (cf. "appointed time" in Ps. 75:2; 102:13)
  2. however, it seems that Eccl. 3:9-11 defines these verses in light of a personal, rather than corporate, emphasis

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAR AND PEACE

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:9-10 The NOUN "profit" (BDB 452, KB 452) is a key term found only in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:11,13; 5:8,15; 7:12; 10:10,11). A related SUBSTANTIVE (BDB 452) is also found in Eccl. 6:8,11; 7:11,16; 12:9,12). It can be translated "advantage," "profit," or "lasting benefit." See note at Eccl. 1:3. The key question is, "Is there any lasting gain or value in human life, human effort, human wisdom?"

At first glance this seems to contradict the "good" of Gen. 1:4,10,12,18,22,25 and the superlative statement of Gen. 1:31. However, Ecclesiastes is dealing with perceived life as it is now. Therefore, I would assume this evaluation is made in light of the terrible consequences of Genesis 3 (see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND).

It seems that humanity is driven to perform certain common tasks (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 2:23), tasks even provided by God (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 2:24; 3:11), but they are unable to understand the purpose or outcome of these tasks. The purpose of these tasks is to show them their dependence on God (cf. Gal. 3:24; Eccl. 3:14,18), which is the opposite of the common experience of the Fall (i.e., independence from God characterized by the recurrent phrase, "under the sun"; see full note at Eccl. 1:3).

3:11
NASB, JB, NEB  "He has made everything appropriate in its time"
NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "He has made everything beautiful in its time"
NRSV, REB  "He has made everything suitable for its time"
TEV  "He has set the right time for everything"
NJB  "all that he does is apt for its time"
JPSOA  "He brings everything to pass precisely at its time"

The key term "appropriate" (BDB 421, KB 423) means "fair" or "beautiful." In context it describes God's sovereign choices that control human circumstances. This is more corporate than individual (i.e., Jewish commentators see Eccl. 3:1-8 as referring to national Israel).

This again shows the sovereignty of God over human events as well as over time.
