 passage of time"
LXX  "he granted eternity in their heart"
JPSOA  "He also puts eternity in their minds"
Peshitta  "also he has made the world dear to man's heart"

The term translated "eternity" (BDB 761, KB 798; lit. "the 'olam") is uncertain. A related Semitic term using the same three consonants means "hidden" or "concealed" (BDB 761).

  1. In later Hebrew it referred to the creation of the world (LXX).
  2. Some scholars try to make this line balance with previous ones ("appropriate in its time"), meaning God controls human situations and destinies.
  3. Some scholars try to take it with the following line about human's inability to understand God's work, which fits the meaning of the Hebrew trilateral root (cf. Eccl. 12:14).
  4. Qoheleth uses a similar root (BDB 761) several times (i.e., 'olam, see SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam), cf. Eccl. 1:4,10; 2:16; 3:14; 9:6; 12:5) in the sense of time.

Poetry is always difficult to lock down. Its beauty and power are often destroyed by exegesis! Its terms are often rare and used in specialized senses. Its meaning is purposefully vague and thought-provoking. The larger context helps us get the general drift of Qoheleth's thought.

The Jerusalem Bible (a French Catholic dynamic equivalent translation) has a good comment on this verse:

"This phrase, however, is not to be taken in the Christian sense; it means simply: God has given the human heart (mind) awareness of 'duration,' he has endowed him with the power of reflecting on the sequence of events and thus of controlling the present. But, the author adds, this awareness is deceptive; it does not reveal the meaning of life" (p. 983 "b").

Humanity longs to understand life but cannot. Humans made in God's image long to fully understand God but cannot (a purposeful philosophical agnosticism, so characteristic of Qoheleth's writings).

▣ "the work which God has done" The NOUN (BDB 795) is from the same Semitic root as the VERB (BDB 793 I, KB 889, Qal PERFECT). This is often done as a creative writing style.

God's work can be understood in two ways:

  1. from eternity
  2. throughout an individual's life

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:12-13
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:12-13 This seems to be a summary strophe, like Eccl. 2:24-26. It suggests that although we cannot understand all of the mysteries of God, we can know

  1. God's love by faith and obedience
  2. enjoy the simple pleasures of life provided by God (cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:12-13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9)

Since we cannot understand or change the events in our individual lives (i.e., Eccl. 3:1-8) or in our world, we must focus on thanksgiving for those common, simple, daily, but really wonderful, things common to all human societies, but that really are a gift from God (cf. Eccl. 2:24; 5:19). These are spelled out in Eccl. 3:13:

  1. food
  2. drink
  3. a sense of purpose in one's labor
  4. from other verses in Ecclesiastes, one's family (cf. Eccl. 9:7-9)

All of these are gifts from God. It is possible that the gift is one's faith perspective which trusts in God although one cannot understand one's own existential circumstances. The Fall (cf. Genesis 3) has affected our ability to comprehend ultimate truth (cf. Eccl. 1:18; 8:16-9:12). It must be revealed, not discovered.

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:14 "I know that everything God does will remain forever"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:14 "I know that everything God does will remain forever" Here again is the emphasis on the eternality and sovereignty of God and the transitoriness of human life (e.g., Ps. 103: 14,15; Isa. 40:6-8; 1 Peter 1:24,25).

Ecclesiastes is as much a book about God as it is about humanity. The theology of a fallen world is only hinted at in the phrase "under the sun," but the reality of a mysterious painful, yet pleasurable, world is characterized in "vanity of vanities, all is vanity." Our mystery is God's clear, purposeful, knowledgeable and comprehensive plan. Knowledge is not as crucial as trust, faith, and obedience (i.e., Job 42).

Some of the texts which characterize the unknowable but present God are

  1. there is a divine plan at work, Eccl. 1:14; 3:10,18; 7:29; 8:16-17
  2. there is a sovereign Lord, Eccl. 1:15 & 7:13; 3:11,14; 9:1; 12:1
  3. there is a daily faith which enables and ennobles, Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18-20 (negatively in Eccl. 6:1-6); 9:7-9
  4. there is an appropriate awe and respect due to God, Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12,13; 12:13
  5. there is/will be a time of evaluation by God of every human being, Eccl. 3:17; (5:1,4, implied); 11:9; 12:14

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

▣ "for God has so worked that men should fear Him" This reflects the truth of Eccl. 3:10 that God has given us a task that we cannot perform so that we will continue to depend on Him (i.e., "fear Him," cf. Eccl. 5:7; 7:18; 8:12,13, which implies a faith worldview) and not on ourselves.

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:15 "That which is has been already, and that which will be has already been"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:15 "That which is has been already, and that which will be has already been" There are several possibilities of this verse:

  1. a reflection on Eccl. 1:9 (i.e., nothing new in human activity)
  2. it is used in a tongue-in-cheek (i.e., "under the sun," cf. Eccl. 3:16)
  3. it could be related to God's revelation to Moses (i.e., do not add or take away from God's revelation, cf. Deut. 4:2; 12:32; Jer. 26:2)
NASB  "for God seeks what is passed by"
NKJV  "God requires an account of what is past"
NRSV  "God seeks out what has gone by"
NJB  "God seeks out anyone who is persecuted"
LXX  "God will seek out that which is past"
REB  "with God summoning each event back in its turn"
JPSOA  "God seeks the pursued"
Peshitta  "and God will avenge him who has been persecuted"

This is a very difficult Hebrew phrase.

  1. Some assume it means "the one who is persecuted" (cf. Peshitta, NJB, JPSOA).
  2. Others go with the traditional translation of "what has been driven away" (the VERB, BDB 134, KB 152, Piel IMPERFECT, has both meanings).
  3. It seems to refer to the general concept of the book of Ecclesiastes that although the experiences of all humans are in a repetitive cycle, there is a divine purpose in this cycle. One day God will judge individual human choices!
  4. The UBS Handbook (p. 108) asserts that this VERB in later Hebrew meant "request" or "ask." If so, then God wants His special creation to pursue:
    1. action at the appropriate time (cf. Eccl. 3:1-8)
    2. daily pleasures (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:22)
    3. eternity (cf. Eccl. 3:11)
    4. His activities (cf. Eccl. 3:14)
    5. His Law (cf.3:15, Deut. 4:2; 12:32)
  5. The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 722, supports the KB, "passed/gone by" (see NASB, NRSV, LXX).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:16 "under the sun"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:16 "under the sun" Again, I think that the book of Ecclesiastes (using this phrase) views life from one of two perspectives:

  1. What is the meaning of life if there is no God?
  2. What is the meaning of life if there is a God?

See note at Eccl. 1:3,9.

▣ "in the place of justice there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness" This seems to show that the two places where the character of God should have been manifested most clearly in human life are

  1. the law courts ("the place of justice," BDB 1048)
  2. the area of worship ("the place of righteousness," BDB 841, see note at Eccl. 1:15)

It is possible that these two words are used in parallel and refer to characteristics of God. However, because of the fallenness of humanity and the unfairness of life in a fallen world, righteousness and justice are not found! Power corrupts (cf. Eccl. 4:1; 5:8; 8:9)! And wickedness (BDB 957, KB 1295, cf. NOUN, Eccl. 3:16 [twice]; 7:25; 8:8; ADJECTIVE, Eccl. 3:17; 7:15; 8:10, 13, 14 [twice]; 9:2) results!

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:17-18 "God will judge both the righteous man and the wicked man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:17-18 "God will judge both the righteous man and the wicked man" There are two aspects given to the statements found in Eccl. 3:16 about wickedness in the place of justice and worship.

  1. The first answer is in this verse and states that God will ultimately judge all humans one day (i.e., an appointed time, cf. Eccl. 11:9; 12:14).

    Verse 17 has often been interpreted as an affirmation of an afterlife. Although this is rare in Ecclesiastes, it is not completely unique. If it is true that God is a fair God, the righteous will prosper and the wicked will be judged (i.e., the two ways, cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; Psalm 1). If it does not happen in this life (sometimes it does, cf. Job 27:13-23; Psalm 73), then the only conclusion is that there must be an afterlife (e.g., Matt. 25:31-46; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 20:11-15).

    SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

    SPECIAL TOPIC: PHARISEES

  2. This is the second answer to the apparent injustice of Eccl. 3:16 and that is that God is surely testing (lit. "purging" or "cleaning," BDB 140, KB 162, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) everything. This is a general truth of the Bible (e.g., Gen. 22:1; Exod. 15:25; 16:4; 20:20; Deut. 8:2, 16; 13:3; Jdg. 2:22; 2 Chr. 32:31; Matt. 4:1; Heb. 12:5-13).

  SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD TESTS HIS PEOPLE

▣ "in order for them to see that they are but beasts" Again, the purpose is to show humans that without God they are only a highly developed animal (i.e., nephesh, Gen. 1:30). God is seeking to put fallen mankind in such a position where they will recognize the futility of life without the spiritual component (God, judgment, eternity).

The JPSOA translates this as "to dissociate them [from] divine beings." I do not see where they got this supposed translation. But, the subject is interesting and relates to the different connotations of elohim (i.e., vv. 17,18). Please look at the following Special Topics.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: godly ones, holy ones

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:19 "For the fate of the sons of men and the fate of beasts is the same"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:19 "For the fate of the sons of men and the fate of beasts is the same" There is a carryover from Eccl. 3:18 to Eccl. 3:19 in the term "beast" (BDB 96, KB 111). If one pursues the concept that this physical realm is all that there is, the consequences are quite discouraging. The death of a human is no different from that of an animal (cf. Eccl. 2:14; 6:6;; 7:2; 9:2,3). However, if there is a spiritual realm and if mankind is made in the image of God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27), then there is an eternal significance for humanity (cf. Eccl. 12:7).

Verses 20-22 are an expansion of the question mentioned in Eccl. 3:19. The term "breath" (BDB 924, KB 1197-1201) is interesting because it goes back to Gen. 2:7. It is true that the breath of life, which made Adam a living soul, or nephesh, is used for both the animals and for Adam. However, although humans certainly do have animal characteristics (eat, breathe, reproduce) and are related uniquely to this planet, there is a uniquely spiritual element in mankind.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

▣  "all is vanity"  This is a major theological term in Ecclesiastes. See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:20 "All go to the same place. All came from the dust and all return to the dust"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:20 "All go to the same place. All came from the dust and all return to the dust" This truth is initially stated in Gen. 3:19 and developed in Ps. 103:14 and 104:29.

The term "dust" (BDB 779, KB 861) is also used in Gen. 2:7 (see notes online) in relation to the special creation of mankind (cf. Gen. 3:19; Job 4:19; 8:19; 10:9; 34:15; Ps. 103:14; 104:29; Eccl. 3:20; 12:7). Humans were made from dust and will return to dust. Qoheleth knew the Genesis account of creation and used its key terms:

  1. nephesh
  2. dust

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:21 "Who knows that"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:21 "Who knows that" Because of the use of this same phrase in Eccl. 2:19 and 6:12 this is obviously a question. It seems though that the same truth is found in Eccl. 12:7 as an affirmation.

The relationship between the questions in Eccl. 3:21 and 22 has been dealt with in a very creative way by the commentator H. C. Leupold in Exposition of Ecclesiastes, pp. 97-101. He asserts that the two questions are really an INTERROGATIVE and a regular ARTICLE, which makes an affirmation. This structure seems to be a better understanding of these two verses. When one consults English translations one finds a question in both Eccl. 3:21 and 22. However, if one compares 12:7 with the question of Eccl. 3:22, they seem to be contradictory. I think that Leupold's technical discussion on the use of the article versus the interrogative is helpful in making Eccl. 3:22 an affirmation instead of a question.

▣ "breath" This Hebrew term ruah (BDB 924) has a wide semantic range:

  1. wind
  2. breath
  3. spirit
    1. God
    2. mankind

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

▣ "upward. . .downward" This is a reflection of the ancient worldview that God's abode was up and Sheol was underground. It is often called "the three storied universe" and is used to try and show that the Bible is an irrelevant ancient book. This is phenomenalogical language, language of the five human senses. Smoke of the sacrifices goes "up" to God! Dead bodies (in Jewish culture) are buried (i.e., in the earth). Before we criticize the ancient world for this kind of descriptive language, remember we moderns speak in the similar imagery.

  1. the sun "rises"
  2. dew "falls"
  3. "mother nature"

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND LTHE THIRD HEAVEN

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL

▣ "what will occur after him" This does not necessarily refer specifically to an afterlife in this context, but perhaps to future events in this life.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 3:22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
3:22 This is another summary statement, like Eccl. 2:24-26 and 3:12-13! This is a recurrent theme (cf. Eccl. 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9). See note at Eccl. 2:24-26

NASB, NRSV  "for that is his lot"
NKJV  "for that is his heritage"
TEV    ——
NJB  "such is the lot of a human being"
LXX, Peshitta, JPSOA  "for it is his portion"
REB  "since that is their lot"

This term (BDB 324, KB 322, II) is used often in Ecclesiastes but is translated in several ways (from NASB 1995):

  1. "reward" ‒ Eccl. 2:10; 5:18,19; 9:6
  2. "legacy" ‒ Eccl. 2:21
  3. "lot" ‒ Eccl. 3:22
  4. "share" ‒ Eccl. 9:6
  5. "portion" ‒ Eccl. 11:1

It refers to that which happens to an individual during his earthly life. Sometimes good, sometimes evil, sometimes fair, sometimes unfair. There is a divine but unknowable plan. Therefore, enjoy what is available to you; enjoy the simple, daily pleasures of an earthly life as they come. Humans are ignorant of the past and future. All they have is the present.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Is this chapter speaking of human actions or divine election?
  2. Does Eccl. 3:2-8 describe the life of all men or only some?
  3. How does Eccl. 3:9-11 relate to Eccl. 3:2-8?
  4. What has God put into man's heart and why is this so frustrating?
  5. What are the simple pleasures of life that God gives and why is this such an important truth in the book of Ecclesiastes?
  6. How does the phrase "under the sun" affect one's interpretation of this book?
  7. Does God really test everyone?
  8. Is the fate of men and animals different or are we simply dealing with a cynic?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:1 "Then I looked again"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:1 "Then I looked again" This reflects Eccl. 3:16.

▣ "the acts of oppression" This first verse of chapter 4 clearly shows that Solomon is not the author. He had the power to confront and correct injustice (cf. Eccl. 3:16; 5:8), but our author sees it and is helpless.

▣ "under the sun" See note about this key theological phrase at Eccl. 1:3,9. Life apart from God is "dog-eat-dog"; "me-at-any-cost"; "power-makes-right" humanity! If fallen humanity is left to itself, it will corrupt everything!

Notice the key terms

  1. "oppress"
    1. NOUN, BDB 799
    2. VERB, BDB 798, KB 897
       (1)  Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE
       (2)  Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  2. "no one to comfort," BDB 636, KB 688, Piel, ACTIVE PARTICIPLE (twice)
  3. "power," BDB 470, KB 468

▣ "they had no one to comfort them" This is speaking (cf. Eccl. 3:16; 5:8) from the governmental perspective.

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. If it is true that the vanity of all life is balanced by Qoheleth's admonition to enjoy the simple pleasures of daily life, then chapters 4 and 5 form a literary unit.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:2-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:2-3 This is such a startling statement.

  1. a hyperbole (see G. B. Caird, The Language and Imagery of the Bible)
  2. a view of pre-birth existence (cf. Job 3:11-19; Ps. 139:13-16; Jer. 1:5)

The pain and frustration of physical life without God, without hope, without help screams out! This is not the world that God intended it to be!!!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:3 "better"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:3 "better" This ADJECTIVE (BDB 373 II, KB 370 I) is used in a comparative sense throughout the book, but translated (NASB) in different ways:

  1. "enjoy yourself" (lit. "consider with goodness"), Eccl. 2:1
  2. "good," Eccl. 2:3,26 (twice); 3:12,13; 4:9; 5:18; 6:12; 7:1,11,18,20; 8:15; 9:2 (twice); 11:6,7; 12:14
  3. "better," Eccl. 2:24; 3:12,22; 4:3,6,9,13; 5:5; 6:3,9; 7:1,2,3,5,8 (twice),10; 9:4,16,18
  4. "be happy," Eccl. 7:14
  5. "pleasing," Eccl. 7:26
  6. "well," Eccl. 8:12,13
  7. "cheerful," Eccl. 9:7

Qoheleth's thought is a comparison on two levels:

  1. life here on earth
  2. the physical compared to the spiritual

Each occurrence of this ADJECTIVE must be interpreted in its context. By the way, this is true of every word!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:4 Life is a competition for food, for shelter, for work, for possessions, for honor, for control! This is the philosophy of atheistic humanism. Power makes right! This is human ego run amuck! Without God the only motive is "me"! This is where laissez faire capitalism is a human curse! This is where communism failed! Every human is envious, every human takes advantage. Every human exploits his fellow human. Life without God is a "dog-eat-dog" life of competition and unsatisfied lust for more-and-more-for-me at any cost.

This is a recurrent theme (cf. Eccl. 1:6,14,17; 2:11,17,26; 4:4,6,16; 6:9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JEALOUSY/ZEAL

▣ "striving after the wind" This is a recurrent phrase for the hopelessness of human effort apart from God (cf. Eccl. 1:6,14,17; 2:11,17,26; 4:4,6,16; 6:9). See note at Eccl. 1:6.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:5 "fool"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:5 "fool" This verse is possibly a proverb or a quote. This kind of mindless self destruction is also seen in Isa. 9:20. Lack of effort leads to destruction, but effort itself has no lasting benefit!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:6 This verse is possibly another proverb (e.g., Prov. 15:16,17; 16:8) or quote. It is meant to highlight the futility of human effort apart from God.

It is possible that "rest" (NASB; MT has "quietness," BDB 629) here represents Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 9:7-9. It so, then the workaholic and the sluggard are contrasted.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:7 This is a recurrent and theologically significant theme. See note at Eccl. 1:3,9.

4:8
NASB  "dependent"
NKJV, JPSOA  "companion"
NRSV    ——
TEV    ——
NJB  "child"
LXX, Peshitta  "a second"
REV  "a friend"

The Hebrew has "a second" (BDB 1041, KB 1604), which is simply the numeral. It can refer to almost anything. Context becomes crucial. You can see by the translations the different relationships possible.

This verse describes a "workaholic." They work for the fun of the work. Work becomes their goal and purpose in life! Work becomes their god!

▣ "his eyes were not satisfied with riches" In many ways (without God) wealth is a curse. Before long it controls us! Those who are wealthy in earthly things never seem to have enough! Life is consumed with more and more; then every effort is made to protect what is accumulated! A good modern example of this strange truth is the disaster of winning a lot of money in the lottery. Statistics show that winning destroys the winners! We need more than wealth and possessions to find true happiness and lasting "gain" (i.e., advantage, profit; see note at Eccl. 1:3). We need God. We were created by Him and for Him. Apart from Him there is no purpose or lasting joy!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:9-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:9-12 This paragraph speaks of the advantage of companionship. This is the same Hebrew term "a second" (BDB 1040, KB 1604) from Eccl. 4:8 used in Eccl. 4:9,10,11,12. Two are always better than one (BDB 25) and three better than two (cf. Eccl. 4:12b).

Another human being changes the equation. Now self is not the only issue. Now the focus and effect of the Fall are reduced. Companionship and community trump isolation and self.

  1. wife
  2. family
  3. neighbor
  4. nation

The Jewish Study Bible asserts that "three cords/strands" is imagery going back to Sumerian culture (the first writing culture of the ANE) of the third millennium B.C." p. 1611.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL FAITH IS CORPORATE

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:13 "poor"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:13 "poor" This Hebrew term (BDB 587, KB 605) is found only four times in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 4:13; 9:15 [twice],16) and means "a poor man."

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. List the areas of life the Qoheleth says is vanity.
  2. What is the meaning of Eccl. 4:2-3?
  3. Are Eccl. 4:5 and Eccl. 4:6 contradictory?
  4. What kind of man is described in Eccl. 4:8?
  5. Does the king in Eccl. 4:13 represent all places of leadership or is he a real king?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 4:13-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
4:13-16 This is so specific. It must refer to a historical incident, possibly

  1. Joseph and Pharaoh
  2. Saul and David

However, the point of the whole paragraph is the fickleness of the populace. No lasting help can come from politics. Fallen humanity cannot be governed into blessings and peace. Selfishness, corruption, and greed will permeate all!

SPECIAL TOPIC: GOVERNMENT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:1 This is verse 17 of chapter 4 in the MT. This is an affirmation of the priority of attitude. Eccl. 5:1-7 deals with warnings associated with religious worship.

NASB, NRSV  "Guard your steps"
NKJV  "Walk prudently"
TEV  "Be careful about going"
NJB  "Watch your step"
JPSOA  "Be not over eager"
REB  "Go circumspectly"
LXX  "Keep your foot"
Peshitta  "Let your conduct be seemly"

The MT has "guard your feet" (BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERATIVE), which is an idiom for proper actioins/motives (i.e., directions in life). Note this same issue spoken so powerfully in Micah 6:6-8 and Amos 5:21-24!

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

▣ "the house of God" This refers originally to the tabernacle, but later to the temple in Jerusalem.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TABERNACLE OF THE WILDERNESS

▣ "to listen" This is an important and common Hebrew term (BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT). It means "to hear so as to do." It focuses on actions, not just information (cf. Eccl. 1:8; 5:1; 7:5 [twice], 21; 9:16,17; 12:13; James 1:22-25).

SPECIAL TOPIC: LISTEN/HEAR (SHEMA)

▣ "to offer" This (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT, "give" or "set") is not the usual word for offering a sacrifice. In context it may refer to sacrifices of the lips (vows).

▣ "the sacrifice of fools" Many do religious things thinking they are right with God because of their actions. God wants a faith relationship before ritual or liturgy. The ritual is not wrong, but only meaningful when done out of faith and commitment (cf. Deut. 10:16; 1 Sam. 15:22; Prov. 21:3,27; Isa. 1:10-17; Jer. 7:22-23; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:22-24; Micah 6:6-8). To put it another way, "God looks at the heart before the hand."

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Chapters 4-5 form a literary unit. Remember, literary units are the original author(s)' way to explain and illustrate the main points of the whole book by means of literary structure.

  2. Chapter 5 begins with a number of commands (warnings) about worship:
    1. "Guard your steps," Eccl. 5:1, BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERATIVE
    2. "Do not be hasty in word," Eccl. 5:2, BDB 96, KB 111, Piel IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    3. "Impulsive in thought," Eccl. 5:2, BB 554, KB 553, Piel IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    4. "Let your words be few," Eccl. 5:2, BDB 224, KB 243, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    5. "Do not be late" (in paying a vow), Eccl. 5:4, BDB 29, KB 34, Piel IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    6. "Pay what you vow," Eccl. 5:4, BDB 1022, KB 1532, Piel IMPERATIVE
    7. "Do not say. . .," Eccl. 5:6, BDB 56, KB 65, Qal IMPERFECT, but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    8. "Fear God," Eccl. 5:7, BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERATIVE
      The paragraph, Eccl. 5:1-7, deals with proper worship attitudes and procedures. The summary command is in Eccl. 5:7 (i.e., #8).
      SPECIAL TOPIC: WORSHIP
      SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

  3. The recurrent conclusions of Qoheleth are
    1. Enjoy each day and the simple God-given pleasures of life as they come (Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).
    2. Fear God (Eccl. 1:7; 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12; 12:13) and keep His commandments (i.e., The Two Ways, cf. Eccl. 12:13)!

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:2 The three verbs in this verse are all IMPERFECTS used as JUSSIVES. Qoheleth warns of thoughtless verbosity (i.e., do not be hasty in word) in God's presence (cf. Prov. 10:19). It is not the eloquence or length of the prayer that impresses God, but the devoted and faithful heart of the one praying!

This verse, in context, may be speaking of making rash vows (cf. Eccl. 5:4; Prov. 20:25).

SPECIAL TOPIC: EFFECTIVE PRAYER

NASB, LXX  "do not be hasty"
NKJV, Peshitta  "do not be rash"
NRSV  "never be rash"
TEV    ——
NJB  "be in no hurry"

The term "hasty" (BDB 96, KB 111, Piel IMPERFECT) has a wide semantic range, but the Piel stem has only two options:

  1. "dismay," "terrify"
  2. "hasten," "make haste"

The second option (e.g., 2 Chr. 35:21; Esther 2:9) fits this context best.

▣ "God is in heaven" See SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEAVENS AND THE THIRD HEAVEN.

▣ "therefore let your words be few" This was proverbial in Israel's literature (e.g., Eccl. 6:11; Prov. 10:19; Matt. 6:7).

5:3
NASB  "For the dream comes through much effort,
  and the voice of a fool through many words"
NKJV  "For a dream comes through much activity,
  and a fool's voice is known by his many words"
NRSV  "for dreams come with many cares, and a fool's voice with many words"
TEV  "The more you worry, the more likely you are to have bad dreams,
  and the more you talk, the more likely you are to say something foolish"
NJB  "From too much worrying comes illusion,
  from too much talking, the accents of folly"

This may have been a well known proverb. It is structured as a balanced double line. The interpretive problem is the word "dream" (cf. Eccl. 5:7, BDB 321). It can refer to

  1. simply sleep (cf. Job 7:14; 20:8; Ps. 73:20)
  2. prophecies given during sleep (cf. Gen. 20:3; 28:12; 37:5,6,9,10; Num. 12:6; 1 Kgs. 3:5; Dan. 2:28)
  3. false prophecies (cf. Deut. 13:2,4,6; Jer. 23:25 [twice],27,28 [twice],32; 27:9; 29:8; Zech. 10:2)

In context, motive, not many words, is the focus of Eccl. 5:1-7. Be careful what you say to God. He takes it seriously! Fools say anything and often!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:4 "When you make a vow to God"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:4 "When you make a vow to God" This is literally, "when you vow a vow." The VERB (BDB 623, KB 674, Qal IMPERFECT) is from the same root as the NOUN (BDB 623). Vows were a covenant with God. You do this and I will do this (i.e., conditional covenant)! They were conditional promises based on certain outcomes. I personally do not believe this (foxhole religion) carries over into the New Covenant!

If you promise, do it (cf. Num. 30:2; Deut. 23:21-23; Ps. 22:25; 50:14; 56:12; 61:8; 65:1; 76:11; Prov. 20:25)! The laws concerning vows are found in Leviticus 27.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:6 This possibly refers to one trying to get out of their promise (vow).

▣
NASB, NKJV  "the messenger of God"
NRSV, NJB, JPSOA  "the messenger"
REB  "the angel of God"
TEV  "God's priest"
NET  "the priest"
Peshitta  "before God"

The KJV has "angel," but the context seems to refer to a priest (i.e., worship setting). The Hebrew word (BDB 521, 1., C) can mean

  1. "priest" (Mal. 2:7)
  2. "angel "(i.e., Ps. 103:20; 148:2)
  3. "messenger" (i.e., the name Malachi)

▣ "it was a mistake" This Hebrew NOUN (BDB 993) denotes an inadvertent sin (see NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 42, #3). It was used in Leviticus for an unintentional sin for which there was a sacrifice (cf. Lev. 4:2,22,27; 5:15,18; Num. 15:24-29).

SPECIAL TOPIC: UNINTENTIONAL SINS

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:7 Human words, though eloquent and multiplied, are vain, empty, and meaningless, be they prayers, dreams (i.e., revelations), or vows. The key is not the sacrifice or the prayer, or the vower, but the object of their address (i.e., God). An attitude of awe and respect (i.e., fear, BDB 431, KB 432, Qal IMPERATIVE) is crucial (cf. Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12,13; 12:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

▣ "dreams" See note at Eccl. 5:3.

▣ "emptiness"  See full note at Eccl. 1:2.

▣ "Rather, fear God" This (BDB 432, KB 432, Qal IMPERATIVE) is a recurrent admonition of Wisdom Literature:

  1. Job 1:1,8; 2:3; 6:14; 28:28
  2. Psalms 15:4; 25:12,14; 31:19; 34:7; 66:16; 103:11,13; 118:4
  3. Proverbs 1:7,29; 2:5; 9:10; 10:27; 14:27; 19:23; 31:30
  4. Ecclesiastes 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12-13;12:13

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:8-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:8-9 These verses pick up on the problem of social injustice (cf. Eccl. 3:16; 4:1; 8:9). The author feels helpless in the face of the pervasive corruption and injustice of government (a strong hint the author cannot be Solomon).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN GOVERNMENT

▣ "the province" See note at Eccl. 2:8.

5:9
NASB  "a king who cultivates the filed is an advantage to the land"
NKJV, Peshitta  "the profit of the land is for all;
  the king himself is served from the field"
NRSV  "this is an advantage for a land; a king for a plowed field"
TEV  "even the king depends on the harvest"
NJB  "the greatest advantage in all the land is his:
  he controls a field that is cultivated"

How do verses 8 and 9 relate to each other? This is the interpretive question. The focus is governmental injustice. Is the king the answer or is the King (God, see Leupold, p. 124) the answer!

Also, the "lasting gain" (i.e., a recurrent theme, BDB 452, cf. Eccl. 2:15; 6:8,11; 7:16; 12:9,12) is a common, shared gift from God (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26).

The Anchor Bible Commentary asserts that "king" should go with the first line (i.e., "and over them all is the king"). This is a possible meaning because the remainder of the thought is "the real wealth of a country is in its cultivated land" (p. 228).

Notice the theories:

  1. God, Himself is the answer.
  2. "Lasting gain" is only from God.
  3. God's gift of the "land" (cf. Gen. 12:13) is the source of wealth in this life for an agricultural community.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:10 "He who loves money will not be satisfied"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:10 "He who loves money will not be satisfied" Money is not the problem but love (BDB 12, KB 17, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) of money (cf. 2 Tim. 6:10). Those who make wealth priority never have enough (i.e., "satisfied," BDB 959, KB 1302, Qal IMPERFECT negated, cf. Eccl. 2:8-11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

NASB, NKJV, LXX  "abundance"
NRSV, JPSOA, Peshitta  "wealth"
TEV  "rich"
NJB  "luxury"

The Hebrew word (BDB 242, KB 250) has a wide semantic range:

  1. sound, murmur, roar
  2. sound of rain falling
  3. tumult, confusion
  4. abundance of numbers
  5. abundance of wealth

It seems that "money" and this term are in a parallel relationship. So, does it refer to:

  1. wealth
  2. crowd applause (i.e., fame)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:11 "When good things increase, those who consume them increase"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 5:11 "When good things increase, those who consume them increase" The phrase "good things" (BDB 375 III, KB 370-372) is purposely ambiguous to cover a range of "good things." When increase (BDB 915 I, KB 1176, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) comes, consumers increase (BDB 912, KB 1174, Qal PERFECT). More of a thing means more workers to help make, distribute, and protect "the thing." More of something often causes the profit margin of the owner to decrease. Is more better?!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:12 "sleep of the working man is pleasant. . .but"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:12 "sleep of the working man is pleasant. . .but" The wealthy are always afraid of losing what is theirs, while the poor man is content with what little he has. Where then is the lasting value?

Again Qoheleth returns to a familiar theme: "enjoy the moment," "smell the roses along the way," "happiness is found in the simple, free, daily life experiences of humans" (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).

Sleep (BDB 445, KB 447) is a gift from God (cf. Ps. 4:8; 127:2; Prov. 3:24; 6:22). Those who do not trust God devise evil on their beds instead of sleeping (cf. Ps. 36:4; Prov. 4:16; Micah 2:1). Earthly possessions rob the owners of sleep (e.g., Prov. 11:28; 18:10-12; 28:11; 30:8-9). The wealthy constantly worry about

  1. losing their wealth
  2. getting more!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:13-16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:13-16 Riches are transitory and temporal. Although one can accumulate much wealth, one can also lose it, and all will leave it behind because humans can take nothing physical into the next life (cf. Eccl. 5:15-17). Riches promise much, but often cannot fulfill the expectation.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

5:13
NASB, NIV, Peshitta  "a grievous evil"
NKJV  "a severe evil"
NRSV  "a grievous ill"
NJB  "grossly unjust"
JPSOA  "a grave evil"
LXX  "an infirmity"

This phrase involves two Hebrew terms:

  1. an ADJECTIVE, BDB 317, KB 316 (the NOUN which denotes an illness or weakness), meaning "severe" or "sore" (cf. Eccl. 5:13,16 and similar form in Eccl. 6:2)
  2. the NOUN, BDB 949, KB 1262 which denotes "evil" (the basic root), "misery," or "distress"

This phrase occurs several times in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 2:17; 5:12,15; 6:1; 10:5).

The term "evil" (BDB 949) is used in Ecclesiastes in several senses. Note NASB and NIV translations.

    NASB NIV
1. Eccl. 1:13 "grievous task" "heavy burden"
2 Eccl. 2:17 "grievous" "grievous"
3. Eccl. 4:3 "evil activity" "evil that is done"
4. Eccl. 4:8 "grievous task" "miserable business"
5. Eccl. 5:1 "doing evil" "do wrong"
6. Eccl. 5:14 "bad investment" "some misfortune"
7. Eccl. 6:2 "sore affliction" "grievous task"
8. Eccl. 8:3 "an evil matter" "for a bad cause"
9. Eccl. 8:5 "trouble" "harm"
10. Eccl. 8:9 "to his hurt" "to his own hurt"
11. Eccl. 8:11 "an evil deed" "to do wrong"
12. Eccl. 8:12 "does evil" "crimes"
13. Eccl. 9:2 "the wicked" "the bad"
14. Eccl. 9:3 "evil" (twice) "evil" (twice)
15. Eccl. 9:12 "treacherous net" "cruel net"
16. Eccl. 10:5 "an evil" "an evil"
17. Eccl. 10:13 "wicked" "wicked"
18. Eccl. 12:14 "evil" "evil"

By this limited comparison you can quickly see the range of meanings for this common NOUN. Qoheleth uses it again and again. He saw this world as sick and unjust because of fallen humanity bent toward self and the terrible exploitation of each other.

5:14
NASB  "a bad investment"
NKJV, NIV  "misfortune"
NRSV, Peshitta  "a bad venture"
TEV  "some bad evil"
NJB, JPSOA  "unlucky venture"

This term (BDB 775, KB 857) is used several times only in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 2:23,26; 3:10; 4:8; 5:3,14; 8:16). Its basic meaning is "task." The NASB translates it as

  1. "task," Eccl. 1:13; 2:23,26; 3:10; 4:8; 8:16
  2. "effort," Eccl. 5:3
  3. "investment," Eccl. 5:14

The NIV translates it as

  1. "burden," Eccl. 1:13; 3:10
  2. "work," Eccl. 2:23
  3. "task," Eccl. 2:26
  4. "business," Eccl. 4:8
  5. "cares," Eccl. 5:3
  6. "misfortune," Eccl. 5:14
  7. "labor," Eccl. 8:16

BDB and KB offer two suggestions on its meaning in Eccl. 5:13

  1. a bad business
  2. a bad affair

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:17 "eats in darkness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:17 "eats in darkness" This phrase refers to (1) a workaholic, (2) a stingy man, or (3) someone once wealthy, but now poor!

The term "darkness" (BDB 365, KB 361; see NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 313-314, #5) is used in several senses in Ecclesiastes and Wisdom Literature:

  1. literal, Eccl. 2:13; Job 26:10 (i.e., day vs. night)
  2. ignorance, Eccl. 2:14; Job 37:19
  3. distress, Eccl. 5:17; 11:8; Job 15:22,23,30; 20:26; 22:11; 23:17; 29:3; Ps. 107:10,14; 112:4
  4. obscurity, Eccl. 6:4 [twice]

The UBS Text Project, p. 578, suggests that this difficult Hebrew phrase means "he eats in obscurity because he lacks even a lamp to give light for his meals."

NASB  "great vexation"
NKJV  "much sorrow"
NRSV, JPSOA  "much vexation"
TEV  "grief"
NJB  "mourning, many sorrows"
NIV  "great frustration"
Peshitta  "much anger"

The term (BDB 494, KB 491, Qal PERFECT with waw) denotes an anger or frustration (cf. Ps. 112:10). It is used twice in Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 5:17; 7:9). It is often used in Scripture for YHWH: in Deut. 4:25; 9:18; 31:29; 32:16,21(twice); Ps. 78:58; 106:29; Jer. 7:18,19; 8:19; 11:17; 25:6,7; 32:29,30,32; 44:3,8.

There are several Hebrew texts that have been suggested (see UBS Hebrew Text Project, v. 3, pp. 577-578. They all understand the phrase in slightly different ways. But all agree the list describes the individual who does not take into account God's presence, gifts, and plan.

  1. lives in darkness
  2. great frustration
  3. sickness
  4. anger

All humans experience the same feelings and hopes but only those who know, trust, and believe have peace, joy, and lasting advantage!

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANTHROPOMORPHIC LANGUAGE USED TO DESCRIBE GOD, C.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:18-19 "to eat, to drink and enjoy oneself in all one's labor. . .which God has given him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:18-19 "to eat, to drink and enjoy oneself in all one's labor. . .which God has given him" Notice the contrast between Eccl. 5:17 and 18! We need to be content with

  1. knowing God
  2. enjoying what He has provided daily (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 8:15; 9:7-9)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

5:18
NASB, NKJV, NRSV  "good and fitting
TEV  "here is what I have found out"
NJB  "so my conclusion is this"
JPSOA  "real good"
Peshitta  "good and comely"
LXX  "good"

The literal phrase is, "what I have seen myself to be good which is beautiful."

The term "good" (BDB 373 II, KB 370-372) is used often in Ecclesiastes (45 times), but translated in several different ways (i.e., Eccl. 2:1, 3, 24 [twice], 26 [twice]).

The second term (BDB 421, KB 423) is literally "beautiful." It occurs eight times in Song of Songs. The NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 495 asserts that it is only in Ecclesiastes that this term means "proper" (cf. Eccl. 3:11; 5:18), which makes it parallel to "good." Remember words only have meaning in a given context. How and why Qoheleth changes the regular meanings (given in other Wisdom books) is uncertain.

NASB  "his reward" [margin "share"]
NKJV  "his heritage"
NRSV, NIV  "our lot"
TEV  "our fate"
NJB  "the lot of humanity"
JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "his portion"

This is a common Hebrew term (BDB 324, KB 322 II) with a wide semantic range, but it is used in Ecclesiastes for temporal benefits for the labor of one who recognizes and respects God's presence and His gifts (cf. Eccl. 2:10,21; 3:22; 5:18,19; 9:6,9; 11:2).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 5:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
5:19 There are two Hebrew VERBS in this context translated "give":

  1. BDB 678, KB 733, Qal PERFECT, very common VERB, cf. Eccl. 2:26 (twice); 5:18,19; 6:2; 11:2; 12:11. God has given wealth and possessions.
  2. BDB 1020, KB 1521, Hiphil PERFECT, much rarer VERB which denotes giving power or enabling, Eccl. 2:19; 5:19; 6:2; 8:9

This second VERB is followed by three Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS that describe what God has given those who respect and obey Him. Eccl. 5:18-20 is similar to Eccl. 2:24-26:

  1. to eat, BDB 37, KB 46
  2. to receive his reward (lit. "to lift"), BDB 669, KB 724
  3. to rejoice in his labor, BDB 970, KB 1333

This series is parallel to Eccl. 5:18:

  1. to eat, BDB 37, KB 46, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  2. to drink, BDB 1059, KB 1667, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  3. to enjoy (lit. "to see"), BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT

▣ "man" This is the generic term for mankind from "adam" (BDB 9, KB 14). It is often used synonymously with ish (BDB 35, KB 43, cf. Eccl. 6:2; Isa. 2:9).

5:20
NASB, NRSV, NIV  "God keeps him occupied"
NKJV, JPSOA  "god keeps him busy"
TEV     ——
NJB  "God keeps his heart occupied"
REB  "God fill is time"

The one VERBAL (BDB 772 I, KB 854 III, Hiphil PARTICIPLE means "to keep someone busy" [from KB]. This same root is used in Eccl. 1:13; 3:10 and translated "task." God gives both "the grievous task" and the relief from it! Again the worldview (i.e., "under the sun"), life without God, brings vanity and meaninglessness, but the worldview of awe, respect, truth, and obedience brings a God-given joy in one's daily labors and family life irresptective of a person's wealth, wisdom, or fame. What a wonderful promise and truth.

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Ecclesiastes 6:1 through 8:15 may be a loosely structured literary unit.

  2. Chapter 6 begins with the folly of (hyperboles):
    1. riches, Eccl. 6:2
    2. many children, Eccl. 6:3
    3. long life, Eccl. 6:6

  3. The reason for the folly is:
    1. the never-ending cycle of human existence
    2. the fact that fallen humanity is never satisfied with physical things (cf. chapters 1-2)

  4. The important question about the meaning of life is asked again in Eccl. 6:12 (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 3:9; 5:16). What does it all mean? Where is the lasting profit/advantage (see note at Eccl. 1:3)?

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

6:1
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, JPSOA, LXX, Peshitta  "an evil"
TEV  "a serious injustice"
NJB, NIV  "another evil"

This is the Hebrew term (BDB 948 II, KB 1250 I) that has been used often by Qoheleth. It starts Eccl. 6:1 (evil) and closes Eccl. 6:2. See note at Eccl. 2:21 and especially at Eccl. 5:13.

▣ "under the sun" This is referring to human values and perspectives only. See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

NASB  "it is prevalent"
NKJV, Peshitta  "it is common"
NRSV  "it lies heavy"
NJB  "which goes hard with people"
LXX  "it is abundant"
REB, NIV  "it weighs heavily"
JPSOA  "a grave one"

This is the ADJECTIVE (BDB 915 I, KB 1176) and a DEMONSTRATIVE ADJECTIVE (BDB 214). As the translations show there are two ways to interpret this phrase:

  1. The evil is common to all humans. (Peshitta)
  2. The evil weighs heavily on humans (MT).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:2 "a man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:2 "a man" This is not the term adam (BDB 9), as in Eccl. 5:19, but ish (BDB 35). These two terms for humanity have

  1. slightly different root meanings
  2. significant semantic overlap

In Ecclesiastes they are synonymous (cf. 2 Kgs. 7:10).

▣ "God has given" This refers to the sovereignty of God in human life and daily affairs (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:14; 5:19). However, His activity is exactly opposite to traditional wisdom (cf. Job's three friends). Mosaic revelation promised abundance for covenant obedience (cf. Leviticus 26; Deutrtonomy 28; 30:15,19), but Qoheleth had seen the prosperity of the wicked (cf. Psalm 73). The traditional theology of "the two ways" did not cover all of life (cf. Job).

▣ "riches. . .wealth. . .honor" See 2 Chr. 1:11, which shows that these things are the desires of all humans. We think these things will make us happy so we pursue them with all our strength and mental focus, but they do not, cannot (i.e., Jer. 9:23-24)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

▣ "God has given. . .God has not empowered" Notice the active presence of God. In Eccl. 5:19 this presence is a blessing ("given" and "empowered"), but here the blessing of material possessions is not balanced with the wisdom to enjoy them! Things, without inner peace, do not bring happiness, contentment, satisfaction, or lasting benefit!

We need to:

  1. enjoy daily life, whatever it may bring (i.e., Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18-20; 7:7-9)
  2. trust in eternal life, whenever and however physical life ceases (i.e., Eccl. 1:3; 3:9; 5:16; 6:11)
  3. honor God (cf. Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12)!
  4. obey God (cf. Eccl. 12:13)!

▣ "soul lacks nothing of all that he desires" See Ps. 17:14; 73:7; Luke 12:19. For notes on nephesh (i.e., soul) see Lev. 17:11 and Gen. 35:18 online.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

▣ "to eat from" This is imagery meaning "to enjoy." Humans work hard but do not enjoy the fruit of their labors.

▣ "foreigner" This (BDB 648, KB 700 II) can refer to

  1. war/invasion
  2. one who is not related by birth (JPSOA)
  3. imagery of the frailty of wealth in this world

In Israel's history it refers to Moses' curses of covenant disobedience in Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28.

NASB  "sore affliction"
NKJV  "an evil affliction"
NRSV  "a grievous evil"
TEV  "just isn't right"
NJB  "grievous suffering"
LXX  "an evil infirmity"
REB  "a dire affliction"
JPSOA  "a grievous ill"
Peshitta  "an evil disease"

This is made up of a NOUN and an ADJECTIVE.

  1. NOUN, BDB 318, KB 318, meaning sickness, cf. Eccl. 5:16; Deut. 28:59,61; Isa. 53:4
  2. ADJECTIVE, BDB 948 I, KB 1250-1253, meaning injury or wrong. See note at Eccl. 5:13.

Life is unfair and unpredictable, yet God is actively present. In the Semitic proverb genre called "role reversal" the same occurs. The seeming prosperity of the wicked (so common in our world) will change (cf. Psalm 73). Lasting happiness and contentment sought after so diligently by godless humans will not bring lasting satisfaction. A righteous God will act, will judge, will right the wrongs of this life (cf. Job).

▣ "vanity"  See note at Eccl. 1:2.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:3 "hundred children"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:3 "hundred children" This is hyperbolic and refers to the harems of royalty or the wealthy. Children are a great blessing from God (cf. Ps. 127:3-5), but they cannot provide a lasting benefit (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:18).

▣ "lives many years" Long life is also a great blessing from God (cf. Prov. 3:16), but it cannot provide a lasting benefit (cf. Eccl. 6:6).

▣ "he does not have proper burial" In Hebrew this can refer to an elaborate funeral. Not to be buried properly was a sign of shame (cf. 1 Kgs. 14:13; 2 Kgs. 9:10,35; Ps. 79:3; Eccl. 6:3; Isa. 14:19-20; Jer. 8:2; 14:16; 16:4; 23:33).

SPECIAL TOPIC: CRUCIFIXION, IV.

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

▣ "Better the miscarriage than he" This is based on the life of a man mentioned in Eccl. 6:1-3. This world's goods and honors (cf. chapters 1-2) do not, by themselves, bring happiness or lasting benefit (cf. Eccl. 4:3). Life without God is not authentic life!

The term "miscarriage" (BDB 658, KB 711) can mean

  1. abortive birth, cf. Job 3:16; Ps. 58:8; NRSV
  2. untimely (i.e., early or late) birth (RSV)

Number 1 fits this context best (cf. Eccl. 4:3).

For "better" see notes at Eccl. 5:18 and 7:1.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:3-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:3-6 The paragraph gives several specific examples which seem to go against traditional wisdom teachings. A man may have

  1. many children (i.e., sexual pleasure and descendants)
  2. a long lifetime (i.e., health and many experiences)
  3. he will find no satisfaction (i.e., no lasting advantage, cf. Eccl. 1:3)
  4. his life has been vain, empty, meaningless (cf. Eccl. 1:2)

Almost as an aside, Qoheleth mentions, "no proper burial," which was very important to Jewish people. The word "proper" is not in the Hebrew text. Even if he had had a proper burial without lasting benefit, he would not be satisfied! Preparation for the afterlife is not made at death, but through life!

The NET Bible has an interesting take on this line (p. 1129). It sees it as related to the previous line and referring to an extended life. It mentions Ps. 49:9 and 89:48 as other examples of this poetic parallelism. I think this interpretation is surely possible and fits the immediate context well!

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SEXUALITY

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN AGING

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:4-5 "it"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:4-5 "it" This refers to the untimely birth of Eccl. 6:3.

  1. Its birth is in vain.
  2. It goes into obscurity (darkness).
  3. Its name is covered in obscurity (darkness).
  4. It never sees the sun (i.e., light).
  5. It never has wisdom.
  6. It is better off!

What a pessimistic view of human life! This challenges OT Wisdom teaching! This author wants us to walk to the brink of existence and look straight into the empty nothingness of atheistic humanism!

For "darkness" see note at Eccl. 5:17.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:5 "never sees the sun"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:5 "never sees the sun" This is an idiom for human life (cf. Ps. 58:8; Eccl. 6:5; 7:11), someone who experiences life on this planet.

▣
NASB, JPSOA  "it is better off than he"
NKJV  "this has more rest than that man"
NRSV  "yet it finds rest rather than he"
TEV  "but at least it has found rest"
NJB  "it will rest more easily than that person"
LXX, Peshitta  "yet this one has more rest than the other"

The "it" refers to the child of untimely birth, which is contrasted with the man who has wealth and honor, but no peace, Eccl. 6:1-3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:6 "thousand years"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:6 "thousand years" This is a symbol of fullness or completeness.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THOUSAND (eleph)

▣ "do not all go to one place" This refers to the common fate of all living things, Sheol (cf. Eccl. 2:14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD? I. B.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:7-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:7-9 This may be poetry (cf. NJB). The parallel lines would be:

  1. all animals toil just to eat (cf. Gen. 3:17-19); yet they can never eat enough to give lasting satisfaction (i.e., they get hungry again), Eccl. 6:7
  2. both the wise and the foolish are caught up in the trials and problems of a fallen world. The second line is uncertain; it seems to give an advantage (i.e., "street smarts") to the poor man who has to perpetually cope with less, Eccl. 6:8
  3. all humans want more than they have, yet when they have much (i.e., chapters 1-2) it is still not enough (i.e., vanity, futility, see note at Eccl. 1:14), Eccl. 6:9

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:8 "advantage"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:8 "advantage" This term (BDB 452, KB 404 cf. Eccl. 6:8,11) is a recurrent key word in Ecclesiastes. See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

▣ "the wise man have over the fool?" There is a helpful comment in NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 1282.

"He queries whether there is any quantitative 'better' that distinguishes sage from fool, righteous from wicked, human from beast. Both wise and foolish must die, and neither is remembered for long. Ultimately, even wisdom is futile (2:12-17; 6:8)."

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:10 "named"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:10 "named" This is either:

  1. a reference to the naming of the animals by Adam, showing his dominion or authority over them (cf. Gen. 2:19-20)
  2. a reference to man being named "Adam" from the Hebrew Adamah (cf. Gen. 2:18-25)
  3. However, in this context it is not the naming of Adam or Adam naming the animals that is the focus, but the repetitive cycle (cf. Eccl. 1:9; 3:15) of humans naming things. This naming was, in a sense, an act of power and authority. Adam had dominion (cf. Gen. 1:28-30), but lost it (i.e., Genesis 3).

▣ "for he cannot dispute with him who is stronger than he is" The "him who is stronger" can refer to:

  1. another human (i.e., one person seeks justice from a physically or socially stronger person, cf. NJB)
  2. imagery of the cycles of time, which have already named everything (over and over)
  3. God (cf. Job 9:32; 40:2; Isa. 45:9)

Number 3 fits the context best.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:11 "many words which increase futility"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:11 "many words which increase futility" The INFINITIVE "many" (BDB 915 I, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) and the PARTICIPLE "increase" (BDB 915 I, KB 1176, Hiphil PARTICIPLE) are word plays on the same Hebrew root, which means, "make much" or "make great."

Israel's Wisdom tradition counseled speaking few words (cf. Prov. 10:19 and Eccl. 5:2-3), because words quickly reveal the person's character and motives.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH

▣ "advantage" This is a major theological issue in Ecclesiastes. See full nte at Eccl. 1:3.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:11-12 Human disputation, either with God or one another, cannot solve the problem of meaningless life without hope.

The famous question of Ecclesiastes is, "What then is the advantage to a man?" This is a repeat of Eccl. 1:3; 2:11,22; 3:9; 5:16! Without a God of justice and mercy there is no joy, benefit, or lasting satisfaction! Life can be good or hard, but what is beyond? Is there a qualitative difference between the fate of a person of faith versus a self-seeking, wicked person?

Human life is fleeting (i.e., like a shadow, cf. Eccl. 8:13; 1 Chr. 29:15; Job 9:9; 14:2; Ps. 102:11; 109:23; 144:4). Human life is a laborious toil. What does the future hold? This is the question (cf. Eccl. 3:22; 7:14; 8:7; 10:14). Is there a fair, just, merciful, unchanging God whose promises can be depended on? This is the faith issue of human existence!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 6:12 "who"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
6:12 "who" Notice there are two questions introduced with "who."

▣ "like a shadow" In this context "shadow" (BDB 853) is used as imagery for the fleeting transitoriness of human life (cf. 1 Chr. 29:15; Job 8:9; 14:1-2; Ps. 102:11; 109:23; 144:4; Eccl. 6:12; 8:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW, SHADE

▣ "under the sun" This is a key phrase in my understanding of how to interpret this book. See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Is this chapter an attack on riches and honor?
  2. How can death or non-existence be preferred to life?
  3. List the ways this chapter teaches the sovereignty of God.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:1 "A good name is better than a good ointment"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:1 "A good name is better than a good ointment" It is the word "good" (BDB 373 II, KB 372), often translated "better" (see BDB 373-375), that links chapters 6 and 7 together (cf. Eccl. 6:3,9,12 and 7:1[twice], 2,3,5, 8[twice], 10, 11,14,18,20,26; often translated as the comparison, "better"; see note at Eccl. 5:18). The interpretative question is, "Where is 'the good' found?"

Gor "better" see full note at Eccl. 4:3.

▣ "A good name" This refers to a godly character and lifestyle through time (cf. Prov. 22:1; Hebrews 11). Who we are (i.e., people of faith) is more important than what we have or do not have!

▣ "good ointment" Good ointment (BDB 1032, KB 1568) is in a contrasting relationship to "good name." Ointment can refer to:

  1. an outward appearance (TEV, "expensive perfume")
  2. a need for healing and restoration
  3. a time of festival (i.e., anointing oneself)

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

▣ "the day of one's death is better" This must be linked with Eccl. 7:1a in regard to the foolishness and destruction (temporal and eschatological) of inappropriate living.

In Eccl. 9:4 life is affirmed, so don't jump to conclusions or proof-text this book!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:1-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:1-10 The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1614, has an interesting comment on vv. 1-10.

"The chapter begins with a section of proverbs, the longest part of which, as in 4.3; 6.3-4, is arranged in a series of 'better than' comparisons concerning wisdom and folly. Wisdom, here in line with 4.2 (cf. 4.3; 6.3-6), is what recognizes that the only certain thing in life is its end, death; fools, on the contrary, focus on life and its illusury pleasures of laughter and feasting."

Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. This chapter, as much of Ecclesiastes, reflects "the two ways" of life (e.g., Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:1,15,19; Psalm 1).
    1. obey the covenant and be blessed by God

    8. Eccl. 7:17, "do not be excessively wicked," BDB 957, KB 1294, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    9. Eccl. 7:17, "do not be a fool," BDB 224, KB 243, Qal JUSSIVE

    11. Eccl. 7:21, "take seriously," BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (lit. "give your heart")
    12. Eccl. 7:23, "be wise," BDB 314, KB 314, Qal COHORTATIVE
    13. Eccl. 7:27, "behold," BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE (lit. "see")
    14. Eccl. 7:29, "behold," BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE (lit. "see")

    17. Eccl. 8:3, "do not join in," BDB 763, KB 840, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense (lit. "stand" or "stop")

  3. The UBS Translator's Handbook on Ecclesiastes (p. 214) asserts that the last two rhetorical questions of Eccl. 6:12 are answered in Eccl. 7:1-14.
    1. 6:12a is answered in Eccl. 7:1-12
    2. 6:12b is linked to 7:13-14 by the phrase "after him" (BDB 29)
     This gives a contextual relationship for interpretation that attempts to follow the intent of the original inspired author. Only the original author (and in some cases, editors) are inspired. No modern preacher, teacher or individual is inspired. They are illumined by the Holy Spirit to understand the major truths and especially gospel implications. Modern interpreters may disagree, but Scripture does not contradict itself. This last statement is tricky to make with a book like Ecclesiastes, where a tongue-in-cheek critique of human culture and life devoid of God is presented! Qoheleth is stating things purposefully in a way that challenges traditional wisdom teaching to help his readers think about the unfairness and injustice so prevalent in this fallen world. Theological, pithy statements do not cover all circumstances!
