    SPECIAL TOPIC: ILLUMINATION

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:2 "house of mourning"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:2 "house of mourning" "House of. . ." (lit. Beth, BDB 108, KB 124 I) is a Semitic idiom (cf. Eccl. 7:4, i.e., Bethel, Bethlehem) used as an ADJECTIVE.

All of the contrasts ("better than. . .") of this chapter are based on the conclusion summary of Eccl. 7:8a. Since life is vanity, its end is preferred to its beginning. 

The NOUN "end" (BDB 693, KB 746) is used only five times in the OT and three of them are in Ecclesiastes:

  1. Eccl. 3:11
  2. Eccl. 7:2
  3. Eccl. 12:13

Qoheleth focuses on the mystery of knowing God and trying to understand His plans and purposes for mankind, but he knows well the inevitable end (i.e., every organic thing becomes inorganic again, i.e., dust-to-dust awaits us all).

▣ "house of feasting" Literally "house of drinking" (BDB 1059, KB 1667 II, cf. Esther 3:15; 7:1) refers to a party event like the birth of a child or a wedding. These two phrases are parallel in Eccl. 7:2-5.

▣ "Because that is the end of every man" Riotous living tends to cause us to live in unreality concerning the common, certain and sudden end of human life (TEV). Pleasure tends to be an emotional, temporary opiate.

▣ "the living takes it to heart" This phrase can have several meanings:

  1. Only the living can understand and have wisdom, not the dead.
  2. The living should reflect on the reality of their own eventual mortality.
  3. The wise ones think about these things (similar to "let him who has an ear hear" of the NT).

If #2 or #3 is correct, then the VERB (BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERFECT) may be functioning as a JUSSIVE.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:3 "Sorrow is better than laughter"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:3 "Sorrow is better than laughter" This parallels Eccl. 7:2. Suffering often brings one to God, while pleasure seldom does (cf. Matt. 5:1; 2 Cor. 7:10). Suffering can have a positive spiritual benefit (e.g., Heb. 5:8; Rom. 5:3-5)!

For "better" see full note at Eccl. 4:3.

SPECIAL TOPIC: SUFFERING (NT)

NASB, JPSOA  "for when a face is sad a heart may be happy"
NKJV  "for by a sad countenance the heart is made better"
NRSV, Peshitta  "for by sadness of countenance the heart is made glad"
TEV  "it may sadden your face, but sharpen your understanding"
NJB  "a joyful heart may be concealed behind sad looks"
NET  "because sober reflection is good for the heart"

In context Qoheleth is

  1. saying that life's difficulties have the potential to awaken a spiritual dimension (TEV). This is the focus of Deuteronomy 27-28, as well as the plagues of Egypt that caused some Egyptians to believe in YHWH (cf. Exod. 12:38); similarly the "seals" and "trumpets" judgments of the book of Revelation.
  2. contrasting the feelings of the immediate (daily life) with the world view of eternity. This life makes us sad; all of us have problems in this world, but if we have faith and obedience, even these sad times give us hope, peace, and strength.

The author is not condemning happiness. Just the opposite, he is advocating an appropriate peace and contentment that is not based on temporal circumstances alone. A book outside the Bible that has helped me in this area is Hannah Whithall Smith's The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "sad" This term (BDB 947, KB 1250-1252) usually means "evil" or "bad," but in a few places it has the connoation of sadness (cf. Neh. 2:2; Prov. 25:20). Context determines meaning!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:4-5
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:4-5 Verses 4 and 5 parallel verses 2 and 3.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY, III. A. #1

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:5 "the rebuke of a wise man"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:5 "the rebuke of a wise man" The term "rebuke" (BDB 172, KB 199) is from the Aramaic verb "cry out." The Bible records two kinds of rebukes:

  1. from God, Job 26:11; Ps. 18:15; 39:11; 76:6; 80:16; 104:7; 106:9; Isa. 50:2; 51:20; 66:5,15
  2. from other humans, Prov. 13:1,8; 17:10; Eccl. 7:5; Isa. 30:17 (twice, NASB, "threat"). It is alluded to in Ps. 141:5; Prov. 6:23; 13:18; 15:31-33; 25:12; Eccl. 9:17.

Rebukes are unpleasant, but a wise person hears and heeds the words of rebuke from a biblically informed person rather than flattering words from a worldly person. This type of pithy statement of truth is common in Proverbs (e.g., Prov. 12:15; 13:14; 25:12).

▣ "the song of fools" This refers to a pleasure oriented life. It is parallel to "laughter of fools" in Eccl. 7:6.

For the term "fool" (BDB 493 I) see SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE (terms)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:6 "the crackling of thorn bushes under a pot"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:6 "the crackling of thorn bushes under a pot" Thorn bushes make poor cooking fires. They burn too hot and too fast (cf. Ps. 58:9; 118:12). There is a Hebrew sound play between "thorn" and "pot." As the fire promises a needed outcome (i.e., cooked food) and cannot deliver, so too, the laughter of fools is deceptive!

▣ "laughter" The term "laughter" (BDB 966, KB 1315) is used often in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 2:2; 3:4; 7:3,5,6). It is used as imagery of the person who seeks instant gratification. It denotes life that focuses on the pleasure of this life in an existential moment, but does not ponder the "lasting benefit."

▣ "futility" For the full note, see Eccl. 1:2.

7:7
NASB, NKJV, NRSV, REB  "oppression"
NJB  "oppressed desires"
TEV, JPSOA  "cheat"
Peshitta, NEB  "slander"
LXX  "extortion"
JPSOA footnote  "riches" (emendation)

This NOUN (BDB 799, KB 897) in this context means "defraud" or "gain by extortion." The JPSOA suggests an emendation to "riches."

  1. oppress ‒ עשׁק
  2. riches ‒ עשׁר

The injustice of life causes many people (even believers) problems (cf. Eccl. 4:1; 5:8) if we don't allow God time to set it straight; sometimes it is not until the afterlife.

▣ "bribe" This is not the normal word for "bribe" (BDB 1005, cf. Exod. 23:8; Deut. 16:19), but is the word "gift" (NJB, BDB 682, KB 655 I), used in a specialized sense (cf. Prov. 15:27). Forms of this same root denoting "a gift" are also found in Eccl. 3:13; 5:19.

It must be recognized that Eccl. 7:7 does not fit into the context easily. The NKJV and NJB see it as relating to the previous verses (i.e., 5-7). From Eccl. 7:1 the text has been referring to how wise men think. However, fallen humanity (i.e., oppression and bribery) can affect even the wise. Wisdom is reflected in how one lives, not just how one thinks.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:8 "The end of a matter is better than its beginning"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:8 "The end of a matter is better than its beginning" This may be (1) a summary statement or (2) related to Eccl. 7:1 about a good name which is acquired with time and must be maintained. Often we judge something or someone too quickly and are disappointed.

▣ "Patience of spirit is better" Verse 8, second line, contrasts two kinds of people by the repeated use of "spirit" (BDB 924, KB 1197, cf. Eccl. 7:9), often translated "breath," "wind," or "spirit" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT). It is imagery for the life of a person. Here there are two kinds of people contrasted:

  1. "Patient," literally "long" (BDB 74, KB 88). This is often used in Proverbs for a person slow to anger (cf. Prov. 14:29; 15:18; 16:32; 19:11). However, its most common usage describes YHWH's merciful character (see SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD [OT], cf. Exod. 34:6; Num. 14:18; Neh. 9:17; Ps. 86:15; 103:8; 145:8; Joel 2:13; Nahum 1:3).
  2. "Haughtiness," literally "high" (BDB 147, KB 171; see SPECIAL TOPIC: LIFTED UP), used of a haughty spirit (ruach).

Notice the other anthropomorphic usages of "high" (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 798)

  1. literally, of tree, but tree as a haughty person, Isa. 10:33
  2. imagery for an arrogant mouth, 1 Sam. 2:3
  3. haughty heart, Prov. 16:15
  4. haughty eyes, Ps. 101:5; Isa. 5:15

People of faith are meant to emulate YHWH. People of faith are encouraged to take the long look, not only the immediate (cf. Eccl. 7:10). The attitude with which people of faith face life is a powerful witness (cf. Prov. 16:32; Gal. 5:22; Eph. 4:2).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:9-10 See Contextual Insight B.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:9 "Do not be eager in your heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:9 "Do not be eager in your heart" The VERB is "eager" (BDB 96, KB 111, Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense, cf. Eccl. 5:2, "do not be hasty in word").

The phrase "heart" is literally "in your spirit." Notice how ruach is used to describe several kinds of people:

  1. "the patient in spirit," Eccl. 7:8
  2. "the haughty in spirit," Eccl. 7:8
  3. "the quick in spirit," Eccl. 7:9

SPECIAL TOPIC: SPIRIT IN THE BIBLE

▣ "angry" The term "angry" (BDB 495, KB 491, cf. Eccl. 5:16; 7:9) is translated "sorrow" in Eccl. 7:3 (also note Eccl. 1:18; 2:23; 11:10). The "slow to anger" God of Eccl. 7:8 can also be angry (e.g., 1 Kgs. 14:9,15; 16:33; 22:54; 2 Kgs. 17:11; 23:19). However, God is angry over human rebellion, but human anger is sparked by self-interest. This emotion quickly reveals the fallenness of humanity (cf. Prov. 14:17; 16:32; James 1:19).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:10 Humans without a sense of God's presence and purpose in their daily lives often seek peace by reflecting on positive circumstances from the past! (i.e. the "good old days")! However, they

  1. cannot be reclaimed
  2. were not that "good" to begin with
  3. often reflect a fallen view of "good"

God is in the mysterious process of molding His covenant partners into the "people of God." This takes time (patience) and faith (i.e., Rom. 5:3-4)! Focusing on human experiences long since past causes one to stumble in the present!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:11-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:11-14 There are several key terms in interpreting this section:

  1. "good" (BDB 373 II, see note at Eccl. 2:26)
  2. "advantage" (BDB 452, see note at Eccl. 1:3)
  3. "the sun" (BDB 1039, see note at Eccl. 1:3)

"Good" and "advantage" point toward more than just a happy life here and now. Happiness and contentment have two foci:

  1. now ("wisdom" and "inheritance," both from previous generations)
  2. afterlife ("under the sun," "see the sun")

However, they are tied together. Our afterlife is affected by physical life now! Verse 12 explains Eccl. 7:11 and relates to this life, while Eccl. 7:13 and 14 relate to God's active presence in this temporal realm, but also to the implication of His continuing presence and care. He is sovereign and He is with us and for us, even when circumstances seem to scream the opposite. If the believer's joy and peace are based on physical blessings (traditional OT wisdom teaching) they can be removed or changed in a moment! No, the eyes of faith take the long look (cf. Eccl. 7:8,10) and trust in God.

I hope as a reader you recognize that my understanding of "under the sun" permeates all of my interpretations of this book. It is a basic presupposition, bias, a priori! Every commentator has these presuppositions (i.e., theological glasses). The first place to analyze an interpretation is the basic presuppositions of the interpreter. All of us have them, you know!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:12 "wisdom. . .knowledge"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:12 "wisdom. . .knowledge" These two terms are in a parallel relationship. Both are inaccessible by human effort. They come only from the hand of God.

▣ "protection" This is the Hebrew word for "shadow" (BDB 853), which offers protection in the desert (e.g., Ps. 17:8; 36:7; 57:1; 61:4; 63:7; 91:1,4). The term "shadow" was used

  1. in the sense of brevity in Eccl. 6:12 and 8:13
  2. here it is used in the sense of God's personal presence and protection (like the Exodus)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW AS A METAPHOR FOR PROTECTION AND CARE

▣ "the advantage" See full note at Eccl. 1:3.

▣ "wisdom preserves the lives of its possessors" Longevity is connected to

  1. the will of a sovereign God
  2. the choices of human beings (cf. Eccl. 7:17; Job 22:16; Ps. 55:23; Prov. 10:27)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:13 "to straighten"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:13 "to straighten" This VERBAL (BDB 1075, KB 1784) occurs in the OT only three times, all in Ecclesiastes. The first two have it contrasted with "crooked" (cf. Eccl. 1:15, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT; 7:13, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT). It is used of human activity in contrast to God's activity.

However, the third occurrence in Eccl. 12:9 is used in connection with human proverbs being "arranged" or "set in order' (Piel perfect). This difference shows the possibility of similar Semitic roots and the uncertainty of the intended nuances and connotations. As the inspiration of Scripture is a faith presupposition, so too, is our ability to understand it. The Spirit is active in both, yet when it comes to translation and interpretation, godly, educated, prayerful believers disagree. It is crucial for all of us affected by sin to search for the main truths of

  1. literary units
  2. paragraph/stanzas
  3. any parallelism

and not fight or build systematic theologies on disputed words or contexts!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:13-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:13-14 See Contextual Insights, C. God is in control (a recurrent theme, e.g., Eccl. 1:15; possibly 6:10) even though we can't always understand the why of our natural or individual circumstances! This inability to understand is purposeful (e.g., Eccl. 3:11; 7:14; 8:17). Faith, not understanding (i.e., Job), is crucial in life and death.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:14 See SPECIAL TOPIC: GOD HARDENED

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:15 The opening phrase of this verse goes back to the literary foil of chapters 1-2 (i.e., Solomon). The author is claiming both extensive observational wisdom, yet he also recognizes its absolute folly and futility. Experience has caused him to become pessimistic about earthly life, but hopeful (though veiled) of God's activity both now and in the future (i.e. "advantage," cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:11; 3:9; 5:16).

This verse states the theological tension over the circumstances of the righteous vs. the wicked. The traditional theology (i.e., "the two ways") stated that God blessed the righteous and destroyed the wicked (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-28; Ps. 37:25; Prov. 2:21ff; 11:19). However, this did not always work out in life, therefore, Job, Psalm 73, and Ecclesiastes begin to question this traditional premise. This is not meant to depreciate obedience or covenant faith, but to place it in the context of a fallen world. This is not the world God intended it to be. A good Christian song at this point would be "This is the day the Lord has made, I will rejoice and be glad in it." Circumstances or earthly things cannot affect true happiness.

NASB  "my lifetime of futility"
NKJV  "my days of vanity"
NRSV  "my vain life"
TEV  "my life has been useless"
NJB  "my futile life"
JPSOA  "my own brief span of life"
LXX, Peshitta  "in the days of my vanity"

The term "futility" (BDB 210, KB 236 I) means "vapor" or "breath," but in Ecclesiastes it is used as imagery to describe the transitoriness and meaninglessness of human, earthly life (see full note at Eccl. 1:2). It is used five times in Eccl. 7:12 and thirty three more times throughout the book (three in Eccl. 12:8). It characterizes human pursuits and activities, including wisdom and righteousness!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:16
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:16 This verse, which seems so strange to us as NT believers, has several unusual VERBS:

  1. "do not be," BDB 224, KB 243, Qal JUSSIVE
  2. "excessively," BDB 915 I, KB 1176, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE
  3. "do not be overly wise," BDB 314, KB 314, Hithpael IMPERFECT
  4. "why should you ruin yourself," BDB 1030, KB 1563, Hithpolel IMPERFECT

The last one denotes a self-deceiving spirit that trusts too much in its own efforts. These, like the self-deceiving wicked, die; sometimes unexpectedly!

The NET Bible (p. 1133) denotes that verb #4 is translated elsewhere in this stem as "to be astonished" (e.g., Ps. 143:4; Isa. 59:16; 63:5; Dan. 8:27), meaning an OT person who had heard the Deuteronomic promises of health, blessing, and prosperity for the obedient covenant partners may be surprised when the unfairness and fallenness of this age takes the life of "righteous" covenant partners early. They are also surprised when an obviously wicked person lives a prosperous, long life (cf. Psalm 73).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:16-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:16-18 We are warned to be careful of

  1. the extremes of legalism and antinomianism
  2. self estimation of one's goodness

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:17 "Why should you die before your time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:17 "Why should you die before your time" See note at Eccl. 7:12.

There are national events related to the different seasons/times of human life. The mind/actions of those who fear God can extend the days of one's life (cf. Eccl. 7:12 and18). Faith effects longevity.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:18 This is a summary statement going back to Eccl. 7:15. From the context Qoheleth seems to encourage

  1. a righteous life
  2. a prolonged life

both of which are related to an appropriate fear and respect for God (cf. Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 8:12,13; 12:13; Prov. 1:7). There is evil in our world and in our hearts! God and His hidden will, goodness, and presence are fallen mankind's (cf. Eccl. 7:23; 3:11; 8:17) only hope. We cannot fully understand Him or our circumstances, but we can trust Him, obey Him, and abide in faith amidst an unpredictable earthly life (cf. Eccl. 12:13)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

NASB  "comes forth with both of them"
NKJV  "will escape them all"
NRSV  "shall succeed with both"
TEV  "will be successful anyway"
NJB  "will find both"
LXX  "all things shall come forth well"
JPSOA  "will do his duty by both"
NIV  "will avoid all extremes"
NET  "will follow both warnings"
Peshitta  "shall follow all these things"

It is obvious from the translations that the phrase is uncertain. Here are the options:

  1. somehow related to Eccl. 7:15-17
    1. will fulfill (i.e., "our duty," from later meaning in Mishnah, JPSOA)
    2. will reject (NET)
    3. will avoid the extremes (NIV)
  2. will be successful (NRSV, TEV)
  3. will accept the warnings (NKJV, Peshitta)

Numbers 2 and 3 are parallel. Life is unpredictable! God's work and will are hidden! Wisdom cannot find ultimate answers! In light of this, live in fear and faith, and leave the outcome to God. Avoid thinking human efforts can ever fully answer or overcome the uncertainties of this life!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:19 Godly wisdom is far stronger than the opionion/wisdom of many political leaders (cf. Eccl. 10:5). Wisdom is a strong ally in this fallen world (cf. Eccl. 7:12; 9:13-18), but it cannot shield the believers from evil, pain, injustice, and bad circumstances.

Please look at the beginning of this chapter where the paragraphing of different modern English translations are compared. Notice that the contextual relationship between Eccl. 7:19-22 is uncertain.

  1. NASB, one paragraph (Eccl. 7:19-22)
  2. NKJV, NRSV, TEV, Eccl. 7:19, Eccl. 7:20, Eccl. 7:21-22
  3. NJB, Eccl. 7:19, Eccl. 7:20, Eccl. 7:21, Eccl. 7:22

These charts at the beginning of each chapter help us decide how many truths are being addressed in each literary unit. Paragraphs or strophes are crucial in discerning related contexts. Every paragraph, or stanza in poetry, has one main truth or thought. All lines or sentences must relate to this truth. Be careful of being sidetracked on illustrations or minor points!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:20 "who never sins"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:20 "who never sins" This is an affirmation of the falleness of all humanity (cf. 1 Kgs. 8:46; 2 Chr. 6:36; Job 15:14-16; 25:4; Ps. 130:3-4; 143:2; Prov. 20:9; Rom. 3:9-18,23; 1 John 1:8-2:1). This shows the foolishness of perfectionism and/or human effort (cf. Eccl. 7:16-18).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:21 "take seriously"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:21 "take seriously" This is literally "give your heart to." It is idiomatic for a strenuous mental search for truth/wisdom (cf. Eccl. 1:17; 7:21; 8:9,16).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:21-22
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:21-22 The writer encourages us not to take ourselves or the words of others too seriously. We often say what we do not really mean!

Another possibility is that all humans are incapable of complete righteousness (all sin, in some ways, at some times). Be careful of judging one another or reacting to insults since you, too, insult people.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:23 "I tested"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:23 "I tested" This VERB (BDB 650, KB 702, Piel PERFECT) denotes the author's approach to finding true wisdom (cf. Eccl. 2:1).

▣ "all this" How far back does this phrase refer (i.e., Eccl. 7:19-22; 15-22; 1-22; or earlier chapters)? Wisdom is hard to find (Eccl. 3:11; 8:17), but must be sought (i.e., Proverbs 1-8).

▣ "I will be wise" This VERB (BDB 314, KB 314, Qal COHORTATIVE) denotes a self determination. However, human effort cannot discover the mysteries of God or the mysteries of a fallen world (cf. Eccl. 1:13-18)!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:23-25
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:23-25 Where does the paragraph or stanza start and stop? Is the major point in Eccl. 7:26 (i.e., NASB, NKJV) the evil woman? Or does this context run through Eccl. 7:29 (cf. NRSV)? These kinds of questions are crucial, but often there are not textual markers, just the interpreter's common sense and context!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:24
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:24 Notice the parallel concepts about the difficulty in fallen humanity's (women singled out in Eccl. 7:28) search for wisdom:

  1. "remote," Eccl. 7:23, BDB 935, KB 1221, "far off"
  2. "exceedingly mysterious," Eccl. 7:24, BDB 771, KB 849, lit. "deep, deep" (i.e., Job 5:9; 11:7; 15:8; Rom. 11:33 (twice)
  3. "who can discover it," Eccl. 7:24, BDB 592, KD 619, Qal IMPERFECT (cf. Job 11:7)
  4. from Eccl. 7:28, "I am still seeking, but have not found" (same VERB as #3)

▣ "discover" This VERB (BDB 592, KB 619) is used nine times in chapter 7:

  1. "discover" (2 times), Eccl. 7:14,24, Qal IMPERFECT
  2. "discovered," Eccl. 7:26 Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE
  3. "discovered," Eccl. 7:27, Qal PERFECT
  4. "to find," Eccl. 7:27, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT
  5. "have not found" (3 times), Eccl. 7:28 (thrice), Qal PERFECT
  6. "found," Eccl. 7:29, Qal PERFECT

Qoheleth discovered he could not discover! His search was sincere, thorough, intensive. God has put in our hearts the desire "to know," "to understand," but it is beyond our current fallen ability. The "desire" probably comes from our being made in the image and likeness of God (cf. Gen. 1:26-27), but sin has damaged our ability (cf. Genesis 3). Yet we still seek, search, yearn, and strive (cf. 1 Cor. 13:9-13)!

7:25
NASB  "I directed my mind"
NKJV, Peshitta  "I applied my heart"
NRSV  "I turned my mind"
TEV  "I devoted myself"
LXX  "I and my heart went round about"
REB  "I went on to reflect"

Literally this is, "I myself turned my heart." This same VERB (BDB 685, KB 738, Qal PERFECT) is used in Eccl. 2:20. It denotes a point in Qoheleth's thinking where he comes to a decision. Maybe we would say "he got his mind around an issue."

The ancients thought "the heart" was the center of thinking, reasoning, feeling.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE HEART

▣ Notice the series of INFINITIVE CONSTRUCTS:

  1. "to know," BDB 393, KB 390, Qal (cf. Eccl. 1:17)
  2. "to investigate," BDB 1064, KB 1707, Qal (cf. Eccl. 1:13)
  3. "to seek," BDB 134, KB 152, Piel
  4. "to know," BDb 393, KB 390, Qal

He wanted to understand or posses:

  1. "wisdom," BDB 315
  2. "an explanation," BDB 363 I, lit. "the sum of things," cf. Eccl. 7:27; 9:10 (#1 and #2 are possibly a hendiadys)

The search from chapter 1 continues by means of

  1. "the evil of folly"
  2. "the foolishness of madness"

Alternately, since Qoheleth has just informed his readers of the impossibility of attaining wisdom (cf. Eccl. 7:23-24,27), this may mean he turned from the search.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:26 "more bitter than death"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:26 "more bitter than death" NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 887, has an interesting comment.

"Attitudes toward death. At best, death was mysterious and fearful, euphemistically called sleep (Ps. 13:3[4]). Those who hate God are said to love death (Prov 8:36), but this, of course, is the language of hyperbole. Usually the prospect of death conjures up feelings of terror (Ps. 55:4[5]), panic (1 Sam 5:11), and bitterness (1 Sam 15:32; Eccl 7:26). There is nothing of the NT idea of death as release or relief, something even to be longed for (2 Cor 5:1-10; Phil 1:21-26)."

"the woman" This verse seems to be out of context, therefore, some have said "the woman" refers to

  1. "godless philosophy" (i.e., wisdom personified, cf. Eccl. 7:4; 9:10)
  2. the "foolishness" (i.e., the word is FEMININE) of Eccl. 7:25
  3. the sin of Eve (cf. Genesis 3)
  4. Proverbs personifies both evil and wisdom in the image of a woman (cf. Proverbs 1-8).

▣ This verse has several images alluding to hunting animals or violence:

  1. "snares," BDB 844 II, cf. Job 19:6
  2. "nets," BDB 357 II
    1. hunter, Micah 7:2
    2. fisherman, Ezek. 26:5,14; 32:3; 47:10; Hab. 1:15,16,17
  3. "chains," BDB 64 (usually referring to human bonds)
  4. "escape," BDB 572, KB 589, Niphal IMPERFECT (usually referring to human deliverance)
  5. "captured," BDB 539, KB 530, Niphal IMPERFECT (military metaphor)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:27-28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:27-28 These verses seem chauvinistic, but males are not much better, only 1/10 of 1% (one man among a thousand). The contextual emphasis is on the rarity of wisdom.

7:27
NASB, NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "the Preacher"
NRSV, NIV  "the Teacher"
TEV  "the Philosopher"
NJB, JPSOA  "Qoheleth"
REB  "the Speaker"

This term (BDB 875, KB 1080) is found only in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 1:1,2,12; 7:27; 12:8,9,10). It may be a Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE (cf. NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 890). In Eccl. 12:8 it has the DEFINITE ARTICLE (twice) denoting not a proper name, but a title (i.e., the who who gathers or assembles, which could denote wisdom or students). See Introduction, Authorship. See note at Eccl. 1:1

▣ "an explanation" This is literally "the sum" (BDB 363 I, KB 360 I). It denotes the conclusion which is reached by human reasoning. This same term is also found in v. 25.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:28
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 7:28 It is possible v. 28 is another allusion to Solomon, who in his older life was allured into idolatry by his young wives. It is also possible this is a reflection of the ANE patriarchal mentality.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 7:29
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
7:29 This verse asserts two truths from Genesis:

  1. Initially all of God's creation was good (cf. Gen. 1:31). Humans can understand and implement God's will.
  2. Fallen humans are creative and energetic in the area of evil and rebellion (cf. Genesis 3-4; 6:5,11-12,13; 11). Though morally capable, humans turn from God's will to self-will at every opportunity (i.e., the lingering results of Genesis 3)!

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why is Eccl. 7:1-14 so hard to interpret?
  2. What is Eccl. 7:16-17 referring to?
  3. Why is wisdom so hard to find?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:1 It is possible that Eccl. 8:1 should go with chapter 7 and conclude that discussion. Rhetorical questions often close units (i.e., Eccl. 6:12). It seems unrelated to what follows unless it deals with how a wise person should act in the presence of a king (i.e., "his stern face"). However, I personally think the "king" refers to God. If not, this is another clue that Solomon is not the author.

▣ "the interpretation of a matter" This term (BDB 833 CONSTRUCT BDB 182) later came to be associated with the interpretation of dreams, especially in Genesis 40-41 (Joseph) and Daniel 2-7 (Daniel), but here it has no such connotation. It is another way of referring to human reason or wisdom.

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION

NASB  "illumines"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "makes his face shine"
TEV  "makes them smile"
NJB, JPSOA  "lights up the face"
LXX  "lighten"

This VERB (BDB 21; KB 24; Hiphil IMPERFECT) is often used of God's face (e.g., Num. 6:25; Ps. 4:6; 31:16; 44:3; 67:1; 80:3,7,19; 89:15; 119:135; Dan. 9:17), but only here of a human face.

▣ "causes his stern face to beam" "Beam" literally means "change" (BDB 1039 I, KB 1600, cf. NKJV). This verse means either

  1. wisdom gives peace and contentment
  2. wisdom helps courtiers keep their true feelings to themselves (cf. Eccl. 8:3; 10:4)
  3. wisdom helps courtiers keep the king's confidence

The terms "illumines" and "beam" seem at first to be parallel, but on closer reading, I think they refer to two different people.

  1. a court sage
  2. a monarch

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

Remember, Ecclesiastes 6:1-8:15 may be a loosely structured literary unit.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:2 "Keep the command of the king"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:2 "Keep the command of the king" "King" (BDB 572 I) is either a reference to God (i.e., the Targums) or to an earthly monarch (i.e., LXX, cf. Rom. 13:1-7).

It seems to me that the real subject of Eccl. 8:2-8 is God, not just an earthly king because

  1. the sovereignty of the king, Eccl. 8:3-4 (God in Eccl. 8:11)
  2. there is a proper time, Eccl. 8:5-6 (cf. chapter 3)
  3. humans have trouble, Eccl. 8:6
  4. there is mystery in human affairs, Eccl. 8:7 (only God knows)
  5. God's authority is emphasized in Eccl. 8:8 (humans do not/should not have it, Eccl. 8:9)
  6. the phrase "he will do whatever he pleases" is always used of God (cf. Ps. 115:3; 135:6; Jonah 1:14)
  7. the vast majority of the uses of "command" (BDB 846) refer to God

Again look at the paragraphing comparison at the beginning of the chapter. This opening section obviously deals with life at court. But how many separate truths are being communicated? Notice how the modern translations answer this question:

  1. NASB, NKJV ‒  two
  2. NRSV, NJB, TEV ‒  one

▣ "oath before God" This refers to an oath (BDB 989, KB 1396) of allegiance

  1. to God
  2. to the king in God's name (BDB 990)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:2-3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:2-3 These two verses have a series of commands:

  1. "keep the command of the king," BDB 1036, KB 1581, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. do not be in a hurry to leave him," first VERB, BDB 96, KB 111, Niphal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  3. "do not join in an evil matter," BDB 763, KB 840, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:3 "in a hurry"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:3 "in a hurry" This word "hurry" is literally "dismayed" or "disturbed" (BDB 96, KB 111, Niphal IMPERFECT but JUSSIVE in use). This root (BDB191) is often linked to another Hebrew root, "hurry," which often has a negative connotation (cf. Eccl. 5:2; 7:9). Even here it has a negative sense (i.e., 2 Chr. 26:20; Esther 6:14; 8:14; Dan. 2:25; 6:19), but not always (i.e., 2 Chr. 35:21; Esther 2:9; Dan. 3:24), where it simply denotes "hurry" or "rapid action." Remember, context determines meaning and connotation of words (i.e., semantic field).

▣ "to leave him" This phrase can refer to

  1. a rebellion (i.e., Akkadian and Ugaritic usages) against God
  2. leaving the king's service

▣ "an evil matter" The word has a wide semantic field as its usage in Job and Ecclesiastes shows (Kohlenberger III, Swanson, The Hebrew English Concordance, pp. 1480-1481).

  1. "evil," Job 1:1,8; 2:3; 21:30; 28:28; 30:26; Eccl. 4:3; 9:3(twice)
  2. "painful," Job 2:7
  3. "trouble," Job 2:10; 31:29
  4. "harm," Job 5:19; Eccl. 8:5
  5. "wicked," Job 35:12; Eccl. 12:14
  6. "heavy," Eccl. 1:13
  7. "grievous," Eccl. 2:17; 6:2
  8. "miserable," Eccl 4:8
  9. "wrong," Eccl. 5:1; 8:11
  10. "misfortune," Eccl. 5:14
  11. "bad," Eccl. 8:3; 9:2
  12. "hurt," Eccl. 8:9
  13. "crimes," Eccl. 8:12
  14. "cruel," Eccl. 9:12

Remember, context determines meaning (not lexicons).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:5 "royal command"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:5 "royal command" This is a Persian word (BDB 846, KB 622) used in reference to an order of the king (or of God, cf. Eccl. 12:13).

NASB  "experiences no trouble"
NKJV, LXX  "will experience nothing harmful"
NRSV  "will meet no harm"
TEV  "you are safe"
NJB  "will come to no harm"
JPSOA  "will not suffer from a dangerous situation"
Peshitta  "will know no evil thing"

For the word's wide semantic range, see Eccl. 8:3, where it is translated "evil matter." Could this refer to the righteous obeying God's laws? Notice the term "procedure" (in Eccl. 8:5 and 6), means "judgment" (BDB 1048).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:6 "proper time"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:6 "proper time" This is reminiscent of chapter 3 (i.e., God's timing).

▣ "procedure" This literally means "judgment" (BDB 1048).

▣ "when a man's trouble is heavy upon him" "Trouble" here literally means "evil" (see note at Eccl. 8:3). The LXX has "knowledge" instead of "trouble." Life is hard and unpredictable, even for the wise, god-fearing person.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:7 This mystery of life (humans do not know why, when, or how problems/joys come) is a recurrent theme (cf. Eccl. 3:22; 6:12; 9:12; 10:14). Human wisdom cannot find the answer to this mystery, so:

  1. enjoy life when you can (cf. Eccl. 9:11)
  2. trust (i.e., fear) in God (cf. Eccl. 9:12,13); see SPECIAL TOPIC: BELIEVE, TRUST, FAITH AND FAITHFULNESS (OT)  and  SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)
  3. obey God (cf. Eccl. 8:5; 12:13); see SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP  and  SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT

This is all we can do (from the sage's OT perspective [cf. Eccl. 6:12]). Thank God there is a New Testament (i.e., Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36)! Thank God for "progressive revelation"

8:8
NASB, NRSV, NJB, Peshitta  "wind" (twice)
NKJV, LXX  "spirit" (twice)
NRSV footnote  "breath"
REB, JPSOA  "breath of life"

The translation of ruah (BDB 924) as "spirit" is an attempt to balance the next phrase ("authority over the day of death"). Humans often cannot affect or change the events of their lives! Surely evil will not help (cf. Eccl. 8:13)!

▣ "those who practice it" This is literally the term "given to it," which reflects a DIRECT OBJECT from the word Ba'al (BDB 127), which means "lord it over" or "rule." Wickedness is personified as an ineffective taskmaster! Paul also uses personification to describe sin/evil (i.e., Rom. 6:16-23; 7:11,14,17; also note 1 Pet. 5:8).

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:9 "under the sun"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:9 "under the sun" This recurrent phrase is one of two keys to my interpretation of the book. Please see notes at Eccl. 1:3 and 9 to fully understand my interpretive stance (i.e., bias) on this Wisdom book.

▣ "a man has exercised authority over another man to his hurt" This is a general summation of the human situation. The dominance (cf. Gen. 1:28) given to humanity in creation has been abused! In Ecclesiastes this usually refers to governmental oppression (cf. Eccl. 4:1; 5:8; 7:7).

This recurrent complaint against the corrupt power of government is a hint that Solomon, who was surely used as a literary foil in chapters 1-2, is not the author of Ecclesiastes. Solomon as King could have reformed government and reduced the corruption.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:10 This verse has several textual problems. The question is, how many people are being referred to and how are they characterized?

  1. the wicked (NASB, NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, NIV)
    1. were given a proper burial (implication elaborately)
    2. attended worship often (i.e., either local synagogue or temple)
    3. were temporarily praised (there is a textual problem involving "forgotten" [BDB 1013, KB 1489, MT, Peshitta, JPSOA, NKJV, NJB] or "praised" [BDB 986 II, LXX, NRSV, REB, NIV, TEV]; see UBS Text Project, p. 584, which gives "forgotten" a "B" rating, meaning some doubt) in the city where they lived (or in Jerusalem) and everyone knew they were evil.
      The two textual options are so similar in form
       (1) "and they are forgotten," וישׁתכחו
       (2) "and they praised themselves," וישׁתבחו
  2. the wicked and the righteous (JPSOA, JAMES MOFFATT Translation)
    1. wicked were buried with praise
    2. righteous were not praised
    3. both were forgotten
  3. the wicked attend worship and boast of it (NEB, REB, NET; this involves a textual change)

The NET Bible has a good technical summary of the exegetical issues, p. 1136.

▣ "futility"  See full note on the recurrent theological term ("vanity") at Eccl. 1:2.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:11 "the sentence"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:11 "the sentence" This is a Persian word for "royal judgment" (BDB 834). In this context it must refer to God. His mercy and slowness to anger is taken by fallen mankind as a license instead of a call to repentance (cf. Rom. 2:4; 2 Pet. 3:9)! Time and opportunity reveal the human heart!

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHARACTERISTICS OF ISRAEL'S GOD (OT)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:12 "may lengthen his life"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:12 "may lengthen his life" This was/is the problem of evil in a fallen world. Evil is in its own environment! It flourishes here. It seems to prevail over the good. Evil persons may "live" longer, but they will face God one day (Psalm 73)! It is this seeming unfairness

  1. in God's world
  2. of traditional Wisdom teaching of the "two ways" (cf. Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:1,15,19; Psalm 1; Prov. 3:2; 9:10-11; 10:27; 14:23; 19:23)

that bothered Job, the author of Psalm 73, Qoheleth, and Habakkuk! Where is the God of promises and justice?! A book that has helped me think through this issue is John W. Wenham, The Goodness of God.

▣ "still I know it will be well for those who fear God" This is a faith statement (i.e., worldview) for Qoheleth (i.e., Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12-13; 12:13; Prov. 1:7,29; 2:5; 9:10). His experience says differently (i.e. Eccl. 8:14-15). Yet, he trusts God (Elohim) for a future vindication (as did Job, cf. Job 14:14-15; 19:25-7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:13 "will not lengthen his days"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:13 "will not lengthen his days" This seems in direct contrast to Eccl. 8:12.

▣ "like a shadow" The concept of shade/shadow was a powerful image for desert people. It can denote

  1. the transitoriness of human life (i.e., Job 8:9; 14:2; Ps. 102:11; 109:23; 144:4; Eccl. 6:12; 8:13)
  2. the protection/care of God (so many, see SPECIAL TOPIC: SHADOW/SHADE)
  3. the approach of death (cf. Job 10:21; 38:17; Ps. 23:4; 44:19)

See note at Eccl. 7:12.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 8:14 This verse screams out at the apparent injustice in life (i.e., Eccl. 8:10-11). Qoheleth affirms God's justice (cf. Eccl. 8:12-13), but yet there is obvious injustice in this life. This verse begins and ends with "futility" (BDB 210 I, KB 286 II; see full note at Eccl. 1:2)! It is in light of this kind of unfairness that the promises of God (i.e., we reap what we sow, e.g., Job 34:11,25; Ps. 28:4; 62:12; Prov. 12:14; 24:12; Eccl. 12:14; Jer. 17:10; 32:19; Ezek. 33:20; Matt. 16:27; 25:31-36; Rom. 2:6; 14:12; 1 Cor. 3:8; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7-10; 2 Tim. 4:14; 1 Pet. 1:17; Rev. 2:23; 20:12; 22:12) are questioned. If the wicked do not reap what they sow in this life, but the righteous often suffer, then there must be an afterlife to verify God's promises and implement God's justice (Psalm 73)!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:15 It is like a summary of the entire book! It is a major recurrent theological theme (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18-20; 8:15; 9:7-9). Trust God; enjoy the moment! This is the conclusion based on the failure of wisdom to understand or affect the unfairness and injustices of this seemingly random earthly life!

Please read each of these Scripture references!

▣ "there is nothing good" See notes at Eccl. 1:1 and 2:24.

▣ "under the sun" This is another major, recurrent theological theme. See note at Eccl. 1:3.

NASB  "stand by him"
NKJV, REB  "will remain with him"
NRSV  "will go with them"
JPSOA, Peshitta  "that much can accompany him"
LXX  "this will attend him"

The VERB (BDB 530 I, KB 522, Qal IMPERFECT) basically means "to be joined to." Enjoyment of the daily gifts of life is to be a companion to daily labor. A contented and positive attitude (worldview) makes a faithful follower's life profitable, not the other physical things (cf. chapter 1-2).

▣ "the days of his life which God has given him" This is the theological affirmation of God's

  1. existence
  2. sovereignty
  3. active involvement in this world

See Eccl. 2:26; 5:18; 6:2; 9:9; 12:7,11.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 8:16-17
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
8:16-17 This is either (1) a summary statement which parallels chapters 1-2 or (2) the introduction to a new section (8:16-9:10, cf. UBS Handbook for Translators, p. 309 or TEV (Eccl. 8:9-9:12).

  1. Wisdom is laborious (i.e., grievous task [cf. Eccl. 1:13,18; 2:23,26; 3:10], lit., "even though one should never sleep day or night"), Eccl. 8:16.
  2. Qoheleth gave himself to it (cf. Eccl. 1:13,14)
  3. Human wisdom cannot discover God's purpose (cf. Eccl. 3:11; 7:23; also note Job 38-41).

This is why Eccl. 8:15 and later 12:13-14 are advocated!

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Is Eccl. 8:1-9 speaking of God or an Eastern Monarch?
  2. Why is Eccl. 8:10 so difficult?
  3. Is there a seeming contradiction between Eccl. 8:12 and Eccl. 8:13?
  4. Why do the wicked prosper and the righteous die early?
  5. Can we know God and His will for man?
  6. Why are there such varied paragraph divisions in this chapter?

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

9:1
NASB  "For I have taken all this to my heart and explain. . ."
NKJV  "For I considered all this in my heart so that I could declare it all:"
NRSV  "All this I laid to heart, examining it all"
REB  "To all this I applied my mind, and I understood‒"
NJB  "Yes, I have applied myself to all this and experienced all this to be so:"
TEV  "I thought long and hard about all this"
NET  "So I reflected on all this, attempting to clear it all up"
JPSOA  "For all this I noted, and I ascertained all this:"

This sounds very much like chapters 1 and 2 (Solomon as literary foil). The author's mind and experience led him to affirm that life is unknowable and unfair.

There is a textual issue at the beginning of v. 1.

  1. "I took to heart"
  2. "I set my heart"

The UBS Text Project suggests option 1, which is followed by RSV, NEB.

▣ Notice the parallelism:

  1. righteous men (BDB 843)
  2. wise men (BDB 314)

Wise persons are righteous persons (cf. Prov. 1:13; 9:9; 23:24). The righteous and the wicked are contrasted in Eccl. 9:2:

  1. the righteous vs. the wicked
  2. the good vs. the bad (LXX)
  3. the clean vs. the unclean
  4. the man who offers a sacrifice vs. the one who does not
  5. the man who does not swear vs. the one who takes oaths lightly

The "wicked" and "righteous" both refer to covenant people (not Gentiles). This follows the theology of Deut. 31:29 and Jdg. 2:19.

NASB  "explain"
NKJV  "declare"
NRSV  "examine"
NJB  "experienced"
LXX  "has seen"
REB  "understood"
JPSOA  "ascertained"
Peshitta  "considered"

This word (BDB 101, KB 116, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) means "to make clear" or "explain" (from the Arabic root, "to examine"). There is some question about the text at this point and some scholars

  1. assume that the VERB is a misprint for "seek out" (BDB 1064, KB 1707), found at Eccl. 1:13; 2:3; 7:25, where the initial t and b are confused
  2. believe that the INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT comes from brr (BDB 140, KB 162), meaning "to be clear" or "to select." It is used in Eccl. 3:18 in the sense of "test" or "purify" (cf. Ps. 18:26)
  3. divide the Hebrew consonants differently (cf. LXX, "seen")

▣ "deeds" This is the only place in the OT where this word (BDB 714), which normally is a VERBAL used of "service to God," is used as a NOUN.

▣ "their deeds are in the hand of God" This is the continuing theme of God's sovereignty ("hand" equals "power," cf. Eccl. 2:24; Job 19:21; 27:11; Ps. 10:12; 17:7; see SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND) and humanity's ignorance of the cause or reason of present events and future events! Fallen humans do not control anything but still have life choices with consequences!

Scripture assures believers that their lives are in the hand (i.e., control) of God (e.g., Deut. 33:3; Job 12:10; Ps. 119:109; Matt. 6:25-34). However, experience teaches that bad things happen to good people. Life is uncertain at best, yet God is sure and faithful. Faith sees through life's uncertainties and beholds God! Life is uncertain and undependable, but God is certain and dependable! Maybe life is a test to see who really trusts God!

For "hand" see SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PROBLEMS AND LIMITATIONS OF HUMAN LANGUAGE

▣ "Man does not know whether it will be love or hatred, anything awaits him" Life is unpredictable and uncontrollable (contra idolatry, cf. Deuteronomy 18), even for those who serve God (cf. Eccl. 9:2,11; 3:22; 6:12; 7:14; 8:7; 10:14). This is the agnostic philosophy that bothered the later rabbis. It totally challenges the "two ways" of traditional wisdom.

The JPSOA sugests an emendation, "even love, even hate, no man can know in advance. All are insignificant." The events of life may be insignificant in the big picture of human history, but they are significant to

  1. the individual and his/her family
  2. the God of creation who has an eternal plan

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:2 "It is the same for all"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:2 "It is the same for all" The same events (i.e., death) occur in the life of the wicked and the righteous (cf. Eccl. 9:3,11; 2:14-15; 3:19-20). If the promises of God are sure, how can this be true? This is the mystery of this fallen age (i.e., the uncertainty of life, but the certainty of death [cf. Rom. 5:12,17,18-19])! True life is more than a physical, earthly experience!

Notice the contrasting pairs used to make the point.

  1. the righteous ‒ the wicked
  2. the clean ‒ the unclean (i.e., ritual purity)
  3. thosel who sacrifice ‒ those who do not (i.e., Eccl. 5:1)
  4. good man ‒ sinner (i.e., Eccl. 2:26; 7:26)
  5. swearer ‒ those who do not swear/vow (i.e., Eccl. 8:2)

The summary is in v. 3, "there is one fate for all men"—death.

The MT, after #1, has "to the good," but does not finish the suggested contrast. The LXX adds "and the bad." If so, then there are six contrasting pairs.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:3 "in all that is done under the sun"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:3 "in all that is done under the sun" This is a major interpretive theme (see full note at Eccl. 1:3). It is used six times in this chapter. It denotes the consequences of earthly life without God.

▣ "one fate for all men" This is a reaction to the traditional OT theology that asserts that if you love and obey God, He will prosper you physically and spiritually (i.e., Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 27-30). It is often called "the two ways" (cf. Ps. 1). The book of Job and Psalm 73 also react against the imbalance of this performance-based worldview when compared to experience (cf. Eccl. 3:19-20).

▣ "the hearts of the sons of men are full of evil" This is the result of the Fall of mankind recorded in Genesis 3, illustrated in Genesis 4, and stated specifically in Gen. 6:5,11-12,13; 8:21; Ps. 14:3; 58:3; notice Rom. 3:10-18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FALL OF MANKIND

NASB  "insanity"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, REB, LXX  "madness"
NJB  "folly"
Peshitta  "grievous error"

This word (BDB 239, KB 242) is used only in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 1:17; 2:12; 7:25; 9:3; and a related form in Eccl. 10:13). It seems to be related to the word for "praise" (same three CONSONANTS but different VOWELS).

Possibly similar to

  1. Saul's experience in 1 Sam. 10:6,10-11
  2. David's in 1 Sam. 21:14 (BDB 237 II)

In Eccl. 1:17 and 2:12 the meaning is parallel to a search for wisdom and does not have a negative connotation. However, in Eccl. 7:25 and 9:3 it is parallel with "evil" and is obviously negative. The first pair describes the author's search for meaning and a lasting advantage, but the last pair describes fallen humanity (cf. Gen. 6:5,11-12,13; 8:21; Rom. 3:9-18). The real theological question is, "Does Qoheleth's thought focus

  1. on Genesis 3 (i.e., sin, cf. Rom. 3:10-31)
  2. on covenant obedience (i.e., Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28; 30:1,15,19)?

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:4 Life is better than death because there still remains the chance to know God (i.e., "there is hope," BDB 105, KB 120 I, lit. "trust," cf. 2 Kgs. 18:19). It is difficult to know when Qoheleth is using sarcasm versus tongue-in-cheek wisdom sayings. At points he seems to contradict himself. At these points several exact opposite interpretations are possible! Is he

  1. totally pessimistic (i.e., "there is no hope)
  2. pessimistic with glimpses of hope here and there (i.e., there is possible hope)
  3. always speaking sarcastically about the fallen world (i.e., there is always hope with God)?

It seems best to me to choose #2. This interpretive stance allows for "under the sun" (see notes at Eccl. 1:3) sarcasm, but also allows hope texts (i.e., Eccl. 8:2:2-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).

The MT has the VERB "chosen" (BDB 103, KB 119, Pual IMPERFECT), but the Masoretic scholars recognized this should read "joined" (Qere, BDB 287, KB 287, LXX, Peshitta), which reverses the first two consonants.

▣ "dog" They were street scavengers (BDB 476) not pets (i.e., Ps. 59:6,14; 1 Kgs. 14:11).

▣ "lion"  The predominant beast of prey in this geography. See SPECIAL TOPIC: LIONS IN THE OT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:5 "for their memory is forgotten"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:5 "for their memory is forgotten" This concept of memory/remembrance is viewed in several ways.

  1. the wicked pagan nations and their leaders/people will not be remembered (Ps. 9:5-6; Exod. 17:14; Deut. 25:19; 32:26; Isa. 26:14)
  2. the righteous will be remembered (Ps. 112:6; Prov. 10:7)
  3. the wicked among the covenant people will not be remembered (Eccl. 8:10; Ps. 34:16; 69:28; 109:13,15)
  4. Qoheleth's reaction to traditonal wisdom, even the righteous will not be remembered (Eccl. 2:16; 9:5)
  5. all memory of human activity will be forgotten (Eccl. 1:11; 2:16; 9:5)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:5-6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:5-6 The "under the sun" logic (sarcasm) of Qoheleth drives him to search for a lasting advantage/profit (see note at Eccl. 1:3). If there is no God, there is no lasting advantage:

  1. the living struggle with the fear of death ("know," BDB 393, KB 562, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE)
  2. the living seek happiness ("reward," BDB 969 I)
  3. the living seek memorials ("no memory," BDB 271), but in the end the life experience of all humans is the same
    1. death (cf. Eccl. 9:2,3,6,11; 3:20)
    2. there is no lasting advantage
    3. no share (i.e., reward, cf. Eccl. 9:6 [BDB 324]) in life!

He comes to this conclusion based on life observances. This is an unfair, unjust, and surprisingly evil world. Often the promises of God seem not to be fulfilled in this life! The wicked prosper and have longevity! What can a godly person do? The book as a whole gives two answers:

  1. enjoy life when and where you can (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9)
  2. trust God and keep the commandments (even if the lasting advantage is not apparent, cf. Eccl. 12:13-14)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:6 This verse describes the fleeting, transitory life of humans. The term "share" (BDB 324, KB 324) is translated

  1. "reward" in Eccl. 2:10; 5:18,19; 9:9
  2. "lot" in Eccl. 3:22
  3. "portion" in Eccl. 11:2

It is the term used for God's allotment of land to the tribes in Deuteronomy and Joshua.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:7 "drink your wine with a cheerful heart"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:7  "drink your wine with a cheerful heart"  See BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE

NASB, NJB, LXX  "for God has already approved your works"
NKJV  "for God has already accepted your works"
NRSV  "for God has long ago approved what you do"
TEV  "It's all right with God"
JPSOA  "for your action was long ago approved by God"
REB  "for God already accepted what you have done"
Peshitta  "for God is pleased with your works"

This cannot refer to sin and rebellion, so it must refer to God's activity within this fallen world (see Eccl. 2:24; 3:13; 5:19; 8:15)! Life is hard, but we are not alone! God has approved those who trust Him. In this context it refers to "eating" and "drinking," which could refer to a daily activity or a religious or social festival (cf. Eccl. 9:8; 8:15).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:7-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:7-9 This is Qoheleth's answer to the futility and uncertainty of human existence! Notice all the commands:

  1. "go," Eccl. 9:7, BDB 229, KB 246, Qal IMPERATIVE
  2. "eat," Eccl. 9:7, BDB 37, KB 46, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:13; 5:18; 8:15
  3. "drink," Eccl. 9:7, BDB 1059, KB 1667, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:13; 5:18; 8:15; see SPECIAL TOPIC: BIBLICAL ATTITUDES TOWARD ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOL ABUSE
  4. "let your clothes be white all the time," Eccl. 9:8, BDB 224, KB 243, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  5. "let not oil be lacking on your head," Eccl. 9:8, BDB 341, KB 338, Qal IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
  6. "enjoy life with the woman. . .," Eccl. 9:9, BDB 906, KB 1157, Qal IMPERATIVE, lit. "see" (see SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SEXUALITY)
  7. "do it with all your might," Eccl. 9:10, BDB 793, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE, cf. Eccl. 2:24; 3:13,22; 5:18; 8:15

Happiness is found not in wisdom, pleasure, or possessions, but in the simple pleasures of daily life.

  1. home, family
  2. work
  3. friends
  4. contentment with gratitude to God for what you have, not what you do not have

Life is a journey, not a destination! Smell the roses, kiss your wife and kids, go to work with joy!

These verses are very similar to the Epic of Gilgamesh (Babylonian Wisdom Literature) 10.3.6-14. This is a good illustration of the transcultural nature of ANE Wisdom Literature.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:8 "Let your clothes be white"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:8 "Let your clothes be white" We cannot control circumstances, but we can control our reaction to them. Those who trust God have a positive mind set, which is not affected by circumstances (see Hannah Whithall Smith's The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life).

▣ "oil" Putting oil on the face and arms was

  1. a sign of gladness (cf. Ps. 23:5; 45:7; 104:15; Isa. 61:3)
  2. preparation for social events

SPECIAL TOPIC: ANOINTING IN THE BIBLE

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:9 "Enjoy life with the woman you love all the days of your fleeting life"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:9 "Enjoy life with the woman you love all the days of your fleeting life" This command ("enjoy" Qal IMPERATIVE) implies monogamy ("love," BDB 12, KB 17, Qal PERFECT, cf. Prov. 5:18-19). Marital contentment is a great blessing from God.

The question remains, does "woman" (BDB 61), without the ARTICLE, refer to "wife" or "woman?" The problem is Qoheleth's seemingly negative view of women found in Eccl. 7:26 and 28. Does this verse encourage monogamous marriage (if so the author cannot be Solomon!)? The Qal PERFECT VERB "love" implies a complete union, not brief encounters!

Wisdom Literature used "woman" in two ways:

  1. wife to be loved, protected, and kept
  2. woman as temptress and symbol of false wisdom or momentary pleasure

As Wisdom Literature used both senses, so too, does Qoheleth!

▣ "your fleeting life" This is the Hebrew NOUN ה (hebel). It was the name of Adam and Eve's second son, Abel (BDB 211 II). It is often used of the breath of humans. Its major usage is as imagery of transitoriness (cf. Eccl. 6:12; 7:15; 9:9; 11:10). In this context it encourages wise humans to enjoy their family life.

This is the same root that occurs in Eccl. 1:2. It is a major theological concept in Ecclesiastes. See full nte at Eccl. 1:2.

▣ "in your toil in which you have labored" The Hebrew root עמל (labor, toil, BDB 765, 766 II) denotes man's labor to support his family (cf. Eccl. 2:10,20,21,22,24; 3:13; 4:4,6,8,9; 5:18; 10:15). It implies hard work.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SEXUALITY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:10 "Whatever your hand finds to do, verily do it with all your might"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:10 "Whatever your hand finds to do, verily do it with all your might" See note at Eccl. 9:7-9, #7. Physical labor originally was not a consequence of sin, but part of Adam's God-given task in the Garden of Eden (cf. Gen. 2:15). After the Fall labor became a curse (cf. Gen. 3:19). In this context labor refers to making a daily living (i.e., food, shelter, home, family, etc). This aspect of life is a gift from God. It takes our minds off the task of trying to discover God and His purposes, which we cannot do. Work is good! From the NT perspective it can glorify God (cf. Eccl. 11:6; John 9:4; Col. 3:17,23; Eph. 6:5-7). Do all you do as unto the Lord Jesus!

SPECIAL TOPIC: GARDEN OF EDEN

▣ "there is no activity or planning or wisdom in Sheol where you are going" The OT (except for Job 14:14-15; 19:25-27; Ps. 16:9-10; 49:15; 86:13) depicts death as a conscious but shadowy existence. The faithful are with their families, but there is no fellowship, joy, or activity. Death is a place or abode, but nothing more (e.g., 1:11; 9:5; Job 3:13-19; 10:21-22). Thank God for the progressive revelation of the New Testament!

Notice the things that humans do not do in Sheol:

  1. activity ("work," BDB 795, cf. Eccl. 2:4,11; 3:17,22; 8:9; 9:7,10)
  2. planning (or "reckoning schemes," BDB 363 I, cf. Eccl. 7:25,27)
  3. pursue knowledge (BDB 395, cf. Eccl. 1:16,18; 2:21,26; 7:12)
  4. gain wisdom (BDB 315, cf. Eccl. 1:13,16 [twice], 18; 2:3,9,13,21; 7:10,11,12 [twice], 19,23; 8:1; 9:10, 15,16 [twice], 18; 10:1,10)

▣ "Sheol" See SPECIAL TOPIC: WHERE ARE THE DEAD? (Sheol/Hades, Gehenna, Tartarus) I. B.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:11-12
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:11-12 These verses highlight the ineffectualness and helplessness of human effort! They again magnify the sovereignty of God. This conclusion is based on the unfairness and injustice that Qoheleth had seen and experienced. Life is unpredictable and uncontrollable (i.e., "for time and chance overtake them all," cf. Eccl. 9:12; 8:7).

His conclusions to this situations are

  1. enjoy life when and where you can; death is coming
  2. trust God even if He is unknown and invisible
  3. there is an afterlife and humans will give an account of the gifts and stewardship of life (cf. Matt. 25:31-46; Rom. 14:10-12; 2 Cor. 5:10; Rev. 20:11-14)

As I sit here writing this, I am so glad I live in a post-resurrection era. Progressive revelation, the life of Jesus, the gospel, the empty tomb are ours! New Testament believers understand so much more of the eternal plans and purposes of God than any OT person. The real question for us is, "What are we doing with this information?"!

9:12
NASB, NJB, Peshitta  "treacherous net"
NKJV, NRSV  "cruel net"
REB  "destroying net"
JPSOA  "fatal net"
NET  "deadly net"

I show these options to illustrate how words have meaning only in sentences. The MT has the ADJECTIVE "evil" (BDB948). This usage carries no connotation of moral evil. Here, it denotes the mechanism of the death of fish. Context, context, context!

This ADJECTIVE appears again in this verse relating to humans. Again the connotation is not "evil" but

  1. "unfortunate" (NET)
  2. "calamity" (JPSOA, NRSV)
  3. "misfortune" (NJB, REB)

Comparing English translations from differing translation theories often helps interpreters see the semantical field and/or connotations of Hebrew roots.

SPECIAL TOPIC: YHWH'S ETERNAL REDEMPTIVE PLAN

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:13-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:13-18 This sounds like a specific historical event that Qoheleth had observed (i.e., a series of eight Qal PERFECT VERBS; LXX makes them SUBJUNCTIVES, implying a hypothetical situation). These verses magnify "wisdom," but in the end it is ignored and forgotten! The wise man can affect things, but so can the sinner (cf. Eccl. 9:18).

9:13
NASB  "it impressed me"
NKJV, NRSV, Peshitta  "it seemed great to me"
NJB  "it strikes me as important"
REB  "I find it of great significance"
JPSOA  "it affected me profoundly"
NET  "it is a great burden to me"

As Qoheleth tried to make sense of life, it was like a stimulant, but he could not figure it out. Life on this planet, in this period, is mysterious, unpredictable, unfair, and deadly!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 9:17-18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
9:17-18 Wisdom has a place in life. It is "better" than. . . ., but it brings no lasting advantage/profit.

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:1 This verse and Eccl. 9:18 are related by contrast. One something can ruin everything! We might say:

  1. one bad apple spoils the bushel
  2. one bad egg spoils the omelet

Foolishness, like leaven, can permeate and affect the whole!

▣ "stink" This translates two Hebrew parallel phrases:

  1. "cause to stink," BDB 92, KB 107, Hiphil IMPERFECT, cf. Prov. 13:5; Exod. 5:21; 16:24; 1 Sam. 27:12
  2. "cause to bubble" (i.e., ferment), BDB 615, KB 665, Hiphil IMPERFECT, cf. Ps. 59:7; 94:4; Prov. 15:2,28
NASB  "weightier"
NKJV, NJB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "outweighs"
TEV  "cancels"
REV  "lose its worth"
LXX  "more precious"

This term (BDB 429, KB 431) is from the same root as "precious," "prized." It is a play on the Hebrew (i.e., Aramaic) concept of that which is heavier (i.e., metals) is more valuable.

▣ "wisdom and honor" These are parallel:

  1. "wisdom," BDB 315, KB 314 so common in Ecclesiastes
  2. "honor," BDB 458 II, KB 457, also a word play on "heavy" (BDB 458, e.g., Eccl. 6:2; Ps. 62:7; 84:11; Prov. 3:16,35; 22:4; 25:2). This term is often translated "glory," e.g., Ps. 3:3; 4:2; 19:1; 24:7, 8,9,10 (twice)

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. It is obvious that a new context starts in Eccl. 9:13 (cf. NKJV, TEV, NJB) and runs through Eccl. 10:20 (NJB takes it to Eccl. 11:6).

  2. Much of it is poetry (NKJV, NRSV, NIV).

  3. The theme is the contrast between the wise person and the foolish person (cf. Eccl. 9:1,2).

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:2 "the right"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:2 "the right" This term (BDB 411, KB 415-416) originally referred to the right hand

  1. which is normally the stronger (i.e., right handed people are more common)
  2. this hand is also the one raised in an oath (religious and civil)
  3. the one that held the shield in battle
  4. since directions were noted by facing east, it refers to the south

SPECIAL TOPIC: HAND

▣ "the left" This term (BDB 969) in Arabic means "unlucky" (cf. JPSOA). It denotes the north.

These two terms are often used as imagery for deviating from the standard of God. God's truth or Torah was seen as a well-worn, clearly marked path (e.g., Ps. 119:105). Deviation from the path (in any direction) meant sin and rebellion (e.g., Deut. 9:12,16; 31:29). It became a cultural idiom (cf. 2 Sam. 2:21).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:3 One's actions reveal one's character (cf. Prov. 12:23; 13:16; 18:2). We would say, "give a person enough rope and he will hang himself."

It is interesting that the phrase "his sense is lacking" is literally, "the fool has no heart" (i.e., he cannot think clearly, he lacks judgment, cf. Prov. 6:32; 7:7; 9:4,16; 10:13,21; 11:12; 24:30).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FOOLISH PEOPLE

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:4 This is advice for those who serve the king (or other leaders). It links up with Eccl. 8:1-4 and 10:16-17,20. This advice on how to act appropriately in a monarch's presense gives evidence that the author of Ecclesiastes was not Solomon.

NASB, NJB  "composure"
NKJV  "conciliation"
NRSV  "calmness"
TEV  "keep calm"
JPSOA  "pardoned"
REB  "amends"
Peshitta  "healing"
LXX  "do not leave your place" (i.e., position or office)

This term (BDB 951, KB 637 II) means "healing," "cure," or "health" (cf. Eccl. 12:18; 13:17; 16:24). Here it is imagery for a sound mind, a calm spirit (cf. Prov. 14:30), which denotes a person not guilty of the charges or anger of the ruler.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:5 "I have seen"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:5 "I have seen" This is a recurrent VERB (BDB 906, KB 1157, used 47 times), which highlights Qoheheth's method of personal observation as the basis of his life philosophy. He focuses on wisdom as practical and observable in daily life. He primarily (not exclusively) uses natural revelation (i.e., Ps. 19:1-6) instead of special revelation (i.e., Scripture, Ps. 19:7-14) to make his points.

▣ "error" This term (BDB 993) implies an inadvertent action or word (e.g., Lev. 4:2,22,27).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:5-7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:5-7 This literary unit also speaks to rulers and the wealthy. As so often in Wisdom Literature, a role reversal occurs (cf. Eccl. 9:13-18; Prov. 29:2).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:8-9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:8-9 This relates several "unexpected consequences" to one's actions:

  1. A person who digs a pit to capture an animal (or person) will be captured by it (cf. Prov. 26:27).
  2. A person breaks through a wall to escape, but in doing so is bitten by a snake hiding there (cf. Amos 5:19).
  3. workers in stone work
    1. quarry
    2. remove stones from a field
    3. construction of walls or buildings
  4. wood cutter activities

It must be admitted that the above interpretation assumes a negative attitude on the part of the worker, which is not easily demonstrated from the text itself. It is possible, however, that the results described are merely accidental and unexpected (cf. Eccl. 10:9). Human actions and words have unexpected consequences (cf. Prov. 26:27).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH, II. A.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:10-11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:10-11 Humans can take actions (i.e., gain wisdom) that will help them live their lives easier and better!

The term "profit" (BDB 452; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 572-573, #4,5) carries significant theological weight, often referring to a lasting or eternal advantage (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:11; 3:9; 5:16; see full note at Eccl. 1:3). Here the focus is on this life, similar to Proverbs.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:11 "charmed. . .charmer"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:11 "charmed. . .charmer" This root (BDB 538, KB 527) can be understood as "whisper" or "charm." This is used of the actions of a medium; see note at Deut. 18:11.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:12-14
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:12-14 There is a play on the term "mouth," "lips," and "swallow" (i.e., "consume"). What we say does make a difference (e.g., Eccl. 10:13,14; Prov. 10:32; 11:11,13; 13:3; 14:3; 18:6,7,21; Matt. 12:37).

SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN SPEECH, II. A., B.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:13 "the end of it is wicked madness"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:13 "the end of it is wicked madness" The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 1040, asserts that this refers to an attitude of life that recognizes no moral law operating in the world. Therefore, this would be taking the imagery of "under the sun" as a life's motto. In my culture it is the idiom, "you only go around once in life, so get all the gusto you can." Ecclesiastes addresses this very attitude (cf. Eccl. 3:17; 9:11; 12:14).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:14 "No man knows what will happen, and who can tell him what will come after him"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:14 "No man knows what will happen, and who can tell him what will come after him" This is a recurrent theme (cf. Eccl. 3:22; 6:12; 7:14; 8:7; 10:14). The future is hidden, even from the wise and godly person! Wisdom is far better than foolishness (cf. Eccl. 10:15), but it is limited in this fallen period of human history!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:15
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:15 There are several ways to view this verse:

  1. work makes a fool tired (i.e., instead of happy)
  2. fools do not like work (i.e., they are lazy)
  3. fools cannot find the path to the city
    1. God's wisdom, cf. Eccl. 10:2-3
    2. the place of employment

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:16-17 "Woe"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:16-17 "Woe" This INTERJECTION (BDB 33 III), often translated "alas," is found only twice in the OT, both in Ecclesiastes (cf. Eccl. 4:10; 10:16), but often in rabbinical literature.

There are two reasons for the woe:

  1. a young, inexperienced ruler
  2. drunken, worldly-minded leadership

It is surprising that "young" (BDB 654, lit. "child") is contrasted with "noble" (BDB 359). Possibly this is related to Eccl. 10:7 (i.e., slave acting like a prince) or to Eccl. 4:13-16, a seeming historical example.

10:17
NASB, NKJV, LXX, Peshitta  "blessed"
NRSV, NJB, REB, JPSOA  "happy"
TEV  "fortunate"

This term (BDB 80, KB 100, e.g., Ps. 32:2; 84:5,12; 119:1; Prov. 3:13; 8:34; 28:14) is the literary opposite of "woe," (Eccl. 10:16). In Psalms it denotes the blessing of being the covenant people of YHWH.

▣ "At the appropriate time" This concept of a divinely appropriate time was first introduced in Eccl. 3:1-11,17; 7:17; 8:5,6,9; 9:8,11,12(twice); 10:17 (esp. Eccl. 3:11).

▣ "for strength" Food is for activity, not for inactivity (drunkenness, see SPECIAL TOPIC: WINE AND STRONG DRINK). We eat to live; we do not live to eat!! One who controls the base appetite to eat probably can control other areas where self takes control. Self discipline is crucial in a leader!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:18
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 10:18 This seems to be an unrelated saying (cf. TEV. NJB), which chastises inactivity (cf. Prov. 24:30-34). It may be related to characteristics of leaders (cf. NKJV, NRSV). Several of the words are rare (i.e., "rafters," BDB 900) and point toward a cultural proverb.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:19
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:19 This verse seems to express the point of view of the foolish.

NASB  "money is the answer to everything"
NKJV  "money answers every thing"
NRSV, REB, JPSOA  "money meets every need"
TEV  "you can't have either without money"
NJB  "money has an answer for everything"
Peshitta  "money brings one low and causes him to go astray in all things"
LXX  "but to money all things will humbly yield obedience"

Ths phrase is not meant to be a negative attack on money. Both food (i.e., "bread") and drink (i.e., "wine") are seen as gifts from God, so too, the means to buy them. It is possible that the VERB (BDB 772 I, KB 851, Qal IMPERFECT) is meant to be understood as in Eccl. 5:20 (the other use of this VERB in Ecclesiastes), "keep him occupied." In this sense money allows "feasts," "parties," "social occasions" for all to keep their minds off

  1. the vanity of all things
  2. the mysteries of God's activities

SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:19 "So, remove. . ."
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:19 "So, remove. . ." The VERB (BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERATIVE is parallel with "put away" (BDB 716, KB 778, Hiphil IMPERATIVE). Humans have the ability to analyze and check their thinking and behavior. Young people are encouraged to eliminate

  1. vexation (BDB 495), referring to emotional distress
  2. pain (BDB 949), here referring to physical issues
▣
NASB  "grief"
NKJV, LXX  "sorrow"
NRSV  "anxiety"
TEV  "worry"
NJB  "indignation"
REB  "vexation"
JPSOA  "care"
Peshitta  "anger"

This term (NOUN, BDB 495, KB 491; VERB, BDB 494) has several possible connotations:

  1. anger of men, Eccl. 7:9
  2. anger of God
  3. grief, Eccl. 1:18; 2:23; 5:16
  4. sorrow, Eccl. 7:3

This verse could fit with #3 or #4. Life is hard; enjoy it when, where and while you can!

▣ "the prime of life" This is possibly related to the concept, "days of black hair" (BDB 1007; NIDOTTE, vol. 4, p. 83, #5), which is the same basic Semitic root as "dawn" (BDB 1007). Youth, as all things, will pass away (lit. "vanity," BDB 210 I). It is fleeting and meaningless!

NASB, JPSOA  "fleeting"
NKJV, NRSV, LXX, Peshitta  "vanity"
NJB  "futile"
REB  "mere futility"

This is the term "breath" (BDB 210 I; see full note at Eccl. 1:2), used here in the sense of "fleeting" (cf. Eccl. 6:12; 7:15; 9:9; Job 7:16; Ps. 39:5,11; 62:9; 78:33; 144:4; Prov. 31:30). Context determines the connotation intended by the original inspired author!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 10:20
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
10:20 The VERB "curse" (BDB 886, KB 1103, used twice) is a Piel IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense.

It is hard to keep reckless words a secret (cf. Luke 12:3)! Those who hear these outbursts often use them for self interest (i.e., tell the king in order to gain favor).

Copyright © 2014 Bible Lessons International

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:1
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:1 This is a recurrent proverb in the Bible relating to one's generosity (rabbinical sources) and God's gracious response (cf. Deut. 15:10; Prov. 11:24-25; 19:17; 22:9; Matt. 10:42; 2 Cor. 9:8; Gal. 6:9; Heb. 6:10).

There are scholars who think the mentioning of "waters" is a reference to marine commerce. Therefore, this verse refers to shrewd investments in sea trade (see NASB Study Bible). There is very little in this context to support this interpretation. But, it does illustrate the difficulty one faces in moderns trying to understand ANE idioms, imagery, and wisdom literature.
