READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Notice that several translations think the last literary unit (i.e., before several brief concluding statements) begins in chapter 11, 11:9-12:8.
    1. Eccl. 11:9-12:8 (NKJV, TEV)
    2. Eccl. 11:7-12:8 (NRSV, NJB)

  2. There are several commands in this chapter:
    1. "cast," Eccl. 11:1, BDB 1018; KB 1511, Piel IMPERATIVE
    2. "divide," Eccl. 11:2, BDB 678, KB 733, Qal IMPERATIVE
    3. "sow," Eccl. 11:6, BDB 281, KB 282, Qal IMPERATIVE
    4. "be idle" (lit. "rest"), Eccl. 11:6, BDB 628, KB 679, Hiphil JUSSIVE
    5. "let him rejoice," Eccl. 11:8, BDB 970, KB 1333, Qal IMPERFECT but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    6. "let him remember," Eccl. 11:8, BDB 269, KB 269, Qal IMPERFECT but used in a JUSSIVE sense
    7. "rejoice," v, 9, BDB 970, KB 1333, Qal IMPERATIVE
    8. "let your heart be pleasant" (lit. "do good"), Eccl. 11:9, BDB 405, KB 408, Hiphil IMPERFECT used in a JUSSIVE sense
    9. "follow" (lit. "walk"), Eccl. 11:9, BDB 229, KB 246, Piel IMPERATIVE
    10. "know," Eccl. 11:9, BDB 393, KB 390, Qal IMPERATIVE
    11. "remove," Eccl. 11:10, BDB 693, KB 747, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    12. "put away," Eccl. 11:10, BDB 716, KB 778, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
    13. "remember," 12:1, BDB 269, KB 269, Qal IMPERATIVE

  3. This paragraph (or stanza depending on the genre, cf. NKJV, NJB), Eccl. 11:1-6, uses agricultural and rural imagery to communicate wisdom teachings.

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:2 "Divide your portion to seven, or even eight"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:2 "Divide your portion to seven, or even eight" This either refers to

  1. diversifying your wealth (NET Bible #5, p. 1143)
  2. more probably in context, helping many people (cf. Matt. 5:42; Luke 6:30)

The Jewish Study Bible, p. 1619, suggests that the sequence of seven. . .eight was a common idiom in both Canaanite and Hebrew literature for "a significant quantity."

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALMSGIVING

NASB, JPSOA, Peshitta  "misfortune"
NKJV, LXX  "evil"
NRSV, NJB  "disaster"
TEV  "bad luck"
REB  "disasters"

This is the term "evil" (BDB 949, KB 1262). See note at Eccl. 2:17 ("grievous") and 9:12 ("treacherous").

  1. It is coming!
  2. Act while you can (Eccl. 11:4,6).
  3. Give while you can (Eccl. 11:1-2).
  4. Enjoy while you can (Eccl. 11:7-8).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:3
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content: 11:3 Humans experience, but cannot predict or control, the events of their lives (a recurrent theme in Ecclesiastes), but we can share our wealth in good times then when the dark days come, others will share with us, similar to the biblical concept of "we reap what we sow" (see full lists of texts at Gal. 6:6-10).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:4
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:4 At first, this verse of two parallel statements implies a warning against inactivity (i.e., referring to giving from Eccl. 11:1-2). However, I prefer the interpretation of the UBS Handbook For Translators, p. 398, which asserts that it is not inactivity (cf. TEV, REB), but timely activity, that is being advocated (also see NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 1018, #2).

  1. Farmers do not sow in a strong wind.
  2. Farmers wait until the wind direction denotes rain, not hot desert winds.
  3. Farmers sow during rainy periods, but reap during rainless periods.

When one is happy and successful, then give to others. If you wait the dark days may come when you cannot give.

11:5
NASB, NKJV, NJB, LXX, Peshitta  "wind"
REB  "living spirit"
NRSV, JPSOA  "breath"
TEV  "life"
Vulgate  "spirit"

Some translations take "wind" (BDB 924, KB 1197) as "spirit" or "breath," thereby connecting the two lines and relating them both to prenatal activity (cf. KJV, NRSV, TEV, REB, JPSOA, NAB). The interpretive question is, "Is there one illustration of mankind's inability to know, or are there two illustrations in Eccl. 11:5?" See SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND, SPIRIT

The big issue is that in some areas (i.e., planting and harvesting times) humans can learn by observation and tradition, but in other areas (mysteries of nature and mysteries of God's activities) humans cannot know. Wisdom, though good, helpful, and desirable, cannot solve all of life's unknowns!

▣ "how bones are formed in the womb" The OT asserts that Yahweh

  1. formed, Job 10:8-11; 31:15; Ps. 139:13-16; Isa. 44:2,24; 46:3
  2. knows, Jer. 1:5; Rom. 9:11
  3. Messianic imagery, Isa. 49:1,5

humans in the womb.

▣ "so you do not know the activity of God" This has been a common theme (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 3:10,11; 8:17). God and His works and ways cannot be completely known by fallen mankind, but we can trust Him because of what we do know!

NASB, REB, JPSOA, LXX  "all things"
NKJV  "all things"
NRSV, TEV  "everything"
NJB, Peshitta  "all"

This is an idiom for the entire creation (cf. Ps. 103:19; 119:91; Jer. 10:16).

NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 730, lists several other phrases that are used to designate the entire creation:

  1. heaven and earth (e.g., Gen. 1:1; Ps. 115:15; 121:2; Prov. 3:19-20
  2. "the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them" (e.g., Ps. 24:1-2; 50:12; 89:11; Jer. 51:48; 1 Cor. 10:26
  3. "in heaven above or on the earth beneath or in the water under the earth (e.g., Exod. 20:4; Ps. 135:6)

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVEN

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:6 "sow"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:6 "sow" Sow (imagery for giving) with confidence and leave the results to God (cf. 2 Cor. 9:6). Verses 5 and 6 are connected by the word "know" (BDB 393, KB 390, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE).

SPECIAL TOPIC: KNOW

▣ "succeed" This Hebrew VERB (BDB 506, KB 503, Qal IMPERFECT) is found only here and in Eccl. 10:10 (Hiphil INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT). The NOUN is found only in Ecclesiastes as well (cf. Eccl. 2:21; 4:4; 5:10), meaning "skill," "success," or "profit." Success is uncertain. It may come (i.e., Eccl. 11:7-8) and it may not (i.e., Eccl. 11:8b). When it does, act (i.e., share).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:7 "light is pleasant"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:7 "light is pleasant" This is imagery for

  1. the enjoyment of life (cf. Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15)
  2. the beginning of life (i.e., "see the son," cf. Eccl. 6:5; 7:11)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:8 This verse seems to relate to Eccl. 11:1-6. Share your wealth and influence while you can because dark days come into every life, and in those days others will share with you.

Live life fully every day. One does not know how many of them will be good and bright!

▣ "the days of darkness" This term "darkness" (BDB 365; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, pp. 312-315) is used as imagery for

  1. death ‒ 1 Sam. 2:9; Job 10:21-22; 15:22,30; 17:13; 18:18; Ps. 88:11-12; 139:11
  2. secrecy ‒ Job 12:22; Isa. 45:3
  3. place of hiding ‒ Job 34:22
  4. distress ‒ 2 Sam. 22:29; Job 15:23; 22:11; 23:17; 29:3; 107:10,14; Eccl. 5:17; 11:8; Isa. 5:30; 9:2; Micah 7:8
  5. terror ‒ Ezek. 32:8; Amos 5:18,20; Nahum v. 8; Zeph. 1:15
  6. mourning ‒ Isa. 47:5
  7. confusion ‒ Job 5:14; 12:25; 19:8; Ps. 35:6
  8. ignorance ‒ Job 37:19; Ps. 18:28; Eccl. 2:14
  9. evil ‒ Prov. 2:13; Isa. 5:20
  10. obscurity ‒ Eccl. 6:4
  11. healing ‒ Ps. 107:14

▣ "futulity"  See full note on this crucial term at Eccl. 1:2 and NIDOTTE, vol. 1, pp. 1003-1006.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
11:9 At this point in the context, Qoheleth begins to talk about the different opportunities and problems that regularly occur during the different stages of life (Eccl. 11:9-12:7).

  1. childhood
  2. youth
  3. young adult
  4. old age

▣ "follow the impulses of your heart" This advice does not refer to evil, but to the natural human instincts of young people:

  1. be with friends
  2. enjoy life at social events
  3. desire a family and children
  4. find one's vocation

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEART

▣ "Yet know that God will bring you to judgment" We are responsible for our choices (cf. Eccl. 3:17; 12:1; 14; Matthew 25-26; Rom. 2:16; 14:10; 2 Cor. 5:10; Gal. 6:7; Revelation 20)! All humans will give an account to God of the gift of life. See note at Eccl. 12:1.

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGMENT IN THE NT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:1 "Remember"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:1 "Remember" This is a Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 269, KB 269), similar to Eccl. 11:9-10. We must live as stewards who will give an account to our Creator (cf. Eccl. 3:17; 12:14; Matt. 10:26; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:16; 14:10-12; 1 Cor. 4:5; Rev. 20:11-15).

▣ "Creator" This is a form of the Hebrew word bara (BDB 135, KB 153, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE, Gen. 1:1). It is exclusively used to describe God as the One who creates! It is interesting that the PARTICIPLE is PLURAL (cf. Job 35:10; Ps. 149:2; Isa. 54:5), which relates to

  1. the "us" passages in Genesis (cf. Gen. 1:26,27; 3:22; 11:7)
  2. the general name for God as creator, Elohim, which is PLURAL (see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, C.), found throughout Genesis 1-2:3
  3. the "us" passage of Isa. 6:8

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEAVENLY COUNCIL OF ANGELIC BEINGS

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

▣ "in the days of your youth" This is a chronological beginning point (i.e., young person still at home, pre-marriage). In Judaism a person is not responsible to keep the law until a period of training and personal commitment (i.e., bar mitzvah, bat mitzvah). From this time forward covenant believers are responsible to God for their actions. See SPECIAL TOPIC: AGE OF ACCOUNTABILITY

Notice that Wisdom Literature informs all stages of life, but starts with young people (cf. Eccl. 11:9). Chapter 12 moves from the opening days of spiritual responsibility throughout life until old age and death. In every state

  1. before evil days, Eccl. 12:1
  2. before old age, Eccl. 12:2
  3. before time of death, Eccl. 12:6

believers must remember God!  Faith is to be lifelong.

The phrase, "in the days of. . .," is using "day" for a period of time.

SPECIAL TOPIC: DAY (yom)

▣ "evil days" In Hebrew this means sickness, sorrow, or here, senility (cf. 2 Sam. 19:35). This term (BDB 949) basically means "evil," "misery," "distress," or "injury" (cf. Eccl. 2:21; 5:12,15; 8:11; 11:8,10). See note at Eccl. 9:12.

▣ "I have no delight in them" The deterioration of the physical body robs life of joy. Remember Qohlelth's repeated admonition of "enjoy daily life now" (i.e., Eccl. 2:24-26; 3:12,13,22; 5:18; 8:15; 9:7-9).

READING CYCLE THREE (see "Bible Interpretation Seminar")

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

  1. Chapter 12 addresses the normal target audience of Wisdom Literature—wealthy young men.

  2. While chapter 11 focuses on youth, this chapter describes old age in colorful imagery. Every part of the body is used to show the deterioration of age.

  3. Many have asserted that the original book concluded at Eccl. 12:8, which is parallel to Eccl. 1:2. Ecclesiastes 12:9-12 and Eccl. 12:13-14 were later added to make the book seem more traditional and theologically acceptable. However, this is only speculation. Both v. 9 and v. 12 start with "besides that" (BDB 452).
    The two textual evidences that point to this conclusion are
    1. the inclusio literary form of Eccl. 1:2 - 12:8 (same words)
    2. Qoheleth is referred to in the third person only in Eccl. 12:9-14 (but alludes to Eccl. 1:1)
    3. the theological emphasis changes from anti-wisdom to traditional wisdom

WORD AND PHRASE STUDY

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:2
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:2 This verse symbolically refers to the use of one's sight or vision (cf. Eccl. 12:3). Even the beauty of seeing God's creation grows dim as one ages. Ecclesiastes 12:2-5 describes old age by a series of images taken from a weather-beaten house. See SPECIAL TOPIC: HUMAN AGING

Although I think a cryptic description of the advance of old age best fits the imagery of Eccl. 12:2-5, there have been other views (cf. Robert Gordis, Koheleth, The Man and His World, A Study of Ecclesiastes, p. 341):

  1. each phrase refers to a different organ of the body
  2. they refer to a storm
  3. they refer to the gradual decay of an estate
  4. each phrase must be taken separately, some literally, some figuratively

▣ "the sun and the the lights, the moon and the stars" This list denotes the "lights" in the sky. It is surprising that "the light" is mentioned alongside "the sun" (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 326, #2c). This may be an allusion to Gen. 1:3-8 vs. Gen. 1:14-19. There was "Light" before the sun!

However, it is possible to see "light" as imagery of a vigorous, young life (Jewish Study Bible, p. 1621).

▣ "and clouds return after the rain" This implies that there is never a clear day, never a sunlit morning. It is always gray and gloomy (i.e., poor eyesight).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:3 "watchman. . .tremble"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:3 "watchman. . .tremble" This refers to the body's arms shaking (from age or fear).

▣ "mighty men stoop" This refers to the muscles of the back and legs.

▣ "grinding ones are few" This refers to the loss of teeth. Arabaic root means "molar teeth."

▣ "windows grow dim" This refers to the eyes, as does Eccl. 12;2. It is surprising they are mentioned twice, separated by other imagery.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:4 "doors on the street shut"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:4 "doors on the street shut" All of verse 4 refers to the lack of hearing.

There seems to be several normal sounds enumerated.

  1. the grinding mill
  2. birds singing
  3. songs in the streets (i.e., normal daily or festival tunes, cf. 2 Sam. 19:36)

▣ "sounding of grinding mill is low" This refers to the ears.

  1. one chewing food (cf. v. 3)
  2. living near a neighborhood grinding mill, usually done by women

▣ "one will arise at the sound of" The reference here is to sleeplessness.

▣ "daughters of song will sing softly" This may be

  1. another reference to bad hearing
  2. a parallel to the aphrodisiac of Eccl. 12:5d (i.e., sexual interest)
  3. notes to a song (NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p 780, #4), possibly sung by women working at a local grinding mill

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:5 "afraid of high places
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:5 "afraid of high places This may refer to standing or a fear of falling.

▣ "terror on the road" This refers to the difficulty of walking.

▣ "almond tree blossoms" Here this refers to white (i.e., gray) hair. The blossoms of the almond tree are white (cf. UBS, Helps for Translators, "Fauna and Flora of the Bible," p. 89).

▣ "grasshopper. . .drags himself" This refers to

  1. the elderly walking bent over
  2. the elderly being overweight (LXX and UBS4, Fauna and Flora of the Bible, p. 54)
  3. full of years
  4. impotence (Talmud, NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 221)
  5. lack of sexual desire (NIDOTTE, vol. 3, p. 221)

▣ "caperberry is ineffective" Normal sexual desire is gone. Caperberries (BDB 2, cf. NASB, NJB, JPSOA, REB) were used to stimulate one's appetite and sexual desire (UBS4 Fauna and Flora of the Bible, p. 102). Some scholars translate (BDB 2, KB 3) as "desire" (i.e., NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NIV).

The JPSOA translation suggests an emendation, "And the caper bush may bud again." This is based on the observation that caper bushes look dead most of the year but sprout out again. However, this is not true of humankind.

▣ "eternal home" The term "eternal" (BDB 761) translates the Hebrew word 'olam. See SPECIAL TOPIC: FOREVER ('olam). The reference is to Sheol (cf. Job 17:13; 30:23).  See SPECIAL TOPIC: SHEOL, I. B.

The old man thinks that the hired funeral mourners (i.e., BDB 704, KB 763, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) are

  1. waiting (BDB 685, KB 738, Qal PERFECT) outside for him to die
  2. in a processional around the bier (NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 46)

Some scholars have asserted that "eternal home" must refer to heaven and the promise of an afterlife. The OT is mostly silent on the afterlife. One wonders how much of the OT was available to the author of Ecclesiastes. Some, for sure! It all depends on the date of the book and the possible OT references to an afterlife.

  1. Job 14:14-15
  2. Job 19:25-26
  3. Ps. 16:9-11 (Messianic)
  4. Ps. 49:15
  5. Ps. 73:24
  6. Isa. 26:19
  7. Dan. 12:2 (clear text)

The Pharisees believed in a bodily resurrection and a future life, much like this one (see SPECIAL TOPIC: PHARISEES). Thank God for "progressive revelation" and the New Testament!

SPECIAL TOPIC: RESURRECTION

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:6
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:6 The NASB asserts that the IMPERATIVE from Eccl. 12:1 is assumed and that God ("Him") is the OBJECT.

The first VERB (BDB 934, KB 1221, Niphal IMPERFECT) basically means "be removed" (only here in the OT). The Septuagint (LXX), Peshitta, and Vulgate have "broken" or "snapped." The Niphal stem denotes no agency in the action. The UBS Text Project, p. 595, gives "is not snapped/not bound" a "C" rating, meaning the translation committee could not decide. The MT has "has not been removed," but the Qere version is "is not snapped."

Notice how all the VERBS of Eccl. 12:6 imply a destruction (i.e., death, cf. Eccl. 12:7):

  1. silver cord is broken, BDB 934, KB 1221, Niphal IMPERFECT
  2. golden bowl is crushed, BDB 954, KB 1285, Qal IMPERFECT
  3. pitcher is shattered, BDB 990, KB 1402, Niphal IMPERFECT
  4. wheel is crushed, BDB 954, KB 1285, Niphal PERFECT (in the ancient language of Carthage this root meant "jar," which fits the parallelism better)

Do all of these VERBS refer to

  1. one event of destruction, one mechanism for obtaining water (Ibn Ezra)
  2. two events of destruction, one for light and one for water
  3. Most modern translations assume two events.

▣ "silver cord. . .golden bowl" This speaks of the value and, yet, the frailty of human life.

▣ "pitcher. . .wheel" These images are from household items or daily chores.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:7
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:7 In light of Qoheleth's questioning of all things, this is a strong affirmation of an afterlife with God.

▣ "the dust will return to the earth" Humans were made from dust (e.g., Eccl. 3:20; Gen. 2:7; 3:19; Job 4:19; 8:19; 10:9; 34:15; Ps. 90:3; 103:14; 104:29; 146:4). We are temporary, fragile creatures!

▣ "the spirit will return to God who gave it" The Hebrew term (BDB 924) can mean "spirit," "wind" (cf. Eccl. 11:5), or "the breath" (cf. Eccl. 3:2 1; Gen. 2:7; Num. 16:22; 27:16; Isa. 57:16; Zech. 12:1). This refers to Gen. 2:7. Qoheleth knew the Torah but does not quote it or even allude to it often. This is a book of "natural revelation."

The return of the "spirit" or "breath" is imagery for death. The only source of life is "the ever living, only living God," YHWH (see SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY, D.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: BREATH, WIND SPIRIT

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:8
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:8 This looks like a concluding summary statement, matching Eccl. 1:2. One wonders how many conclusions were originally a part of Ecclesiastes and how many were added later.

Before I try to answer this question, let me affirm that this is a hermeneutical question, not an inspiration question. When dealing with OT texts as they now stand (A.D. 900s, for the Masoretic Text), we are dealing with edited texts. The date and number of edits is uncertain. It is a faith presupposition that the Bible as it now exists is inspired. The exact mechanism of this inspiration is unknown. The Spirit was active in the original authors and also in the later editors or compilers of the OT. To add to this uncertainty is the issue of textual problems. The text we have now was not the original text.

  1. the different versions of the Septuagint
  2. the different versions of the Hebrew Bible in the first century
  3. the different versions of the Hebrew Bible found in the Dead Sea Scrolls
  4. the suggested emendations of the Masoretic scholars (marginal notes to MT, Qere)

Even though we do not have the exact words of the original authors, we believe the Spirit was active in preserving the essential truths!

Therefore, to ask how many conclusions are there to Ecclesiastes is not an attack on inspiration, but an attempt to deal with what looks like two, three, or four conclusions:

  1. Eccl. 12:8 (Qoheleth's conclusion matching Eccl. 1:2)
  2. Eccl. 12:9-10 (a positive postscript)
  3. Eccl. 12:11-12 (a negative postscript)
  4. Eccl. 12:13-14 (a traditional postscript)

The Jewish Study Bible has two divisions: Eccl. 12:9-11; Eccl. 12:12-14 (p. 1621).

The UBS Handbook For Translators assumes that Eccl. 1:1 and 12:9-14 were later editions (p. 434), combined with two postscripts, Eccl. 9-11, 12-14.

These last verses are an editorial on Qoheleth. He is referred to in the third person (i.e., describes his activities), which never occurs in the rest of the book, except the very beginning (Eccl. 1:1) and the very end (Eccl. 12:9-14).

SPECIAL TOPIC: INSPIRATION

SPECIAL TOPIC: TEXTUAL CRITICISM

NASB, NKJV, LXX  "the Preacher"
NRSV  "the teacher"
TEV  "the Philosopher"
NJB  "Qoheleth"

The term (see introduction) is used only here with the DEFINITE ARTICLE, which implies a title, not a name.  See full note at Eccl. 1:1.

▣ "vanity of vanities" This book is characterized by two phrases. This is one of them (see full note at Eccl. 1:2). The second is "under the sun" (see full note at Eccl. 1:3). The author is using satire, irony, and tongue-in-cheek statements as a way to force fallen humanity to come to grips with the fleeting frailty, purposelessness, and hopelessness of life without God.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:9-10
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:9-10 Notice the activities of a sage:

  1. "taught the people knowledge," Eccl. 12:9, BDB 540, KB 531, Piel PERFECT
  2. "pondered," Eccl. 12:9, BDB 24 II, KB 27, Piel PERFECT, only here in the OT (same root common as "to give ear to")
  3. "searched out," Eccl. 12:9, BDB 350, KB 347, Piel PERFECT, only here in OT
  4. "arranged," Eccl. 12:9, BDB 1075, KB 1784, Piel PERFECT, the word's basic meaning is "to be straight" (cf. Eccl. 1:15; 7:13). Piel stem only here. This activity is part of the editing/compiling process, which took place over many years.
  5. "sought to find delightful words," Eccl. 12:10, BDB 134, KB 152, Piel PERFECT, BDB 592, KB 619, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT. This refers to powerful literary impact
  6. "to write words of truth correctly," Eccl. 12:10, BDB 507, KB 503, Qal PASSIVE PARTICIPLE, these men had a sense of God's presence and power, using them to communicate His will to others. Qoheleth did not see himself as a rebel against the truth, but against some wisdom concepts.

This is similar to a description of a scribe's work in Ezra 7:10 (study, practice, teach).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:9
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:9 The UBS, Handbook For Translators makes an interesting observation about the initial word of Eccl. 12:9 and 12 (BDB 452, KB 452), translated several ways in Ecclesiastes:

  1. "extremely" (i.e., excess), Eccl. 2:15; 7:16
  2. "advantage," Eccl. 6:8,11; 7:11
  3. "anything" (untranslated by NASV)
  4. "in addition," Eccl. 12:9

BDB 452 gives the basic meaning as "superiority," "advantage," or "excess." The theologically interesting aspect is that a closely related term (BDB 452) is used in Qoheleth's introductory question, "What advantage does man have in all his work?" (i.e. Eccl. 1:3). This key term is repeated several times (cf. Eccl. 1:3; 2:11,13; 3:9; 5:8,13; 10:10,11). It denotes the futility of any lasting advantage in human performance or human knowledge apart from God (i.e., "under the sun," cf. Eccl. 1:3).

It is surely possibly that this key term (and its derivatives) begin and close the book. There is no lasting benefit or hope apart from God and His word!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:11
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:11 There is a reverse parallelism (chiasm, see SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW POETRY, III):

  1. the words of wise men
    the masters of these collections
  2. like goads (BDB 201)
    like well-driven nails (BDB 702)

As #1 above refers to the same group (there is some variety possible):

  1. "the words of scholars," NKJV
  2. "collected sayings," NRSV
  3. "they guide the assembled people," REB
  4. "their collected sayings," NIV
  5. "these wise words left us by many masters," Knox)

So, #2 above refers to the same thing (i.e., an animal prod, a long staff with a metal point firmly attached).

Wisdom Literature was to be a guide and discipline from God (i.e., "One Shepherd," cf. NAB, NKJV, TEV, NIV) to challenge and encourage humans in this life and point them to the next.

▣ "goads" This form is found only here. These long, pointed (from the same root, "to sharpen," cf. 1 Sam. 13:21) sticks (BDB 201) were used to prod animals into activity. These truths should motivate humans into godly action.

▣ "given" This VERB (BDB 678, KB 733) is a Niphal PERFECT. This VERB is often used in Ecclesiastes to refer to God's activity (cf. Eccl. 1:13; 2:26; 3:10; 5:18,19; 6:2; 8:15; 9:9; 12:7,11).

▣ "by one Shepherd" This title (both royal and divine) was often used of God (cf. Gen. 48:15; 49:24; Ps. 23:1; 80:1; 95:7; Isa. 40:11; Jer. 31:10; Ezek. 34:11). This verse emphasizes the fact that God inspires these truths (i.e., recognition of inspiration and later canonicity).

Jewish tradition identifies "the one shepherd" with Moses (i.e., Targums, Rashi). However, Moses is never called shepherd, but he does carry the "rod of God" (shepherd's staff). But remember, this book does not use special revelation (Scriptures) but natural revelation (observation). Elohim is referred to often and fits "Shepherd" (capitalized in NASB).

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:12 "my son"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:12 "my son" In Israel's Wisdom Tradition the teacher was called "father" and his male students "sons" (i.e., Prov. 1:8; 4:1).

▣ "be warned" This VERB (BDB 264, KB 265) is a Niphal IMPERATIVE found in Wisdom Literature only three times (once in Ps. 19:11 and twice in Eccl. 4:13; 12:12). This at first seems to contradict the author's plea to search for wisdom, but apparently as Eccl. 12:11 asserts God's authorship of some literature (i.e., canonical texts), Eccl. 12:12 must refer to other non-canonical wisdom literature. It is similar to Eccl. 1:18.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HEBREW CANON

SPECIAL TOPIC: WISDOM LITERATURE

NASB  "excessive devotion"
NKJV, NRSV, TEV, NJB, JPSOA, NIV, REB, LXX, Peshitta  "much study"

The VERBAL "excessive" (BDB 915 I, KB 1176, Hiphil INFINITIVE ABSOLUTE) is used twice in this verse:

  1. making of many books
  2. excessive devotion

The NOUN (BDB 529, KB 1176; NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 760) is found only here in the OT. In Arabic it means "to be devoted," "to be attached," or "to apply oneself assiduously to something."

It is uncertain whether (1) the writing; (2) the compiling; or (3) the study of books is the focus of the warning. The problem is that human wisdom is helpful, but not ultimate!

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:13 "The conclusion"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:13 "The conclusion" This term (BDB 692, KB 747) means "end" (cf. Eccl. 3:11; 7:2; 12:13), used in the sense of "summary," "conclusion," or "result of investigation."

▣ "fear God" This is the first of two Qal IMPERATIVES (BDB 431, KB 432). This admonition is a repeated theme (cf. Eccl. 3:14; 5:7; 7:18; 8:12-13; Job 1:1; 28:28; Prov. 1:7; 9:10; 15:33). Respect Him and recognize His presence, power, and provision (hidden though it may be) in our daily lives.

Fear of God is the beginning of true wisdom (cf. Job 28:28; Ps. 111:10; Prov. 1:7; 9:10; Eccl. 12:13).

SPECIAL TOPIC: FEAR (OT)

▣ "keep His commandments" This is the second Qal IMPERATIVE (BDB 1036, KB 1581, cf. Eccl. 8:5). The terms "fear" and "commandments" appear together in Ps. 112:1, which describes a "blessed" person. Like the book of James in the NT, this book asserts the need for faith in action!

SPECIAL TOPIC: KEEP

SPECIAL TOPIC: WAYS OF REVELATION, II. E.

▣ "this applies to every person" No one is excluded from the demand for respect and obedience to God.

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 12:14 "Because God will bring every act to judgment"
entries.author: Dr. Bob Utley
entries.content:
12:14 "Because God will bring every act to judgment" God is going to set things straight, if not in this life, then in the next (cf. Eccl. 3:17; 11:9; Gal. 6:7-9).

SPECIAL TOPIC: JUDGMENT IN THE NT

▣ "everything which is hidden" The VERB "hidden" (BDB 761 I, KB 834, Niphal PARTICIPLE) refers to intentional and unintentional sins (cf. Ps. 19:12; 90:8; 139:23-24). Fallen humans will give an account to God for the stewardship of the gift of life (cf. Matt. 10:26; 25:31-46; Rom. 2:16; 14:10-12; 1 Cor. 4:5; Rev. 20:11-15).

SPECIAL TOPIC: UNINTENTIONAL SINS

▣ "whether it is good or evil" Everyone will give an account of his actions (cf. 1 Cor. 3:10-15; 2 Cor. 5: 10).

DISCUSSION QUESTIONS

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

These discussion questions are provided to help you think through the major issues of this section of the book. They are meant to be thought-provoking, not definitive.

  1. Why is this book seemingly so self-contradictory?
  2. What is the purpose of Ecclesiastes in the Canon?
  3. What is the final word from the author?
  4. Why is this book so relevant today?
